0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was arrogant about it; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther set the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae), and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Corinth in the 50s AD was a boom town. Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, it was refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves, and grew rich on trade between its two harbours on either side of the isthmus. It hosted the Isthmian Games and was full of people climbing the social ladder: one inscription found there records that a man called Erastus paved a street at his own expense in return for public office, perhaps the same Erastus, “the city treasurer”, who sent greetings in Romans 16:23. Status, eloquence, wisdom and success were prized. Paul spent eighteen months planting the church there (Acts 18), and a few years later, from Ephesus, he wrote this letter after hearing of serious problems.

The first problem is division. Church members were lining up behind favourite teachers (Paul, Apollos, Peter, even “Christ”) as though they were rival schools of philosophy. Paul’s answer goes to the root: the gospel itself overturns human ideas of wisdom and status. Its message is a crucified Messiah, which sounded like nonsense to Greeks and like an outrage to Jews, yet it is God’s power and wisdom. God deliberately chose ordinary, unimpressive people, so that no one could boast except in the Lord, who has given us Christ as our wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, writing with a colleague called Sosthenes, introduces himself as an apostle by God’s calling. He addresses the church in Corinth as God’s own people, made holy in Christ and called to be saints, together with believers everywhere who call on the name of Jesus, the Lord of all, and wishes them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul’s self-designation as an apostle “by the will of God” is not modesty but theology. The divine will is the only ground of any apostolic or ministerial commission. This will become crucial in the letter: when the Corinthians reject Paul’s apostleship, they are not rejecting a self-appointed teacher but the will of the God who sent him. The same logic applies to their own calling: they are saints not because they volunteered but because they were called (v. 2). The sovereignty of grace is the foundation of every sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s apostolic authority was contested at Corinth by those who preferred Apollos’s rhetorical polish or Cephas’s Petrine prestige. His opening — “called by the will of God” — quietly answers the challenge before it is raised. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still the same: divine calling, not human talent. The pastor who grounds his authority in his own gifts is standing on sand; the one who grounds it in the call of God can stand when the culture turns against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians is Paul’s letter to a gifted but troubled church. Chapter 1 does two things. First, Paul greets and thanks God for them: they are a church of God, sanctified in Christ, enriched with every gift, and God will keep them to the end (vv. 1–9). Then he takes up the first problem: the church is splitting into fan clubs around favourite leaders, Paul, Apollos, Peter, even Christ (vv. 10–17). His answer goes to the root. The Corinthians were impressed by worldly wisdom and polished speech, but the gospel is the message of the cross, which the world thinks foolish and weak, and which is in fact the power and wisdom of God (vv. 18–25). God proved this by whom he chose: not many wise, powerful or noble, but the foolish and weak and despised, so that no one can boast before him (vv. 26–29). Everything the believer has, wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption, is found in Christ, so let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (vv. 30–31). Divisions are cured not by better leaders but by a fresh look at the cross.

Setting and background. Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church on his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–18; 1 Corinthians 16:8). He had stayed eighteen months. Since then he had written an earlier letter (5:9), heard reports from Chloe’s people (1:11), and received a letter from the church with questions (7:1). 1 Corinthians answers both the reports and the questions: divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection.

Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Called” (klētos): Paul did not choose the job; God called him (Galatians 1:15). “Apostle” (apostolos, one sent with authority): an authorised messenger of Christ, a witness of the risen Lord (9:1; 15:8). In a church where some questioned his authority (4:3; 9:3), Paul begins with the basis of it: the will of God, not his own ambition.

And our brother Sosthenes. Key words. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth (Acts 18:17). If so, the man who once led opposition is now a brother, and is with Paul as he writes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean apostles still exist today in Paul’s sense. The apostles of Christ, eyewitnesses of the risen Lord, laid the foundation of the church once (Ephesians 2:20). Their authority continues in their writings, the New Testament.

In a sentence. Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,

On a Tuesday. Whatever place you hold in your church or work, see it as God’s calling, not your achievement. That keeps you humble and steady.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Setting and background. Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, with ports on two seas. It had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. It was proud, competitive, status-conscious and famous for its immorality; to corinthianise had become a Greek word for sexual vice. It hosted the Isthmian Games and many temples.

To the church of God that is in Corinth. Key words. Church (ekklēsia, assembly, those called out). It is the church of God, not of Paul or Apollos or any faction. It belongs to him.

To those sanctified in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Sanctified” (hagiazō, set apart as holy) is a perfect tense: they have been made holy, once for all, by union with Christ (6:11). This is definitive sanctification: God has set them apart as his own. Remarkable, given how unholy they were behaving.

Called to be saints. Key words. Saints (hagioi, holy ones) is what all believers are, not a special class. Called: effectively summoned by God. Their calling is to live up to what they already are.

Together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours. Key words. The Corinthians were not the only church, and not independent of the rest. To call on the name of the Lord is the Old Testament language for worshipping the LORD (Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13). To call on Jesus is to worship him as God.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Paul’s standard greeting, joining the Greek greeting (grace) and the Hebrew (shalom, peace), and filling both with gospel meaning. Grace from the Father and the Son together: Jesus is placed alongside the Father as the source of divine blessing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians were already perfect in conduct. They were saints in Christ who were behaving badly. Paul addresses them first by what God has made them, then corrects them.

In a sentence. To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be his holy people, together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you are a saint, set apart for God. Thank him, and ask him to make your life match your name.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus of Greece, with two ports and a mixed, mobile population. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God constantly for the grace given to the Corinthians in Christ. They have been enriched in every way, especially in their speech and knowledge, because the message about Christ took firm root among them, and so they lack no spiritual gift as they wait for Christ to be revealed. Christ will keep them firm to the end, so that they will be blameless on his day. God is faithful, and it was he who called them into fellowship with his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 — “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” — is one of the great perseverance texts in Paul. The guarantee of the Corinthians’ ultimate confirmation (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling is God’s act; the fellowship is God’s gift; the sustaining is God’s work. Reformed theology has always grounded the doctrine of perseverance here: the saints persevere not because they are strong but because the God who called them is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing before God and their superiority over others by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving subtly reorients them: the gifts are something you “were enriched in” — given, not earned. Now: The same pride attaches to spiritual accomplishment in every generation — the sense that one’s theological sophistication or spiritual experience gives one a higher standing. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—

I give thanks to my God always for you. Key words. Even for this troubled church, Paul gives thanks. He sees God’s work in them before he deals with their sin.

Because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus. Key words. The cause of thanksgiving is not their goodness but God’s grace.

That in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge. Key words. The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge, the very gifts they were later misusing (8:1; 13:1–2; 14). “Speech” (logos) and “knowledge” (gnōsis). Paul thanks God for them, because they were real gifts. The problem was not the gifts but pride in them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is flattering them. He means it; and later he will show that gifts without love are nothing (13:1–3).

In a sentence. Paul always thanks his God for you because of his grace given you in Christ Jesus. For in him you have been enriched in every way, with all kinds of speech and with all knowledge,

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise your church, thank God for what he has given it. It changes how you speak.
verseByVerse.note: The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge — the very gifts later misused.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you—so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,

Even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you. Key words. The testimony (martyrion) about Christ is the gospel Paul preached. Confirmed (bebaioō, made firm, established): it took root and was shown true in their lives, including through spiritual gifts.

So that you are not lacking in any gift. Key words. “Gift” (charisma): spiritual gifts, which chapters 12–14 discuss at length. They had everything they needed.

As you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Revealing” (apokalypsis, unveiling): Christ’s return, when he will be seen in glory. The gifts are for the time of waiting. Some Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived (4:8); Paul reminds them they are still waiting (13:8–12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every individual had every gift (12:29–30). The church as a whole lacked nothing.

In a sentence. God thus confirming our testimony about Christ among you. Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly wait for our Lord Jesus Christ to be revealed.

For worship. Thank God that he gives his church what it needs to wait well for Christ. Pray for his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who will sustain you to the end. Key words. “Who” refers to God (or Christ). “Sustain” (bebaioō, the same word as in v. 6: confirm, establish, keep firm). As God confirmed the gospel among them, he will confirm them to the end. “To the end”: to the last day.

Guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Guiltless” (anenklētos, unaccused, blameless, no charge can be brought). The day of the Lord: the day of judgement and Christ’s return. On that day, believers will stand without accusation, because Christ’s righteousness is theirs (Romans 8:33–34; Colossians 1:22).

Where Christians differ: perseverance. Some teach that true believers may fall away and be finally lost. Verdict: Paul says God will sustain them to the end. If it were up to the Corinthians, with all their failings, they would not stand. But God keeps his people. True believers may fall into serious sin, as the Corinthians did, and must be corrected; but God will not let them go (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; Westminster 17.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean sin does not matter. The rest of the letter calls them to repent. God keeps them partly by such warnings.

In a sentence. He will also keep you firm to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Your assurance rests not on your strength but on God’s keeping. When you fail, run back to him; he is holding you.

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

God is faithful. Key words. The reason for the confidence of verse 8. “Faithful” (pistos): reliable, true to his word. A key phrase in this letter (10:13).

By whom you were called. Key words. God called them, effectively, into union with Christ. What God begins, he finishes.

Into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. Key words. “Fellowship” (koinōnia, sharing, partnership, common life). They have been called into a shared life with Christ: union with him, sharing in all he is and has. And since every believer shares in Christ, they share in one another. This is the answer to their divisions (v. 10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean fellowship is just friendly activity. It is first participation in Christ, from which friendship with one another flows.

In a sentence. God is faithful, who has called you into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

For worship. God is faithful. Rest your weight on that today.

parallels.desc: the faithful God

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul appeals to them, in Christ’s name, to agree with one another and end their divisions. Members of Chloe’s household have told him about quarrels: each person has a favourite, Paul, Apollos, Peter or Christ. Is Christ split into pieces? Was Paul crucified for them, or were they baptised into Paul’s name? He is glad he personally baptised only a handful of them, so no one can claim to be his disciple. Christ sent him not mainly to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with clever rhetoric, which would empty the cross of its power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions are a cautionary tale about what happens when human personality becomes the centre of Christian community. This text is a permanent warning: the church that rallies around a preacher’s gifts, style, or personality rather than around the crucified Christ has already drifted from the gospel. The preacher is, at most, a herald — the one who announces a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal to preach with “eloquent wisdom” is not anti-intellectualism; it is a deliberate choice to let the gospel speak in its own register, with its own power, rather than dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and sophistry: you attached yourself to the most impressive teacher, displayed his influence on your life, and measured your social standing by his. The Corinthian factions are simply the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity pastor culture is the contemporary version. The church that streams a famous preacher rather than investing in local pastors, or that divides over which theological tradition’s champion to follow, is still choosing Apollos over Christ — a more impressive package over the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.

I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Appeal” (parakaleō, urge, plead). By the name of Christ: by his authority, the one name they all share. Notice Christ has been named ten times in the first ten verses.

That all of you agree. Key words. Literally, that you all say the same thing: speak with one voice, rather than shouting rival slogans (v. 12).

And that there be no divisions among you. Key words. “Divisions” (schismata, tears, splits, from which we get schism). The word was used of a tear in a garment (Mark 2:21). The church had not yet split into separate congregations, but there were cliques and rivalries.

But that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. Key words. “United” (katartizō, mended, restored, put in order, as of mending nets, Mark 1:19). Paul wants the torn garment mended. Same mind (nous, way of thinking) and same judgement (gnōmē, opinion, purpose).

For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you. Key words. Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business, perhaps slaves or employees travelling between Corinth and Ephesus. Paul names his source openly, not secret gossip. “Quarrelling” (erides, strife, rivalry).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must agree on every opinion (Romans 14). It means unity in the gospel, in mind and purpose, without factions.

In a sentence. Paul appeals to you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree with one another in what you say and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly united in mind and thought. Some from Chloe’s household have informed him that there are quarrels among you.

On a Tuesday. If you have a complaint about someone in your church, speak openly and to the right person, not in whispers. And work for mending, not tearing.
verseByVerse.note: Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business who had travelled to Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul.” Key words. Literally, I am of Paul: I belong to Paul. Some were proud to follow the church’s founder.

Or “I follow Apollos.” Key words. Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. He was an eloquent Jew from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24–28). Some preferred his polished style.

Or “I follow Cephas.” Key words. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name. Some, perhaps Jewish believers, claimed the leading apostle of the Twelve.

Or “I follow Christ.” Key words. Perhaps the most dangerous party: those who claimed Christ for themselves, as if they were more spiritual than everyone else, and needed no human teachers.

Is Christ divided? Key words. Has Christ been split up and shared out among factions? The church is his body; to divide it is to tear him.

Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? Key words. Absurd questions with obvious answers. Only Christ died for them; they were baptised into his name, meaning into his ownership. Paul refuses to be the head of a party.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should have no preferences among teachers, or that denominations are always sinful. It means no human leader may take Christ’s place, and no preference may divide the church.

In a sentence. What he means is this: one of you says, “I follow Paul”; another, “I follow Apollos”; another, “I follow Cephas”; still another, “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in the name of Paul?

For worship. Thank God for the preachers and authors who have helped you. Then remember: none of them died for you. Only Christ did.
verseByVerse.note: Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)

I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius. Key words. Crispus was the synagogue ruler who believed with his household (Acts 18:8). Gaius later hosted the whole church (Romans 16:23). Paul baptised only a few, probably leaving most baptisms to others.

So that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. Key words. Paul is glad, given the factions, that no one can claim a special bond with him through baptism.

I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Key words. Stephanas and his household were the firstfruits of Achaia, and devoted themselves to serving the saints (16:15–17). Paul corrects himself honestly as he dictates.

Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else. Key words. An honest admission of a gap in memory. Inspiration does not mean Paul had a perfect memory of every detail; it means what he wrote is true, including his statement that he does not remember.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Some argue from household baptisms (here, and Acts 16:15, 33) that infants of believers should be baptised. Verdict: The New Testament never mentions an infant in any household baptism. The household of Stephanas is described as devoting themselves to serving the saints (16:15), which suggests believers old enough to serve. Baptism in the New Testament follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12). So the app holds believer’s baptism, while warmly recognising paedobaptist brothers and sisters as faithful Christians who read the covenant differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19). Paul simply refuses to let it become a badge of loyalty to him.

In a sentence. Paul is thankful that he did not baptise any of you except Crispus and Gaius, so no one can say that you were baptised in his name. (Yes, he also baptised the household of Stephanas; beyond that, he does not remember if he baptised anyone else.)

On a Tuesday. Do not tie your faith to a particular minister. Your baptism joined you to Christ, not to a person.

parallels.desc: Crispus
Gaius
Stephanas

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel. Key words. A Hebrew way of stressing priority: not this but that, meaning that first. Paul’s main commission (Acts 26:16–18) was preaching (euangelizō, to announce good news). Baptism followed, and others could do it.

And not with words of eloquent wisdom. Key words. Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators (sophists) were celebrities, paid for their performances and judged by their style. The Corinthians wanted their preachers to be impressive. “Eloquent wisdom” is literally wisdom of word: clever rhetoric and human philosophy.

Lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. Key words. “Emptied” (kenoō, made void). If the preacher dazzles with style, people believe because of the performance, and the cross’s own power is hidden. The power is in the message of the crucified Christ, not in the messenger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should be careless or dull, or that learning and clear speech are bad. Paul himself argued and reasoned (Acts 17:2; 19:8). It means preachers must not rely on technique or try to make the gospel attractive by hiding its offence.

In a sentence. For Christ did not send Paul to baptise, but to preach the gospel, and not with wisdom and eloquence, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, do not worry about being impressive. Speak simply about Christ crucified. The power is in the message.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators were admired like celebrities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Scripture foretold that God would confound the wisdom of the wise. Where are the sages, the scholars and the debaters now? God has made the world’s wisdom look foolish. Since the world in its wisdom did not come to know God, God was pleased to save believers through the apparent foolishness of preaching. Jews want miraculous signs and Greeks want wisdom, but Paul preaches a crucified Messiah, an offence to Jews and nonsense to Gentiles, yet to those God calls, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom. God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and his weakness stronger than human strength.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross (Theologia Crucis)

Luther’s distinction between the theology of the cross and the theology of glory is nowhere more clearly grounded than in 1:18–25. The theologian of glory sees God in power, success, and wisdom that makes sense on human terms. The theologian of the cross sees God revealed precisely in weakness, foolishness, and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross is not the means to something better; it is the place where God is most fully known. The cross was never Plan B after the fall. It was the plan from eternity — the place where the justice and the love of God were both satisfied at the same moment, in the same event, in the same Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul wrote into a culture where crucifixion was the ultimate symbol of shame, defeat, and criminal status. To preach a crucified Messiah was not merely theologically offensive but socially disqualifying. The early Christians were not brave about something trivial; they were staking their social standing and their lives on an executed criminal. Now: The pressure to make the gospel more palatable — to lead with Jesus-as-life-coach rather than Jesus-as-sin-bearer, to emphasise personal fulfilment rather than atonement — is the contemporary version of Paul’s Corinthian problem. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age. The answer is still to preach it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”

For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing. Key words. The word (logos) of the cross: the message that God saves through a crucified man. To those who are perishing it is folly (mōria, from which we get moron): absurd, idiotic. Perishing (apollymenoi) is a present participle: they are on the way to destruction.

But to us who are being saved it is the power of God. Key words. “Being saved” is also present: salvation is begun and continuing, to be completed at Christ’s return. The cross is not merely a message about power; it is God’s power at work, saving people (Romans 1:16). The same message divides humanity into two groups.

For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.” Key words. From Isaiah 29:14. In Isaiah, the wise men of Judah relied on their clever political plans instead of on God. God promised to bring their wisdom to nothing. The same happens with human wisdom that rejects the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is irrational or that Christians should despise thinking. It means human wisdom, as a way to know and reach God, fails. Only God’s revelation can save.

In a sentence. For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.”

For worship. If the cross is precious to you and not foolish, that is because God has saved you. Praise him for opening your eyes.

parallels.desc: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.

Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Key words. Echoes of Isaiah 19:12 and 33:18. The wise man: the Greek philosopher. The scribe: the Jewish expert in the law. The debater (syzētētēs): the clever arguer of either kind. Where are they? Their wisdom could not save.

Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? Key words. By the cross, God showed that all human wisdom was foolish in the matter of knowing him.

For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom. Key words. In God’s wise plan, he arranged things so that the world, with all its philosophy and religion, could not find him by its own wisdom (Romans 1:21–22). This was deliberate, so that salvation would be by grace.

It pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe. Key words. “What we preach” (kērygma): the content of the message, not just the act of preaching. God chose a message that seems foolish, and a means, preaching, that seems weak, to save those who believe. Not those who are clever, but those who believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean general revelation is worthless. Creation shows God’s power and divine nature (Romans 1:20). But it cannot bring saving knowledge; only the gospel can.

In a sentence. Where is the wise person? Where is the teacher of the law? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to be clever to be saved, only to believe. And you do not need to be clever to share it.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

For Jews demand signs. Key words. Many Jews wanted miraculous proofs of power before they would believe, like the Exodus wonders (Matthew 12:38; John 6:30). They expected a powerful Messiah who would defeat Rome.

And Greeks seek wisdom. Key words. Greeks wanted a philosophy that satisfied the mind and was elegantly argued.

But we preach Christ crucified. Key words. Paul gives neither. He preaches a crucified Messiah. “Crucified” is a perfect participle: the one who was crucified and remains the crucified one. The cross is the heart of the message, not an embarrassing detail.

A stumbling block to Jews. Key words. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels. For Jews, it also meant being under God’s curse, for anyone hanged on a tree is cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). A crucified Messiah seemed a contradiction. “Stumbling block” (skandalon, scandal).

And folly to Gentiles. Key words. To Greeks and Romans, worshipping a crucified Jew was madness. The earliest picture of the crucifixion is a mocking graffito from Rome showing a man worshipping a crucified donkey.

But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks. Key words. The called: those effectively summoned by God, not just invited. The same message is heard by many; to the called, it is life.

Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Key words. The Jews wanted power; the Greeks wanted wisdom. In Christ crucified, both find what they were really looking for: the true power of God that saves, and the true wisdom of God that plans salvation.

Where Christians differ: the general call and the effectual call. Some think that God’s call is only an invitation, which people accept or reject by their own power. Verdict: The gospel is offered to all who hear it, and all are commanded to believe (the general call). But Paul here speaks of those who are called as distinct from the rest who hear and stumble. This is the effectual call, God’s inward work by the Spirit that makes the gospel powerful in the elect, so that they come freely (Romans 8:30; Westminster 10.1). The difference between those who believe and those who mock is God’s calling, not human cleverness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean signs and arguments are always bad. Jesus did signs, and Paul reasoned. It means that the cross must stay at the centre, and neither signs nor arguments can replace it.

In a sentence. Jews demand signs and Greeks look for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those whom God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

For worship. Look at the cross today. There is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Worship the crucified Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels; for Jews, a crucified man was under God’s curse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

For the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Key words. Paul speaks ironically. What looks like foolishness on God’s part, saving through a crucified man, is wiser than all human wisdom combined.

And the weakness of God is stronger than men. Key words. The cross looked like weakness: the Son of God helpless, mocked, dying. But by it, God defeated sin, death and Satan (Colossians 2:15). What looks weakest in God is stronger than all human power.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is actually foolish or weak. Paul is speaking from the world’s viewpoint.

In a sentence. For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength.

On a Tuesday. When God’s ways look foolish or weak in your situation, remember the cross. His weakness wins.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to look at their own church. Not many of them were clever, powerful or well-born by worldly standards. God deliberately chose what the world thinks foolish, weak, low and contemptible, even what counts for nothing, to put the proud and the important to shame, so that no human being can boast before him. It is God who has placed them in Christ Jesus, and Christ has become for them wisdom from God: their righteousness, their holiness and their redemption. So, as Scripture says, anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Doctrine of Boasting: Sola Gratia Applied

The logic of vv. 28–29 is the logic of grace pushed to its social conclusion: God chooses the things that are “not” to bring to nothing the things that “are” — “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” This is the pastoral and sociological outworking of sola gratia. If salvation were partly dependent on human wisdom, power, or birth, then at least some people could boast. But when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors, and the socially marginal, the only conceivable boast is in the grace that did what human merit could never have achieved. God’s choosing of the lowly things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness but a deliberate demolition of every ground of human pride before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social hierarchy was steep and rigid: Roman citizens over freedpersons over slaves; the educated over the illiterate; patrons over clients. The church at Corinth crossed every one of these lines — and the crossing was theological, not merely sociological. It was evidence of the same gospel that the cross proclaimed. Now: The church that unconsciously mirrors the class and status structures of its surrounding culture is denying with its sociology what it affirms with its theology. The cross creates a community where the only legitimate boast is in the Lord — which means no other boast is legitimate at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;

For consider your calling, brothers. Key words. Look at yourselves. Look at who was in the church when God called you.

Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. Key words. Literally, according to the flesh. Most were not educated, influential or high-born. Many were slaves, freedmen, workers. Note “not many,” not “not any”: there were some, like Erastus (Romans 16:23) and Crispus.

But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise. Key words. “Chose” (eklegomai): three times in verses 27–28. God’s choice was deliberate. He passed by the people the world admires and chose the people it overlooks.

God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong. Key words. “Shame” (kataischynō, put to shame, disgrace). By saving the weak, God shows that salvation has nothing to do with human strength.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never saves the wise or wealthy, or that poverty earns salvation. It means God does not choose people because of their worldly advantages.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, think of what you were when you were called. Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were influential; not many were of noble birth. But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong.

For worship. If you are not impressive by the world’s standards, rejoice: God chose you. If you are, rejoice too, but know that your advantages had nothing to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.

God chose what is low and despised in the world. Key words. “Low” (agenē, without family, of no birth). “Despised” (exouthenēmena, treated as nothing).

Even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are. Key words. Things that are not: people who count for nothing in the world’s eyes, nobodies. Things that are: the somebodies. God uses nobodies to nullify (katargeō) the somebodies, as he created the world out of nothing (Romans 4:17).

So that no human being might boast in the presence of God. Key words. The purpose of election. “No human being” (literally no flesh). If God had chosen people for their wisdom, power or birth, they could boast. By choosing nobodies, he excludes all boasting (Romans 3:27; Ephesians 2:8–9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God chose people because they were lowly. Lowliness is not merit either. God chose freely, and the lowliness of those chosen displays that freedom.

In a sentence. God chose the lowly things of this world and the despised things, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, so that no one may boast before him.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to feel superior to other Christians, remember: none of us has anything to boast of before God.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,

And because of him you are in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Because of him” is literally from him: God is the source of your being in Christ. Union with Christ is God’s work, not yours.

Who became to us wisdom from God. Key words. Christ himself is our wisdom. The Corinthians were seeking wisdom; it was standing in front of them, in Christ. Paul then explains what this wisdom consists of, in three words.

Righteousness. Key words. Christ is our right standing before God. His righteousness is counted to us: justification (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9).

And sanctification. Key words. Christ is our holiness. In him we are set apart for God (v. 2), and from him we receive the Spirit who makes us holy.

And redemption. Key words. Christ is our release, bought by the price of his blood (Ephesians 1:7). Final redemption includes the body at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

Where Christians differ: imputed righteousness. Some deny that Christ’s righteousness is counted to believers, saying instead that God makes us righteous inwardly, and accepts us on that basis. Verdict: Christ became our righteousness. Our right standing with God is not our own inner goodness but Christ’s obedience counted to us, received by faith alone (Romans 4:5–6; 5:19). Sanctification, which follows, is the inward renewal; it is distinct from justification but never separated from it. Both are found in Christ, so the one who has Christ has both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ gives us these things as separate packages to collect. He is them. Have Christ, and you have all of them.

In a sentence. It is because of God that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God, that is, our righteousness, holiness and redemption.

For worship. Christ is your wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption. You need nothing more and no one else. Rest in him.

parallels.desc: the LORD is our righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

So that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” Key words. A summary of Jeremiah 9:23–24: let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, the mighty in his might, or the rich in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows the LORD. Notice how Jeremiah’s list, wisdom, might and riches, matches verse 26. In Jeremiah, the Lord is Yahweh; Paul applies it to Christ, the Lord Jesus. Boasting itself is not wrong; the question is what we boast in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never take joy in anything else. It means our glory, confidence and pride rest in the Lord alone.

In a sentence. Therefore, as it is written: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

On a Tuesday. Notice what you boast about today: your work, your children, your church, your opinions. Turn it into boasting in the Lord.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me

Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?<sup>14</sup>I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,<sup>15</sup>so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name.<sup>16</sup>(I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)<sup>17</sup>For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.<sup>18</sup>For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.<sup>19</sup>For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”<sup>20</sup>Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?<sup>21</sup>For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.<sup>22</sup>For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom,<sup>23</sup>but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles,<sup>24</sup>but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.<sup>25</sup>For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.<sup>26</sup>For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.<sup>27</sup>But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;<sup>28</sup>God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,<sup>29</sup>so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.<sup>30</sup>And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,<sup>31</sup>so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Paul continues his answer to a church that prized clever speech and secret wisdom. He reminds them how he first came to Corinth: not as a dazzling orator, but weak, nervous and resolved to speak of nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power rather than on human brilliance. Yet the gospel is not anti-intellectual. There is a wisdom Paul speaks among the mature, but it is God’s wisdom, hidden in the past and now revealed, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

This wisdom cannot be discovered; it must be revealed, and God has revealed it by his Spirit, who knows God’s depths as a person’s own spirit knows his thoughts. The apostles have received that Spirit, and they speak in words he teaches. A person without the Spirit cannot accept these things; they seem foolish to him, because they can be understood only by the Spirit. But the person with the Spirit can discern them, and believers have the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recalls his arrival in Corinth. He did not come with impressive rhetoric or a display of cleverness to announce God’s message. He had made up his mind to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, crucified. He came in weakness, fear and great trembling, and his preaching did not rely on persuasive technique but on a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that their faith would rest not on human wisdom but on God’s power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s deliberate simplicity in proclamation is not a pastoral strategy; it is a doctrinal commitment. The power of the gospel is the power of the Spirit working through the word of the cross — not the power of the preacher, the brilliance of the argument, or the emotional manipulation of the audience. Reformed theology has always insisted on this: it is the Spirit who regenerates, convicts, and converts; the preacher is the instrument, not the cause. If people are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything the preacher can add.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth, the travelling sophist was a celebrity figure — a rhetorical virtuoso who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee, and move on. The Corinthians expected their teacher to perform at that level. Paul’s refusal to do so was not incompetence but protest: he would not compete on the sophists’ terms. Now: The contemporary equivalent is the pressure to make church services “compelling” through production values, platform charisma, and emotional manipulation. Paul’s counter-word is not to be deliberately boring, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: actually save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 2 carries on the argument against the Corinthians’ love of worldly wisdom. First, Paul reminds them how he preached when he came: not with impressive rhetoric, but with Christ crucified, in weakness, so that their faith would rest on God’s power, not human cleverness (vv. 1–5). Second, there is a true wisdom, but it is God’s wisdom, hidden and now revealed: his plan of salvation in Christ, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (vv. 6–9). Third, this wisdom is known only by the Spirit. The Spirit searches the depths of God and reveals them to his apostles, who speak them in Spirit-taught words (vv. 10–13). The natural person, without the Spirit, cannot receive these things; the spiritual person, taught by the Spirit, can, and has the mind of Christ (vv. 14–16). The chapter is one of the Bible’s key passages on revelation, inspiration and illumination.

And I, when I came to you, brothers. Key words. Paul goes back to his first visit to Corinth, about AD 50 (Acts 18:1).

Did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. Key words. “Lofty” (hyperochē, superiority, excellence). He did not come as a showman orator. Some manuscripts read “mystery of God” instead of “testimony of God”; the ESV notes this. Either way, the content is God’s message about Christ.

For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. Key words. “Decided” (krinō, judged, resolved): a deliberate choice. Not that Paul knew nothing else, or spoke of nothing else, but that everything he taught was centred on and measured by Christ crucified. The cross was not one topic among many; it was the lens for all of them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only on the crucifixion and nothing else. He taught the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), including ethics, marriage, the church and the resurrection, as this letter shows. But all of it flowed from the cross.

In a sentence. And so it was with Paul, brothers and sisters. When he came to you, he did not come with eloquence or human wisdom as he proclaimed to you the testimony about God. For he resolved to know nothing while he was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

On a Tuesday. Let Christ crucified be the centre of your faith. Measure your opinions, priorities and plans by the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.

And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling. Key words. Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens (Acts 17:32–34), after being driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, and he was alone. The Lord had to reassure him in a vision: do not be afraid, but go on speaking (Acts 18:9–10). Paul was not a confident superstar. He was weak, afraid and trembling.

And my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom. Key words. “Plausible” (peithos, persuasive): the techniques of rhetoric designed to win over an audience.

But in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. Key words. “Demonstration” (apodeixis, a proof, a technical term in rhetoric for a compelling argument). The proof of Paul’s message was not his technique but the Spirit’s power: convicting hearts, bringing new birth, perhaps accompanied by miracles (2 Corinthians 12:12; 1 Thessalonians 1:5).

So that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God. Key words. If their faith had been produced by clever speech, a cleverer speaker could undo it. Faith that rests on God’s power stands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should be nervous to be faithful, or that preparation is unspiritual. It means the effectiveness of preaching depends on the Spirit, not the preacher.

In a sentence. Paul came to you in weakness with great fear and trembling. His message and his preaching were not with wise and persuasive words, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom, but on God’s power.

For worship. If you feel weak and afraid when you speak of Christ, you are in good company. Pray for the Spirit’s power, and speak.
verseByVerse.note: Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet Paul does teach wisdom among those who are mature, though not the wisdom of this age or of its rulers, who are passing away. It is God’s secret wisdom, hidden until now, which God planned before time for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood it; if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. As Scripture says, no one has seen, heard or imagined what God has prepared for those who love him, but God has revealed it to us by his Spirit, who searches even the depths of God. Just as only a person’s own spirit knows his inner thoughts, only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. Believers have received not the world’s spirit but God’s Spirit, so that they may understand what God has freely given. The apostles speak of these things in words taught not by human wisdom but by the Spirit. The unspiritual person rejects them as foolishness and cannot understand them, because they are discerned only through the Spirit. The spiritual person can evaluate everything but is not subject to merely human judgement. Who has known the Lord’s mind to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum). Calvin’s Institutes ground the believer’s certainty about Scripture not in external proofs but in the Spirit’s own witness to the heart. Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned; the Spirit of God alone can reveal them; the Spirit has been given to those who are in Christ. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos) is not merely unwilling but unable to receive spiritual things — a direct support for the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its noetic dimension.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for Apollos’s sophisticated rhetoric over Paul’s plain proclamation was, at root, a preference for a wisdom they could evaluate by their own natural capacities. Paul’s response: the real wisdom — the wisdom that saves — cannot be evaluated that way. It requires the Spirit to receive it. Now: The recurring temptation to evaluate the gospel by academic or cultural criteria — to ask whether Christianity can hold its own in the university seminar — misses Paul’s point. The knowledge of God is not the endpoint of human inquiry; it is the gift of the Spirit to the humble heart. This is why apologetics serves evangelism but cannot replace it: ultimately, only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.

Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom. Key words. Paul is not against wisdom. There is a true wisdom. “Mature” (teleioi, complete, grown up): here, all who have the Spirit and accept the gospel, as opposed to the natural person (v. 14). Some in Corinth thought they were the mature elite; Paul redefines maturity.

Although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. Key words. The rulers of this age are the political and religious leaders who crucified Jesus (v. 8): Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas. Some also see behind them the spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12). They are being brought to nothing (katargeō), passing away with this age.

But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God. Key words. Literally, God’s wisdom in a mystery. Not a secret for an elite few, but God’s plan once hidden and now revealed (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:4–6).

Which God decreed before the ages for our glory. Key words. “Decreed” (proorizō, predestined, determined beforehand). Before time began, God planned salvation through Christ crucified. For our glory: the goal is the glorification of believers, sharing Christ’s glory (Romans 8:30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is a secret higher teaching for advanced Christians beyond the gospel, as the later Gnostics claimed. The wisdom is the gospel itself, understood more deeply.

In a sentence. We do, however, speak a message of wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. No, we declare God’s wisdom, a mystery that has been hidden and that God destined for our glory before time began.

On a Tuesday. God planned your glory before the ages. On a hard day, remember where your story is going.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

None of the rulers of this age understood this. Key words. The rulers did not grasp God’s plan. They thought they were getting rid of a troublemaker. In fact they were carrying out God’s plan of salvation (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28).

For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Key words. “Lord of glory”: a title of God in the Old Testament (Psalm 24:7–10; Acts 7:2). The one they crucified was the Lord of glory himself. A stunning phrase: God the Son, the glorious Lord, crucified. Because Christ is one person with two natures, what is true of either nature can be said of the person: the Lord of glory died, in his human nature.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the rulers were innocent because they were ignorant. Jesus prayed for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34), but they were guilty (Acts 3:17; 4:10).

In a sentence. None of the rulers of this age understood it, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

For worship. The Lord of glory was crucified for you. Let that astonish you again.

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”—these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.

But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined.” Key words. A loose quotation of Isaiah 64:4 (with echoes of Isaiah 65:17). Human senses and imagination could never discover God’s plan of salvation.

“What God has prepared for those who love him.” Key words. Those who love him are believers. What God has prepared includes salvation in Christ now, as well as glory to come.

These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. Key words. The verse is often quoted as if it were only about heaven, beyond our knowledge. But Paul says God has revealed these things. “Revealed” (apokalyptō, unveiled). “Us” here refers first to the apostles, through whom God gave the revelation that became the New Testament, and then to all believers who receive it.

For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. Key words. “Searches” (eraunaō): not that the Spirit is ignorant and must look, but that he knows everything thoroughly. The depths of God: his inmost thoughts and purposes. Only someone who is himself God can know the depths of God. This is a strong text for the Spirit’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know everything about heaven. Much remains unseen (1 John 3:2). But the heart of God’s plan is revealed.

In a sentence. However, as it is written: “What no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what no human mind has conceived, the things God has prepared for those who love him,” these are the things God has revealed to us by his Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit who knows the depths of God has revealed God’s heart in Scripture. Open it today, and ask him to show you.

parallels.desc: from of old no one has heard or perceived

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.

For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? Key words. An analogy. No one can know what you are thinking unless you tell them. Only your own spirit knows.

So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Key words. In the same way, only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. The Spirit is to God as a person’s spirit is to the person: one with God, sharing his inner life. Yet the Spirit is also a distinct person who reveals (v. 10) and teaches (v. 13).

Now we have received not the spirit of the world. Key words. The spirit of the world: the mindset and wisdom of fallen humanity, perhaps also the evil spirit at work in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2).

But the Spirit who is from God. Key words. Believers have received the Holy Spirit, the Spirit from God (Romans 8:9).

That we might understand the things freely given us by God. Key words. “Freely given” (charizomai, given by grace). The Spirit enables us to understand what God has given us in Christ: forgiveness, adoption, glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have private revelations beyond Scripture. The Spirit helps us understand what God has given and revealed in his word.

In a sentence. For who knows a person’s thoughts except their own spirit within them? In the same way no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. What we have received is not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may understand what God has freely given us.

For worship. Thank God for the gift of his Spirit, who lets you know God’s heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.

And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit. Key words. Not only the thoughts but the words of the apostolic message are taught by the Spirit. This is a key text for verbal inspiration: the Spirit guided the apostles’ very words (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21).

Interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual. Key words. The Greek is compressed: literally, combining spiritual things with spiritual. It may mean explaining spiritual truths in spiritual words, or explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people (ESV). The ESV notes these alternatives. Either way: the Spirit’s truths are conveyed in the Spirit’s words and received by the Spirit’s people.

Where Christians differ: inspiration. Some say the Bible contains God’s word but that its words are merely human, and may contain errors. Verdict: Paul says the words, not only the ideas, were taught by the Spirit. Scripture is God-breathed in all its parts, without error in all it affirms, while using the personalities and styles of its human authors (Westminster 1.4–5, 8). The Spirit did not dictate mechanically, but guided the writers so that what they wrote was exactly what God intended.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the human authors were passive, or that every Christian’s words are inspired as the apostles’ were. This was a unique gift for giving Scripture.

In a sentence. This is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, explaining spiritual realities with Spirit-taught words.

On a Tuesday. Treat the words of Scripture with care. Every one was taught by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.

The natural person. Key words. The “natural person” (psychikos, soulish, living only by natural human life) is someone without the Spirit. Not just a crude or unintelligent person; it can be a brilliant philosopher. The issue is not intellect but spiritual life.

Does not accept the things of the Spirit of God. Key words. “Accept” (dechomai, welcome, receive). He may understand the words but does not welcome the truth.

For they are folly to him. Key words. The same word as 1:18. To him the gospel seems foolish.

And he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned. Key words. “Not able” (ou dynatai): a lack of ability, not just willingness. “Discerned” (anakrinō, examined, judged): spiritual truths can only be evaluated rightly by the Spirit’s help. The natural person needs new birth (John 3:3).

Where Christians differ: total inability. Some teach that unbelievers have the natural ability to receive the gospel if they choose to, and God’s grace only assists them. Verdict: Paul says the natural person is not able to understand the things of the Spirit. Sin has darkened the mind and enslaved the will (Ephesians 4:18; Romans 8:7). This is total inability: not that unbelievers are as bad as they can be, but that they cannot turn to God by their own power. Only the Spirit, by regeneration, opens the heart (Acts 16:14; Westminster 9.3; 10.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should not reason with unbelievers or present evidence. Paul did. But we must pray, because only the Spirit can open their eyes.

In a sentence. The person without the Spirit does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God but considers them foolishness, and cannot understand them because they are discerned only through the Spirit.

For worship. Pray for an unbelieving friend. Ask the Spirit to open their eyes as he opened yours.
verseByVerse.note: The “natural person” is someone without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.

The spiritual person. Key words. The spiritual person (pneumatikos) is anyone who has the Spirit: every true believer. Not a superior class of Christian, as some Corinthians thought.

Judges all things. Key words. “Judges” (anakrinō, discerns, evaluates): the same word as verse 14. With the Spirit, a believer can evaluate everything rightly in the light of God’s truth, including the world’s wisdom.

But is himself to be judged by no one. Key words. The natural person cannot properly evaluate the spiritual person, because he lacks the Spirit. The world cannot rightly judge the Christian’s faith, any more than a blind person can judge colours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are infallible, or above correction or church discipline. Paul himself corrects the Corinthians throughout, and tells them to judge one another’s prophecies (14:29) and to discipline sin (5:12). It means unbelievers are not qualified to judge spiritual truth.

In a sentence. The person with the Spirit makes judgements about all things, but such a person is not subject to merely human judgements.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shaken when the world mocks your faith. It cannot see what you see.

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” Key words. From Isaiah 40:13 (also Romans 11:34). No human can know God’s mind by their own wisdom, much less teach him.

But we have the mind of Christ. Key words. A breathtaking claim. In Isaiah, the mind of the Lord is the mind of Yahweh; Paul equates it with the mind of Christ. We cannot reach God’s mind ourselves, but we have Christ’s mind given to us by the Spirit: his way of thinking, revealed in the apostolic gospel. “We” is first the apostles, then all believers who receive their teaching.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know everything Christ knows, or that we can never be wrong. It means we share his outlook through his word and Spirit, and grow into it (Philippians 2:5; Romans 12:2).

In a sentence. For, “Who has known the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

For worship. Ask God to give you more and more of the mind of Christ: his humility, his love, his way of seeing the world.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?
