5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Paul now deals with a scandal. A man in the church is living with his father’s wife, probably his stepmother, a relationship forbidden by the law of Moses and condemned even by Roman society. Worse, the church is proud of itself instead of grieving. Perhaps they thought their freedom in Christ meant the body did not matter. Paul, though absent, has already made his judgement: when they assemble with the Lord’s power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him outside the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Paul uses a Passover picture. Just as Jewish households swept every scrap of yeast out of the house before the feast, the church must get rid of the old yeast of sin, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding of an earlier letter. He never meant them to avoid all contact with immoral people in the world, which would mean leaving the world altogether. He meant that they must not share fellowship with someone who claims to be a believer but persists in serious sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge those inside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has heard that there is sexual immorality in the church of a kind not even found among pagans: a man is living with his father’s wife. And instead of mourning and removing him, they are proud. Though absent in body, Paul is present in spirit and has already judged the man. When they gather in the name of the Lord Jesus, with Paul’s spirit and the Lord’s power present, they are to hand him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Their boasting is wrong. Do they not know that a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough? They must clear out the old yeast so that they may be a new, unleavened batch, as in fact they are, for Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. So they should keep the festival, not with the old yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

The Reformed tradition has always identified church discipline as one of the marks of the true church (alongside Word and sacraments). Calvin’s Institutes IV.12 grounds discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the holiness of the community is not a human achievement but a participation in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the final word against the sinner but the penultimate word, designed to produce repentance. The church that refuses to discipline its members — in the name of grace, tolerance, or avoiding conflict — is, paradoxically, acting without grace: it is allowing the leavening of unrepentant sin to compromise the whole community and denying the sinner the painful mercy of confrontation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian pride in tolerating this relationship may reflect the influence of the “strong” in the community — those with social status and rhetorical sophistication who had reinterpreted gospel freedom as moral permissiveness. The man involved may have been a patron of the church, someone whose loss the community feared. Paul overrides all such calculations: the gospel has higher priorities than keeping wealthy members comfortable. Now: The contemporary church’s allergy to any form of discipline is well-documented and widely lamented. Churches afraid to confront unrepentant sin in their members have, ironically, become communities shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 5 turns from divisions to a case of open, scandalous sin, and to the church’s failure to deal with it. A member is living with his stepmother, and the church is proud of its tolerance instead of grieving (vv. 1–2). Paul, though absent, has already judged the case: when they gather in the Lord’s name and power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him out of the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord (vv. 3–5). Sin tolerated spreads like yeast through dough; since Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, the church must clean out the old yeast and live in sincerity and truth (vv. 6–8). Finally, Paul clears up a misunderstanding of an earlier letter: the call to separation applies not to unbelievers in the world, but to anyone who calls himself a brother and lives in open, unrepentant sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge its own (vv. 9–13). This chapter is the New Testament’s clearest teaching on church discipline.

It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you. Key words. “Actually” (holōs, everywhere, widely): it is common knowledge. “Sexual immorality” (porneia): any sexual sin outside marriage.

And of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans. Key words. Even Roman law and pagan moral sense condemned it. Cicero called such a union an unbelievable crime.

For a man has his father’s wife. Key words. “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it (Leviticus 18:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). “Has” suggests an ongoing relationship, perhaps living together or married. The father may have died or divorced her. Since Paul says nothing about disciplining the woman, she was probably not a believer.

And you are arrogant! Key words. “Arrogant” (physioō, puffed up). Perhaps they boasted of their freedom and tolerance, thinking that the body did not matter spiritually (6:12–13). Or they were proud in spite of the sin.

Ought you not rather to mourn? Key words. “Mourn” (pentheō, grieve as for the dead). The right response to sin in the church is grief, not pride or indifference.

Let him who has done this be removed from among you. Key words. The man must be put out of the fellowship of the church.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should expel members for every sin. All believers sin. Church discipline is for serious, open sin persisted in without repentance (Matthew 18:15–17).

In a sentence. It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that even pagans do not tolerate: a man is sleeping with his father’s wife. And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have gone into mourning and have put out of your fellowship the man who has been doing this?

On a Tuesday. When sin is exposed in your church, do not gossip or shrug. Grieve, and pray for repentance.
verseByVerse.note: “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it, and Roman law condemned it too.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,

For though absent in body, I am present in spirit. Key words. Paul is in Ephesus, but he is with them in thought and concern, and with his apostolic authority (Colossians 2:5).

And as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. Key words. The facts are public and clear. Paul does not need further investigation. “Pronounced judgement” (krinō, judged, decided).

When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus. Key words. Discipline is not the action of one man, even an apostle, but of the gathered church. Assembled in Jesus’ name: under his authority, as he promised (Matthew 18:17–20).

And my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus. Key words. Paul’s apostolic authority and Christ’s own power stand behind the church’s action. When a church disciplines rightly, Christ acts through it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is present as a ghost. It means his authority and judgement are joined with the church’s action.

In a sentence. For Paul’s part, even though he is not physically present, he is with you in spirit. As one who is present with you in this way, he has already passed judgement in the name of our Lord Jesus on the one who has been doing this. So when you are assembled and he is with you in spirit, and the power of our Lord Jesus is present,

For worship. Christ is present in his gathered church with authority. Pray for your church leaders as they exercise care and discipline.

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.

You are to deliver this man to Satan. Key words. To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, which lies under Satan’s power (1 John 5:19; Ephesians 2:2). Inside the church, he was under the protection and care of God’s people; outside, he is exposed. Paul uses the same phrase of Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:20).

For the destruction of the flesh. Key words. “Flesh” (sarx) here probably means his sinful nature, his fleshly desires. The hope is that the misery of being cut off will break the power of his sin and bring him to repentance. Some think it means physical suffering or even death (11:30). The first fits the hope that follows better.

So that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. Key words. The goal of discipline is restoration and salvation, not destruction. Discipline is a severe mercy. This appears to have worked: 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 may describe the man’s (or another offender’s) repentance and restoration.

Where Christians differ: church discipline. Many churches today never practise discipline, thinking it unloving or judgemental. Others practise it harshly, for minor issues. Verdict: Church discipline is commanded by Christ and the apostles (Matthew 18:15–17; 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15; Titus 3:10). It is one of the marks of a true church, alongside the preaching of the word and the right use of the sacraments (Belgic Confession 29). Its purposes are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church, and the honour of Christ (Westminster 30.3). It should be done carefully, in stages, with love and prayer, and only for serious, persistent, unrepentant sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church can damn someone or curse them. It means the church formally recognises that the person is acting as an unbeliever and treats him as one in need of the gospel.

In a sentence. hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you are ever disciplined, see it as God’s severe mercy. If you see it done, pray for the person’s return.
verseByVerse.note: To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, where Satan rules, in the hope that he will repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

Your boasting is not good. Key words. Their pride (v. 2) is unfitting, especially with this sin in their midst.

Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Key words. A proverb (also Galatians 5:9). Leaven (zymē, yeast): a small piece of old fermented dough worked through new dough. A little spreads through the whole. Tolerated sin spreads. If the church accepts this, others will think it acceptable.

Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump. Key words. Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7). Searching out every crumb became a symbol of removing sin. The church must remove the sinner and the sin he represents.

As you really are unleavened. Key words. Be what you are. In Christ, they are already a new, unleavened lump: holy, sanctified (1:2). Now they must live like it.

For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Key words. The reason. At the first Passover, the lamb was killed and its blood put on the doorframes, so that God passed over and spared the firstborn (Exodus 12). Christ is our Passover lamb: his blood shields us from God’s judgement. He died at Passover time (John 19:14, 36). The sacrifice has been made; now the feast of unleavened bread must follow: a life free of the old yeast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep the Jewish Passover. Christ has fulfilled it. The Lord’s Supper is the new covenant meal (11:23–26).

In a sentence. Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough? Get rid of the old yeast, so that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

For worship. Christ our Passover lamb was sacrificed for you. Let that make you hate sin and long to be clean.
verseByVerse.note: Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Let us therefore celebrate the festival. Key words. The festival is the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which followed Passover for seven days (Exodus 12:15–20). Since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the Christian life is a continual festival: joyful, grateful, holy.

Not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil. Key words. The old yeast: the sins of the old life. Malice (kakia, ill will, badness) and evil (ponēria, wickedness).

But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Key words. Sincerity (eilikrineia, purity, transparency, perhaps from being tested in the sunlight) and truth. A life with no hidden yeast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean holiness is a burden. It is a feast, a celebration of what Christ has done.

In a sentence. Therefore let us keep the festival, not with the old bread leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

On a Tuesday. Live today as a celebration. Throw out the old yeast of grudges and hidden sins. Live openly, honestly, joyfully.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul clarifies what he wrote in an earlier letter about not associating with sexually immoral people. He did not mean people of this world who are immoral, greedy, swindlers or idolaters; to avoid them entirely they would have to leave the world. He meant that they must not associate with anyone who calls himself a brother or sister but lives in sexual sin or greed, worships idols, slanders, gets drunk or swindles, and they should not even eat with such a person. It is not Paul’s business to judge outsiders; God will judge them. But the church must judge those inside it, and, as the law says, expel the wicked person from among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside the community (v. 12–13) defines the scope of church discipline with precision. The church is not called to police the world; it is called to maintain the integrity of its own fellowship. “God judges those outside” — this is not indifference to the world’s sin but a recognition that the church is not the world’s court of law. The church’s mission to the world is evangelism, not judgment; its internal discipline is precisely what enables it to be a credible witness in the world it is trying to reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. Misapplied teaching on holiness tends in two directions: either becoming a withdrawal sect (refusing all contact with sinful unbelievers) or collapsing into permissiveness (refusing all internal accountability). The Corinthians had managed both: they read the earlier letter as a call to leave the world, and they were lax about discipline inside the church. Now: The same confusion persists: churches that are either socially withdrawn from the world (failing at evangelism) or internally undisciplined (failing at community). Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.

I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people. Key words. The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived. “Associate” (synanamignymi, mix together with): close fellowship.

Not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world. Key words. The Corinthians had misunderstood, perhaps deliberately, thinking Paul meant they must avoid all immoral people, which was impossible, and so ignored the instruction altogether.

Or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. Key words. Greedy (pleonektai, those who always want more). Swindlers (harpages, robbers, extortioners). Idolaters: worshippers of false gods. Paul lists sins of money and worship alongside sexual sin.

Since then you would need to go out of the world. Key words. Christians must live among unbelievers, work with them, be friends with them, and witness to them (John 17:15). Withdrawal from the world is not the answer.

Where Christians differ: the lost letter. Some argue that if an apostolic letter was lost, the New Testament canon must be incomplete. Verdict: Not everything an apostle wrote was meant by God to be Scripture for the whole church in all ages. God, in his providence, preserved exactly the books he intended to be the canon (Westminster 1.2, 1.8). The canon is closed and complete, sufficient for all faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The lost letter’s point is preserved here anyway.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should approve of the world’s sins. It means they should not try to escape the world, but live in it as witnesses.

In a sentence. Paul wrote to you in his letter not to associate with sexually immoral people, not at all meaning the people of this world who are immoral, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world.

On a Tuesday. Do not hide from unbelievers. Love your non-Christian neighbours, colleagues and friends, and be salt and light among them.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.

But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother. Key words. “Bears the name”: calls himself a Christian, claims to be a brother. The separation is from professing believers who live in open sin.

If he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler. Key words. Paul adds two to the list: reviler (loidoros, one who abuses others with words, a verbal bully) and drunkard (methysos). These describe a pattern of life, not a single fall. Notice greed and verbal abuse are on the list alongside sexual sin.

Not even to eat with such a one. Key words. Table fellowship expressed acceptance and friendship. The church must not carry on as if nothing were wrong. This probably includes the Lord’s Supper, and ordinary social meals. The purpose is to make the person feel the seriousness of his sin (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean refusing all contact, or treating him as an enemy. Paul says to warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Family members still have family duties. It means the church withdraws the normal signs of Christian fellowship until there is repentance.

In a sentence. But now Paul is writing to you that you must not associate with anyone who claims to be a brother or sister but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or slanderer, a drunkard or swindler. Do not even eat with such people.

For worship. Pray for anyone you know who calls himself a Christian but lives in open sin. Pray for genuine repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”

For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Key words. Outsiders: unbelievers. It is not the church’s job to discipline the world.

Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? Key words. The church is responsible for its own members. “Judge” here means exercise discipline, not condemn eternally.

God judges those outside. Key words. Unbelievers are in God’s hands. He will judge them. Our task toward them is to preach the gospel.

“Purge the evil person from among you.” Key words. A refrain from Deuteronomy (17:7; 19:19; 22:21, 24; 24:7), used when Israel had to remove a serious offender. In Israel this involved the death penalty. In the church, the equivalent is removal from fellowship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not speak out about sin in society, or that the church has no prophetic voice. It means church discipline applies only to church members.

In a sentence. What business is it of Paul’s to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked person from among you.”

On a Tuesday. Hold yourself and fellow believers to God’s standard. Be gentle and gracious with unbelievers, who do not yet know Christ.

parallels.desc: so you shall purge the evil from your midst

Let him who has done this be removed from among you.<sup>3</sup>For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing.<sup>4</sup>When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,<sup>5</sup>you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.<sup>6</sup>Your boasting is not good. 6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Two more problems show the Corinthians living by the standards of their city rather than of Christ. First, church members were suing each other in the public courts. In Roman Corinth, civil litigation was a contest of status: the wealthy and well connected usually won, and lawsuits were a way to humiliate rivals. Paul is appalled that believers, who will one day judge the world and even angels, cannot settle disputes among themselves, and that they would rather drag one another before unbelieving judges than suffer wrong. He reminds them that the unrighteous, including thieves and swindlers, will not inherit God’s kingdom, and that some of them used to be exactly that, before they were washed, made holy and justified in Christ by the Spirit.

Second, some were using slogans like “all things are lawful for me” and “food for the stomach and the stomach for food” to justify sleeping with prostitutes, as if what the body does did not matter to the soul. Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord and will be raised. A believer’s body is a member of Christ, and union with a prostitute makes the two one flesh. So they must run from sexual immorality. Their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit; they are not their own; they were bought at a price, and must honour God with their bodies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul is shocked that when a believer has a dispute with another, he dares to take it before unbelieving judges instead of before God’s people. Do they not know that the saints will judge the world, and even angels? Then surely they are competent to settle everyday matters. Why appoint as judges those whom the church has no reason to respect? Is there really no one wise enough among them to decide between brothers, so that brother sues brother in front of unbelievers? The very fact that they have lawsuits against each other is already a defeat. Why not rather be wronged or cheated? Instead they themselves wrong and cheat, and they do it to their own brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul’s argument from eschatology — “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2) — is a characteristic move: the future reality of the believer’s status shapes present behaviour. The saints who will participate in Christ’s eschatological judgment (Dan 7:22; Rev 20:4) have already, in their union with Christ, been granted a dignity that makes recourse to pagan courts for petty disputes absurd. The inconsistency Paul exposes is not merely practical but theological: why would those destined for cosmic judicial authority submit their neighbourhood disputes to judges who do not acknowledge Christ?
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Going to court was not merely a legal act but a social strategy. Paul refuses the framework: the cross creates a community in which the willingness to absorb loss is a greater display of power than the ability to win in court. Now: The Christian instinct to reach for legal remedies when wronged by a fellow believer is understandable but reveals how deeply the world’s categories of justice and self-protection have shaped us. Paul’s question — “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — is among the most countercultural sentences in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 6 deals with two more failures that show the Corinthians had not grasped what it means to belong to Christ. First, believers were suing one another in pagan courts. Paul is appalled: the saints will one day judge the world and even angels, so they ought to be able to settle disputes among themselves; better still, they should be willing to be wronged rather than wrong a brother (vv. 1–8). Second, he reminds them that the unrighteous, the sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, the greedy and others, will not inherit God’s kingdom. Some of them had been such people, but they have been washed, sanctified and justified in Christ and by the Spirit (vv. 9–11). Third, he takes apart the Corinthian slogans that excused sexual sin: all things are lawful, food for the stomach. The body is for the Lord. It will be raised; it is joined to Christ; it is a temple of the Holy Spirit; it was bought with a price. So flee sexual immorality and glorify God in your body (vv. 12–20).

Setting and background. Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were often used by the wealthy and powerful against those of lower status, and judges could be swayed by bribes or social rank. Taking a brother to court was a way of shaming him publicly.

When one of you has a grievance against another. Key words. “Grievance” (pragma, a matter, a case): a civil dispute, probably about property or money (v. 7).

Does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Key words. “Dare” (tolmaō): how can you be so bold? The unrighteous: unbelieving judges, outside God’s people. The saints: fellow believers in the church.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? Key words. One of six times in this chapter Paul asks, do you not know? (vv. 2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19). At the last day, believers will share in Christ’s judgement of the world (Daniel 7:22; Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4).

And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? Key words. Trivial cases: everyday disputes, small compared to the last judgement. If you will judge the world, can’t you judge this?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never use the courts, or that crimes should not be reported to the authorities. Paul himself appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and Romans 13 gives the state authority to punish wrongdoers. Paul is speaking of civil disputes between believers.

In a sentence. If any of you has a dispute with another, do you dare to take it before the ungodly for judgement instead of before the Lord’s people? Or do you not know that the Lord’s people will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?

On a Tuesday. If you have a dispute with a fellow Christian, go to them first, and then to wise believers, before going public.
verseByVerse.note: Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were a way for the powerful to win status.

parallels.desc: judgment was given for the saints of the Most High

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!

Do you not know that we are to judge angels? Key words. Probably the fallen angels, who await judgement (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Believers will share in Christ’s judgement even of them. An astonishing dignity.

How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life! Key words. “Matters pertaining to this life” (biōtika, everyday matters, the stuff of daily living). If you will judge angels, you can handle property disputes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be judges independently of Christ. They share in his judgement, as his people united to him.

In a sentence. Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!

For worship. God has destined you for such dignity that you will judge angels. Live today with that in mind.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?

So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? Key words. Those who have no standing (exouthenēmenoi, despised, counted as nothing) in the church: the pagan judges, whose values the church does not share. Some read the verse as an ironic command: appoint even the least regarded church members as judges.

I say this to your shame. Key words. The Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom. Paul says: you should be ashamed.

Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers? Key words. Ironic. A church so proud of its wisdom (1:5; 3:18) cannot find one wise person to settle a quarrel?

But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers? Key words. Double shame: brothers fighting, and doing it publicly before unbelievers, who would mock the church.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have the power of a civil court. The church can mediate and advise, and discipline members who refuse to be reconciled.

In a sentence. Therefore, if you have disputes about such matters, do you ask for a ruling from those whose way of life is scorned in the church? Paul says this to shame you. Is it possible that there is nobody among you wise enough to judge a dispute between believers? But instead, one brother takes another to court, and this in front of unbelievers!

On a Tuesday. Churches should have wise people ready to help members settle disputes. Pray that yours does, and be one of them.

parallels.desc: able men to judge the people

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!

To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Key words. “Defeat” (hēttēma, loss, failure). Whoever wins the case, the church has already lost. The very existence of such lawsuits shows a failure of love.

Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Key words. The way of Christ (Matthew 5:39–40; 1 Peter 2:23). Better to lose money than to lose a brother and dishonour Christ. A radical, cross-shaped answer.

But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers! Key words. The real problem: some in Corinth were not the victims but the cheaters. They were defrauding fellow believers, and using the courts to do it.

Where Christians differ: may a Christian ever sue a Christian? Some say never, under any circumstances. Others say the courts are open to Christians like anyone else. Verdict: Paul’s rule is that disputes between believers should be settled within the church, and that it is often better to accept loss than to sue a brother. But this assumes both parties are willing to submit to the church. Where a professing believer refuses church correction, he is to be treated as an unbeliever (Matthew 18:17), and there may be cases where legal protection is necessary, especially for the vulnerable, or where crimes are involved. Abuse, violence and fraud should be reported to the authorities whom God appointed to punish evil (Romans 13:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean victims of crime should stay silent to protect the church’s reputation. That would be a grave misuse of this passage.

In a sentence. The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means you have been completely defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated? Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, and you do this to your brothers and sisters.

For worship. Is there a wrong you need to let go of for the sake of peace and Christ’s honour? Bring it to him, and release it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be deceived: the unrighteous will not inherit God’s kingdom. Those who live in sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery or homosexual practice, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, slanderers and swindlers will not inherit it. Some of the Corinthians had lived exactly like that. But they were washed, set apart as holy and declared righteous in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The triad of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — covers the full scope of soteric transformation. Reformed theology typically orders justification before sanctification logically; Paul here places sanctification before justification in the list, which suggests he is not giving a logical order but a rhetorical one: moving from the most experientially tangible (washing, cleansing from the pollution of past sin) to the most legally decisive (justification, right standing before God). All three are accomplished “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — trinitarian to the root.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street — not foreign or distant behaviour but the lives many of the congregation had lived and from which the gospel had extracted them. Paul is not writing to people who need to be warned away from exotic sins; he is reminding them of who they used to be, so they understand what they now are. Now: The church in every generation contains people whose past is on the list in vv. 9–10. The three words of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — are the most liberating words any of them will ever hear about that past. It was real; the transformation is realer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Key words. A link with verses 1–8: the “unrighteous” (adikoi) are the same word as the pagan judges of verse 1. Those who wrong (adikeō, v. 8) are acting like the unrighteous. To inherit the kingdom: to receive eternal life in God’s coming reign.

Do not be deceived. Key words. Some in Corinth were deceiving themselves that how they lived did not matter if they had knowledge or gifts.

Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers. Key words. The sexually immoral (pornoi): all sexual sin outside marriage. Idolaters: worshippers of other gods. Adulterers (moichoi): those unfaithful to their marriage.

Nor men who practice homosexuality. Key words. The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind this phrase refer to the passive and active partners in consensual homosexual acts. The first (malakoi, literally soft ones) was used of the passive partner. The second (arsenokoitai, literally male-bedders) appears to be formed from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male. Paul uses the terms to cover homosexual acts generally.

Nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers. Key words. Sins of property and speech too: theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, extortion. The list is broad. No one can look down on others.

Will inherit the kingdom of God. Key words. Those whose lives are characterised by these sins, unrepentant, show they are not God’s people.

Where Christians differ: homosexuality. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative relationships, such as pederasty or prostitution, not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Verdict: The terms Paul uses draw directly on Leviticus, which forbids homosexual acts as such, without reference to exploitation. Elsewhere Paul grounds his teaching in creation (Romans 1:26–27), and Jesus defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman (Matthew 19:4–6). The historic Christian teaching is that sexual relations belong only within marriage between a man and a woman. This must be held with deep compassion. Same-sex attraction is a real and often painful experience, not chosen, and believers who experience it and live faithfully are brothers and sisters to be loved and supported. Homosexual sin is listed alongside greed, drunkenness and slander, sins all of us need forgiveness for. And verse 11 shows the gospel’s welcome to all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that anyone who has ever done one of these things is lost. Verse 11 says some of them were such people. It means that unrepentant, habitual practice of such sins is incompatible with belonging to God’s kingdom.

In a sentence. Or do you not know that wrongdoers will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral nor idolaters nor adulterers nor men who have sex with men nor thieves nor the greedy nor drunkards nor slanderers nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Do not deceive yourself. If a sin on this list rules your life, run to Christ today. He washes, sanctifies and justifies.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind “men who practice homosexuality” refer to the passive and active partners in homosexual acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

And such were some of you. Key words. Past tense. Some of the Corinthian believers had been immoral, idolaters, thieves, drunkards, practising homosexuals. That is who they were. It is no longer who they are.

But you were washed. Key words. “Washed” (apolouō, washed clean): cleansed from sin’s filth. Probably a reference to new birth, of which baptism is the sign (Titus 3:5; Acts 22:16).

You were sanctified. Key words. Set apart as holy to God: definitive sanctification (1:2). God claimed them as his own.

You were justified. Key words. Declared righteous before God: their guilt removed, Christ’s righteousness counted to them (Romans 5:1). Paul does not list these in logical order; all three happen together at conversion.

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. Key words. All of it through Christ’s work and the Spirit’s application. Notice the Trinity: the Lord Jesus, the Spirit, our God (the Father).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that former temptations will never return. But a believer’s identity is no longer defined by past sins or present temptations. You are washed, sanctified, justified.

In a sentence. And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

For worship. Whatever you once were, if you are in Christ: you were washed, sanctified, justified. Praise him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes up slogans the Corinthians were using. “Everything is permitted for me”, they said; yes, but not everything is helpful, and Paul will not be mastered by anything. “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food”, they said, meaning that the body’s appetites, including sex, do not matter; God will do away with both. But the body is not meant for sexual immorality. It is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body, and God, who raised the Lord, will raise us too. Believers’ bodies are members of Christ; should they unite them with a prostitute? Never. Whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her, for Scripture says the two become one flesh, but whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. So they must flee sexual immorality. Other sins are outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who lives in them, given by God. They do not belong to themselves; they were bought at a price, so they must honour God with their bodies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul’s argument for sexual ethics is grounded in resurrection theology: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a temporary shell to be discarded but the vehicle of the self that God will raise — the same body, transformed. This is why what we do with the body matters eternally. The body-soul dualism that dismisses bodily sins as theologically insignificant — a common Gnostic error in the ancient world — is precisely what Paul is refuting. The resurrection of the body is the theological foundation of a robust, embodied Christian ethics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a prostitute in Corinth was a normal feature of social life — not perceived as transgression but as participation in the city’s religious and social fabric. The Corinthian with a “strong” theology might have regarded it as religiously meaningless (the idol is nothing) and biologically natural. Paul’s counter-argument changes the frame entirely: it is not religiously meaningless because the Holy Spirit inhabits the believer’s body; the body is not yours to give away because it was bought with a price. Now: The sexual ethics of any age are shaped by whatever account it gives of the body. Paul’s account — the body as Spirit-indwelt, resurrection-destined, cross-purchased — is the most exalted account of human physicality in any worldview.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.

“All things are lawful for me.” Key words. The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth. Perhaps they had twisted Paul’s own teaching on Christian freedom into a licence to do anything, including sexual sin. Paul partly agrees, then qualifies sharply.

But not all things are helpful. Key words. “Helpful” (sympherō, beneficial, profitable). The question is not only, is it allowed? but, is it good for me and others?

“All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything. Key words. A wordplay: “lawful” (exestin) and “dominated” (exousiasthēsomai, brought under the authority of). I have authority to do all things, but I will not let anything have authority over me. Freedom that leads to slavery is not freedom. Many things that are permissible become addictions.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul believed literally everything is lawful. He has just listed sins that exclude from the kingdom. The slogan applies at most to things God has left free.

In a sentence. “I have the right to do anything,” you say, but not everything is beneficial. “I have the right to do anything,” but Paul will not be mastered by anything.

On a Tuesday. Is there something permitted that has started to master you: your phone, food, entertainment, alcohol? Freedom means being able to say no.
verseByVerse.note: The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth, which Paul quotes and then corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

“Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food.” Key words. Another slogan. The Corinthians argued that bodily appetites are natural and do not matter spiritually. Eat when hungry; have sex when you desire it. Many Greeks thought the body was unimportant compared to the soul.

And God will destroy both one and the other. Key words. Possibly also part of the slogan: the body will perish anyway, so what we do with it does not matter. Paul agrees that food and stomach are temporary, but rejects the conclusion.

The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord. Key words. The body (sōma) is not like the stomach. It is the whole person in bodily existence, and it belongs to the Lord. Sexual immorality is not just an appetite; it involves the whole person.

And the Lord for the body. Key words. A stunning statement. The Lord is for the body: he cares about it, redeemed it, and will raise it. The body is not unimportant to God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil or that food is wrong. It means the body is precious to God and must be used for his purposes.

In a sentence. You say, “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy them both.” The body, however, is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

For worship. Thank God that your body matters to him. Offer it to him today (Romans 12:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!

And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Key words. The body is not destroyed at death for good. As God raised Christ’s body, he will raise ours (15:20–23). What will be raised matters now. This is why chapter 15 is so important to the letter.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Key words. Members (melē, limbs, parts). Believers are united to Christ, body and soul. Your hands, eyes and whole body are parts of Christ.

Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Key words. Prostitution was common in Corinth, sometimes connected with temples. To have sex with a prostitute is to take what belongs to Christ and join it to her.

Never! Key words. Mē genoito, absolutely not. Unthinkable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who falls into sexual sin is no longer joined to Christ. It shows the horror and contradiction of such sin.

In a sentence. By his power God raised the Lord from the dead, and he will raise us also. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ himself? Shall Paul then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!

On a Tuesday. Your body is a part of Christ. Do not take it anywhere, or do anything with it, that you would not take Christ to.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.

Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? Key words. “Joined” (kollaō, glued, cleaved to). Sex is never merely physical. It unites two persons. Even a casual encounter creates a real union.

For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” Key words. From Genesis 2:24, God’s design for marriage. Sexual union is meant to express and seal the lifelong covenant union of husband and wife (Matthew 19:5–6). Used outside marriage, it still creates a union, but a false and destructive one.

But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him. Key words. The same word, joined. Believers are united to Christ in a spiritual union, by the Spirit, which is even deeper than marriage (Ephesians 5:31–32). Sexual immorality sets up a rival union.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a sexual encounter creates a marriage. It means sex has a meaning that cannot be emptied out, which is why it belongs in marriage.

In a sentence. Do you not know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.” But whoever is united with the Lord is one with him in spirit.

For worship. You are joined to the Lord, one spirit with him. Let no other union compete with that.

parallels.desc: they shall become one flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.

Flee from sexual immorality. Key words. “Flee” (pheugō, run away from, present tense: keep fleeing). Not argue with it, flirt with it, or test your strength against it, but run. Joseph fled from Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39:12; 2 Timothy 2:22).

Every other sin a person commits is outside the body. Key words. Possibly another Corinthian slogan: every sin is outside the body. Or Paul’s own statement, meaning that sexual sin is unique.

But the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Key words. Sexual sin is unique in its relation to the body. It is not that it is the worst sin, but that it involves giving one’s own body to another in a union meant only for marriage. It defiles the body that is the Lord’s and the Spirit’s temple.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sexual sin is unforgivable. It is washed away like every other sin (v. 11). Nor does it mean other sins (like drunkenness) have no bodily effects.

In a sentence. Flee from sexual immorality. All other sins a person commits are outside the body, but whoever sins sexually sins against their own body.

On a Tuesday. Plan your escape routes: what you will do, where you will go, whom you will call, when temptation comes. Then flee.

parallels.desc: Joseph fled

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you. Key words. In 3:16 the church together is God’s temple; here each believer’s body is. Temple (naos): the inner sanctuary where God dwells. The Holy Spirit lives in your body. Sexual sin brings the Holy One into the brothel.

Whom you have from God? Key words. The Spirit is God’s gift (2:12). You did not earn him.

You are not your own. Key words. The opposite of the modern slogan, my body, my choice. The believer does not own himself.

For you were bought with a price. Key words. “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market. Christ purchased you with his own blood (1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9). You belong to your new master. And he is a master who bought you to set you free.

So glorify God in your body. Key words. The conclusion. Use your body to show God’s worth: in purity, service, work, worship. Some later manuscripts add “and in your spirit, which are God’s”; the shorter reading is original.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you must hate or neglect your body. It means you care for it and use it as God’s property, for his glory.

In a sentence. Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honour God with your bodies.

For worship. Pray: Lord, I am not my own. You bought me with your blood. Use my body today for your glory.
verseByVerse.note: “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints?<sup>2</sup>Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?<sup>3</sup>Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!<sup>4</sup>So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church?<sup>5</sup>I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers,<sup>6</sup>but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?<sup>7</sup>To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?<sup>8</sup>But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!<sup>9</sup>Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality,<sup>10</sup>nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.<sup>11</sup>And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.<sup>12</sup>“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.<sup>13</sup>“Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other.
