7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
From chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The first concerns sex and marriage. Some in Corinth had swung to the opposite extreme from the immorality of chapter 6: they said it was better for a man not to touch a woman at all, even in marriage, and perhaps that believers should divorce unbelieving spouses or not marry. Roman society, by contrast, pressed people to marry: the emperor Augustus had passed laws penalising the unmarried. Paul steers between both pressures.

Married couples should not deny each other sexually, except briefly by agreement for prayer. Singleness is good and Paul himself prefers it, but it is a gift, and those without it should marry. Believers should not divorce, as Jesus taught; a believer married to an unbeliever should stay if the unbeliever is willing, but is not bound if the unbeliever leaves. In general, each person should serve God in the situation in which he was called, whether circumcised or not, slave or free, though a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Because the time is short and the world in its present form is passing away, and because of a present crisis, Paul advises the unmarried to consider staying single, so as to serve the Lord without divided concerns. But marriage is no sin, and a widow may remarry, only to a believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the questions in their letter, beginning with the claim that it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. Because sexual immorality is a real danger, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Husband and wife owe each other sexual intimacy; neither has sole rights over their own body, for each belongs to the other. They should not deprive each other except by mutual agreement for a limited time of prayer, and then come together again, so that Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control. Paul says this as a concession, not a command. He wishes everyone could be single as he is, but each person has his own gift from God. To the unmarried and widows he says it is good to stay single as he does, but if they cannot control themselves they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with desire.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

Reformed theology has always resisted the Catholic elevation of celibacy above marriage as the spiritually superior state. The Reformers read 1 Corinthians 7 as affirming both callings as genuine gifts of God, neither intrinsically superior. Luther’s own marriage was a theological act — a public demonstration that marriage is not a second-class spiritual status. Paul’s careful handling of both callings in vv. 7–9 supports this reading: celibacy is a charisma, a grace-gift, as is marriage. Neither is commanded; both are honoured.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics who were advocating celibacy within marriage may have been influenced by the same Gnostic-adjacent body-negativity that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6 — but in the opposite direction: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul’s answer refuses both the libertine and the ascetic extremes. Now: The Christian tradition has tended to err in one direction or the other in every generation: either treating sexuality as a dangerous force to be suppressed, or (more recently) treating it as a sovereign identity that cannot be questioned. Paul’s account makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant obligation, eschatologically relativised.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 7 is the Bible’s longest discussion of marriage and singleness. Some in Corinth swung the opposite way from the immorality of chapter 6: they thought sex itself was unspiritual, and that believers should abstain even in marriage, or leave their marriages. Paul answers their questions one by one. Marriage is good, and sexual union within it is a mutual duty and gift; married couples should not deprive each other (vv. 1–7). Singleness is also good, and a gift, but those who burn with desire should marry (vv. 8–9). Married believers must not divorce; if one is married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, the believer should stay; if the unbeliever leaves, the believer is not bound (vv. 10–16). In general, Christians should remain in the situation in which God called them, whether married or single, Jew or Gentile, slave or free, for what matters is keeping God’s commands (vv. 17–24). Finally, because the time is short and this world is passing away, singleness has real advantages for undivided devotion to the Lord; but marrying is no sin (vv. 25–40). The chapter honours both marriage and singleness as callings from God.

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote. Key words. From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. “Now concerning” (peri de) marks each new topic: marriage (7:1), virgins (7:25), food offered to idols (8:1), spiritual gifts (12:1), the collection (16:1), Apollos (16:12).

“It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” Key words. Literally, not to touch a woman, a polite expression for sexual relations. This is probably a slogan from the Corinthians’ letter, which Paul quotes and then qualifies. Some ascetics in Corinth were saying that even married couples should abstain.

But because of the temptation to sexual immorality. Key words. Literally, because of immoralities. In a city like Corinth, and given the strength of sexual desire, enforced abstinence would lead to sin.

Each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Key words. “Have” here probably means have sexual relations with, within marriage. One wife, one husband: monogamy. Marriage is God’s good provision for sexual desire.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the only reason to marry is to avoid sin. Scripture gives many purposes for marriage: companionship (Genesis 2:18), children (Genesis 1:28), a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32), and the prevention of immorality (Westminster 24.2). Paul is answering a specific question here.

In a sentence. Now for the matters you wrote about: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But since sexual immorality is occurring, each man should have sexual relations with his own wife, and each woman with her own husband.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the good gift of marriage, and for sex within it. It is not unspiritual; it is his design.
verseByVerse.note: From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The ESV notes that “to have sexual relations” is literally “to touch.” The quoted saying was probably a slogan of some at Corinth.

parallels.desc: it is not good that the man should be alone

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights. Key words. “Conjugal rights” is literally what is owed (opheilē, debt). Sexual relations in marriage are a duty each spouse owes the other. Notice Paul speaks first of the husband’s duty to his wife.

And likewise the wife to her husband. Key words. Complete mutuality. Each owes the other.

For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Key words. “Have authority” (exousiazō, the same word as 6:12). In marriage, each gives the other a claim on their body.

Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Key words. In the ancient world, the first statement was ordinary; the second was revolutionary. A husband’s body belongs to his wife. Paul establishes equal mutual belonging in the marriage bed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean either spouse may force or coerce the other. The passage is about giving, not taking. Love does not insist on its own way (13:5), and husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25). Abuse is never justified by this verse.

In a sentence. The husband should fulfil his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body but yields it to her husband. In the same way, the husband does not have authority over his own body but yields it to his wife.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, ask: am I giving myself to my spouse generously, or withholding? Love gives.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

Do not deprive one another. Key words. “Deprive” (apostereō, rob, defraud, the same word as 6:7–8). Refusing sex in marriage is a kind of defrauding.

Except perhaps by agreement for a limited time. Key words. Three conditions for abstaining: mutual agreement, a limited time, and a spiritual purpose.

That you may devote yourselves to prayer. Key words. A season of special prayer, perhaps with fasting.

But then come together again. Key words. Abstinence in marriage is the exception, not the rule.

So that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. Key words. Satan uses unmet desire to tempt to adultery and other sins. Paul is realistic about human weakness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sexual relations are less spiritual than prayer. Both are good. It means that devotion to prayer should not become an excuse to neglect a spouse.

In a sentence. Do not deprive each other except perhaps by mutual consent and for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again so that Satan will not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

For worship. Pray together as a couple, if you are married. And thank God for the gift of each other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.

Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. Key words. “Concession” (syngnōmē, allowance, permission). What is “this”? Probably the permission to abstain for a time for prayer (v. 5). Paul does not command it.

I wish that all were as I myself am. Key words. Paul was unmarried at this time, perhaps a widower; as a former Pharisee and member of the council, he may once have been married. He found singleness a great freedom for ministry.

But each has his own gift from God. Key words. “Gift” (charisma, the same word for spiritual gifts in chapter 12). Both singleness and marriage are gifts from God. Paul does not say only singleness is a gift.

One of one kind and one of another. Key words. God gives different callings to different people.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier? The medieval church came to treat celibacy as a higher, more spiritual state, and required it of clergy. Verdict: Paul values singleness highly, but he calls both singleness and marriage gifts from God. Neither is holier. Forbidding marriage is described as a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and church leaders may be married (1 Timothy 3:2; 9:5). The Reformers rightly restored the honour of marriage, including for ministers. Each believer should seek to serve God in the calling he has given.

What it does not mean. It does not mean singleness is a gift only for those who feel no desire. It means God gives each person their present situation as his gift, to be used for him.

In a sentence. Paul says this as a concession, not as a command. He wishes that all of you were as he is. But each of you has your own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.

On a Tuesday. Whether you are single or married today, see it as God’s gift to you for now, and use it for him.

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

To the unmarried and the widows. Key words. The unmarried (agamoi) may mean widowers here, paired with widows, or all unmarried people.

I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. Key words. “Good” (kalos, fine, fitting): not commanded, but a good option.

But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. Key words. “Exercise self-control” (enkrateuomai, a word used of athletes in training, 9:25). If someone is not able to live a chaste single life, marriage is the right path.

For it is better to marry than to burn with passion. Key words. “Burn” (pyroō): burn with sexual desire. Not burn in hell. Paul is honest: strong desire is a legitimate reason to marry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is a second-best choice for the weak. It means God has provided marriage for the many who are called to it.

In a sentence. Now to the unmarried and the widows Paul says: it is good for them to stay unmarried, as he does. But if they cannot control themselves, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

For worship. If you are single and long to be married, bring that desire to God honestly. He knows and cares.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To married believers Paul passes on the Lord’s own command: a wife should not separate from her husband, and if she does she must remain unmarried or be reconciled; and a husband must not divorce his wife. To others, in cases Jesus did not address, Paul gives his own apostolic instruction. A believer married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay should not divorce. The unbelieving spouse is made holy through the believer, and so are their children. But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so; the believer is not bound in such cases, for God has called us to peace. And who knows whether the believer may yet save the unbelieving spouse?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s careful distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” vs. “I, not the Lord”) is a fascinating window into apostolic hermeneutics. It does not mean that vv. 12–16 are less authoritative Scripture — Paul is writing under inspiration. It means that vv. 10–11 apply a dominical teaching directly, while vv. 12–16 extend the principle to a situation Jesus did not address. Both are authoritative; they are transparent about their different relationship to the dominical tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Divorce was common and easy in the Roman world, and Corinth’s fluid social culture made marriage instability familiar. The question of what to do in a mixed marriage — especially if the unbeliever wanted out — was live and urgent for many in the community. Now: The “Pauline privilege” continues to be one of the most practically significant and debated passages in NT ethics, applied to situations ranging from desertion to abuse. The governing principle — God has called you to peace — is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.

To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord). Key words. Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce (Mark 10:9–12; Matthew 5:32; 19:6–9). Here he can quote the Lord directly. “Married” here means where both spouses are believers.

The wife should not separate from her husband. Key words. “Separate” (chōrizō) was a common word for divorce in that time. Some Corinthian women may have wanted to leave their husbands to live a more spiritual, celibate life.

But if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. Key words. If a believing wife does leave (without biblical grounds), she has two options: stay single or be reconciled. She is not free to marry someone else.

And the husband should not divorce his wife. Key words. “Divorce” (aphiēmi, send away). The same rule for husbands. In Greek and Roman law, divorce was easy for both sexes. Christ forbids it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is ignoring the exception Jesus gave for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9). He is giving the general rule, without listing every exception. It does not mean a spouse must stay in danger. Separation for safety from abuse is not the same as seeking divorce, and church leaders and authorities should help.

In a sentence. To the married Paul gives this command (not he, but the Lord): a wife must not separate from her husband. But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.

On a Tuesday. If your marriage is hard, do not look for a way out; look for help. Seek counsel, pray, and work toward reconciliation.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.

To the rest I say (I, not the Lord). Key words. Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer after marriage. So Paul gives his own apostolic ruling. This does not mean it has less authority. It means Paul cannot quote a saying of Jesus, but he speaks with the authority Christ gave him (v. 40; 14:37).

If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. Key words. Some new believers may have thought they must leave an unbelieving spouse, perhaps fearing they were defiled by the union. Paul says: no. If the unbeliever is willing to stay, stay.

If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. Key words. The same for wives. In the ancient world, a wife was expected to follow her husband’s religion. A believing wife of a pagan was in a hard place. But she should stay if he is willing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may marry unbelievers. Paul forbids that (v. 39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). He is speaking of those already married when one came to faith.

In a sentence. To the rest Paul says this (he, not the Lord): if any brother has a wife who is not a believer and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. And if a woman has a husband who is not a believer and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him.

For worship. Pray for believers married to unbelievers. Ask God to make their faithfulness a witness.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer; Paul applies his authority as an apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife. Key words. “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing spouse. The believer is not defiled by the marriage; rather, the marriage is sanctified, set apart, acceptable to God. The unbeliever is exposed to the gospel and the influence of a godly spouse (v. 16).

And the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Key words. The same in reverse.

Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy. Key words. If the marriage were unclean, the children would be too. But the children of a believing parent are holy: set apart, under the influence of the gospel and a believer’s care, and in that sense distinct from the children of two unbelievers.

Where Christians differ: holy children and baptism. Some argue from this verse that the children of believers are in the covenant and should therefore be baptised as infants. Verdict: The verse says the unbelieving spouse is also made holy, yet no one would baptise an unbelieving spouse. So holy here cannot mean qualified for baptism. It means set apart in a special relation to God’s people and blessing. Baptism in the New Testament is for those who repent and believe. The app holds this credobaptist reading, while recognising with charity that paedobaptist brothers and sisters read the covenant signs differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children of believers are automatically saved. They need to be born again and believe, like everyone else. But they are greatly privileged.

In a sentence. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.

On a Tuesday. If you are the only believer in your home, your presence matters. God has placed you there for your family’s good.
verseByVerse.note: “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing partner.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.

But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. Key words. If the unbeliever insists on leaving, permanently, do not try to force them to stay. “Separates” (chōrizō): divorces, departs.

In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. Key words. “Enslaved” (douloō, bound as a slave). The believer is not bound to the marriage. This is a strong word: the believer is free.

God has called you to peace. Key words. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.” Either way, God does not call believers to endless conflict trying to hold on to a spouse who has left.

Where Christians differ: desertion and remarriage. Some say a deserted believer may separate but never remarry while the former spouse lives. Verdict: Not enslaved means the marriage bond is broken, and the deserted believer is free to remarry, in the Lord. Paul uses similar language about being free to remarry after a spouse’s death (v. 39; Romans 7:2–3). Scripture recognises two grounds for divorce with freedom to remarry: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied by the church or civil authority (Westminster 24.6). Divorce is always a tragedy, and churches should handle each case with care and wise counsel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer may push an unbelieving spouse to leave, or use this as an excuse to end a hard marriage.

In a sentence. But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so. The brother or the sister is not bound in such circumstances; God has called us to live in peace.

For worship. If you have been abandoned, God has not abandoned you. He calls you to peace. Rest in his care.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Key words. This may be read two ways. Positively: who knows, you might win him to Christ, so stay if he is willing (1 Peter 3:1–2). Or as a reason to let him go: you cannot be sure your staying will save him, so do not cling to a spouse who wants to leave. The second fits verse 15 more closely; the first fits the whole passage’s encouragement to stay.

Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? Key words. “Save” here means be God’s instrument in bringing them to salvation (9:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believing spouse can save their partner by their own power. Only God saves. But God often uses a faithful spouse.

In a sentence. How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or, how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

On a Tuesday. If your spouse is not a believer, live with gentleness and quiet faithfulness. God may use it to win them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul states a general rule he teaches in every church: each person should live the life the Lord assigned and in which God called him. If a man was circumcised when called, he should not try to undo it; if uncircumcised, he should not seek circumcision. Neither counts for anything; what counts is keeping God’s commands. Each should remain in the situation in which he was called. A slave who was called should not let it trouble him, though if he can gain his freedom he should take it. For a slave called by the Lord is the Lord’s freed person, and a free person called is Christ’s slave. They were bought at a price, so they must not become slaves of human beings. Each should remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain — remain as you are — is not social conservatism but theological prioritisation. The gospel relativises every earthly status by subjecting it to a higher identity: in Christ. This does not mean social structures are indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good), but that the gospel’s transformative work operates from the inside out, transforming the meaning of every condition before changing the condition itself. This is the seed from which the ultimate abolition of slavery grew in Christian history: not immediate political revolution but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which eventually made the institution of slavery theologically intolerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. The question of whether conversion required a change of social status was real and practically urgent. Paul’s answer guards against two errors: treating social change as spiritually necessary (legalism applied to status), and treating social change as spiritually forbidden (quietism about injustice). Now: The principle “remain as you are” guards against the modern Christian anxiety that effectiveness for God requires a different job, a different social location, a different cultural context. You were placed where you are by Providence; bloom there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.

Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. Key words. The principle of verses 17–24. “Assigned” (merizō, apportioned): God has given each person their place in life. “Called”: the moment God called them to faith. Becoming a Christian does not mean you must change your outward situation. Serve God where you are.

This is my rule in all the churches. Key words. Not a special rule for Corinth (4:17).

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Key words. Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision, to avoid mockery at the public baths and gymnasiums (1 Maccabees 1:15). A Jewish believer need not become a Gentile.

Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. Key words. A Gentile believer need not become a Jew (Galatians 5:2–6).

For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God. Key words. A startling statement for a Jew, since circumcision was itself a commandment. But Paul means the moral commandments, the law of love, which applies to all (Galatians 5:6; 6:15). Ethnic identity markers do not matter before God; obedience does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians can never change jobs or circumstances (see v. 21). It means that our outward situation is not what makes us acceptable to God, so we need not rush to change it.

In a sentence. Nevertheless, each person should live as a believer in whatever situation the Lord has assigned to them, just as God has called them. This is the rule Paul lays down in all the churches. Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man uncircumcised when he was called? He should not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commands is what counts.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a new situation to serve God. Serve him in the job, family and place you are in today.
verseByVerse.note: Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)

Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Key words. The principle repeated.

Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. Key words. A bondservant (doulos, slave). Perhaps a third of people in Corinth were slaves. Roman slavery was not based on race; people became slaves through war, debt or birth, and many were freed by age thirty. Some slaves were educated professionals. But slaves had no legal rights and could be badly treated. Paul says: do not let your status trouble you. You are fully a Christian, with full dignity before God.

(But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.) Key words. The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead,” meaning stay a slave even if offered freedom. The Greek is ambiguous. The ESV’s main reading is more likely: freedom is better, so take it if you can. Paul goes on to say do not become slaves of men (v. 23).

Where Christians differ: did the Bible approve of slavery? Some say the New Testament approved of slavery because it did not demand its abolition. Verdict: The New Testament did not call for violent revolution, but it planted principles that undermine slavery: all humans bear God’s image; slave and free are equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11); masters must treat slaves justly, knowing they have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9); slave-trading is condemned (1 Timothy 1:10); and here slaves are encouraged to gain freedom. Christians like William Wilberforce rightly drew on these truths to fight for abolition. The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by the law of Moses itself (Exodus 21:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should accept injustice passively. It means our worth and calling do not depend on our circumstances.

In a sentence. Each person should remain in the situation they were in when God called them. Were you a slave when you were called? Don’t let it trouble you, although if you can gain your freedom, do so.

For worship. Thank God that in Christ, your worth does not depend on your status. Pray for those who are enslaved or exploited today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead.” Slaves could sometimes buy or be granted their freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.

For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Key words. “Freedman” (apeleutheros, a freed slave). The slave who becomes a Christian is spiritually free: freed from sin, guilt and death by the Lord. He has the highest freedom there is.

Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. Key words. And the free person who becomes a Christian is now Christ’s slave, under his total ownership. Every believer is both free and a slave, whatever their social status.

You were bought with a price. Key words. As in 6:20. Christ purchased us with his blood.

Do not become bondservants of men. Key words. Do not sell yourself into slavery, a common way of escaping debt; and do not let human opinions or powers control you spiritually. You belong to Christ.

So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God. Key words. The third statement of the principle (vv. 17, 20, 24). “With God”: in his presence, with him. The most important thing is not your situation, but that you are with God in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good. It means that the gospel relativises social status: in Christ, the slave is free and the free man is a slave.

In a sentence. For the one who was a slave when called to faith in the Lord is the Lord’s freed person; similarly, the one who was free when called is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Brothers and sisters, each person, as responsible to God, should remain in the situation they were in when God called them.

On a Tuesday. At work, you serve your employer, but your true master is Christ. Work for him (Colossians 3:23–24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the question of those who have never married, Paul has no command from the Lord, but gives his judgement as one the Lord has made trustworthy. Because of the present crisis, he thinks it good for people to stay as they are. Those who are married should not seek to separate; those who are free should not look for a wife. But marrying is no sin, though married people will face hardship, and Paul wants to spare them. The time is short. From now on, married people should live without being absorbed in marriage, mourners as if not mourning, the joyful as if not rejoicing, buyers as if they owned nothing, users of the world as if not engrossed in it, because the world in its present form is passing away. Paul wants them free from anxiety. The unmarried can focus on the Lord’s affairs and how to please him; the married must also think about the world and how to please their spouse, so their interests are divided. He says this for their benefit, not to restrict them, but so that they may serve the Lord with undivided devotion. A man engaged to a woman may marry her if he feels he should; it is no sin. But one who has firmly decided not to marry does well too. Marriage is good, but staying single is better in present circumstances. A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry anyone she wishes, provided he belongs to the Lord. Paul thinks she will be happier if she stays as she is, and he believes he too has God’s Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as if not” framework is one of the most pastorally liberating texts in the NT for the believer under pressure. It is not an ascetic refusal of the world’s goods but an insistence that no good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying — all are real; none are final. The person who holds them “as if not” is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress” — the compressed time between the first and second coming, with its attendant pressures. He is not issuing universal commands but pastorally calibrated counsel. Now: The eschatological urgency has not diminished — we are closer to the end than Paul’s Corinth was. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, is not less relevant but more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.

Now concerning the betrothed. Key words. A new question from their letter. “Betrothed” is literally virgins (parthenoi): unmarried young women, probably those engaged to be married.

I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment. Key words. Jesus had not spoken directly on this. Paul gives his considered advice (gnōmē, opinion, judgement).

As one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. Key words. Paul is a trustworthy guide, made so by God’s mercy. His advice is inspired wisdom, even if not a command (v. 40).

I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is. Key words. The “present distress” (anankē, necessity, pressure) may refer to famine, persecution or the general trouble of the last days. There were famines in Greece around this time. Whatever it was, it made marriage and family life especially hard. Paul’s advice is: stay as you are, for now.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s advice here has no authority. It means it is wise counsel given for a specific situation, not an absolute command for all times.

In a sentence. Now about virgins: Paul has no command from the Lord, but he gives a judgement as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. Because of the present crisis, he thinks that it is good for a man to remain as he is.

For worship. Ask God for wisdom in your big decisions, especially in hard times. He gives it generously (James 1:5).
verseByVerse.note: The “present distress” may refer to famine, persecution or the pressures of the last days.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Key words. If you are married, or engaged, do not try to get out.

Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Key words. If you are unmarried, do not rush to find a spouse, given the present distress.

But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Key words. Marriage is not sin. Paul is firm against the ascetics in Corinth.

Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that. Key words. Literally, trouble in the flesh: the pressures and anxieties of married and family life, especially in hard times. Paul wants to spare them that. Pastoral care, not a rule.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is bad. It means it carries burdens as well as joys.

In a sentence. Are you pledged to a woman? Do not seek to be released. Are you free from such a commitment? Do not look for a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face many troubles in this life, and Paul wants to spare you this.

On a Tuesday. If you are thinking of marriage, count the cost as well as the joy. Both are real.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.

This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. Key words. “Appointed time” (kairos): the season between Christ’s first and second comings. “Grown very short” (synestalmenos, compressed, like a sail being furled). The end is on its way. This shapes everything.

From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none. Key words. Not neglecting their wives (v. 3), but not letting marriage become their ultimate concern. Marriage is for this age only (Matthew 22:30).

And those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing. Key words. Grief and joy are real, but not final. The Christian mourns with hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13) and rejoices without clinging.

And those who buy as though they had no goods. Key words. Buy, but hold possessions loosely. You are a steward, not an owner.

And those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. Key words. Use the world, its goods and systems, but do not be absorbed by it. “Have no dealings” (katachraomai, use fully, use up).

For the present form of this world is passing away. Key words. “Form” (schēma, outward shape, like a scene in a play). The world as it now is will not last (1 John 2:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be cold, detached or careless. It means they should live with eternity in view, holding everything in this world with an open hand.

In a sentence. What Paul means, brothers and sisters, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they do not; those who mourn, as if they did not; those who are happy, as if they were not; those who buy something, as if it were not theirs to keep; those who use the things of the world, as if not engrossed in them. For this world in its present form is passing away.

For worship. Hold everything you love with an open hand today. Only God and his kingdom will last.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,

I want you to be free from anxieties. Key words. “Free from anxieties” (amerimnos, without care). Paul’s advice is pastoral: he wants to spare them worry.

The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. Key words. Here “anxious” (merimnaō) is used positively: concerned for, devoted to. The single person can give full attention to the Lord’s work.

But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife. Key words. Worldly things here are not sinful things, but the things of ordinary life: providing, caring, household concerns. A married man rightly has to think about pleasing his wife. That is his duty, not his sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean married people cannot serve the Lord, or that pleasing a spouse is unspiritual. It means their attention is rightly divided.

In a sentence. Paul would like you to be free from concern. An unmarried man is concerned about the Lord’s affairs, how he can please the Lord. But a married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife,

On a Tuesday. If you are single, use your freedom for the Lord. If you are married, pleasing your spouse is part of pleasing the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.

And his interests are divided. Key words. Pulled in two directions: the Lord and his wife. Both are legitimate.

And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. Key words. Holy here means devoted to God, set apart for his service, in her whole person.

But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. Key words. The same for wives.

I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you. Key words. “Restraint” (brochos, a noose, a halter). Paul is not trying to trap them or impose rules.

But to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord. Key words. “Good order” (euschēmon, what is fitting, seemly). “Undivided devotion” (aperispastōs, without distraction, as Martha was distracted, Luke 10:40). His aim is that each one be wholly devoted to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are automatically more devoted, or that married people cannot be devoted. It means singleness offers a particular opportunity for undistracted service.

In a sentence. and his interests are divided. An unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the Lord’s affairs: her aim is to be devoted to the Lord in both body and spirit. But a married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. Paul is saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but that you may live in a right way in undivided devotion to the Lord.

For worship. Whatever your situation, ask the Lord for undivided devotion to him.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.

If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed. Key words. The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally virgin, and that the passage could also be read of a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage. The ESV takes it as an engaged man and his fiancée, which fits the language of passions better.

If his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. Key words. If desire is strong, marry. No sin.

But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control. Key words. If he is settled, not under pressure, in control of his desire, and has decided not to marry,

And has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. Key words. To remain engaged but not marry, in view of the present distress, is also good.

So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better. Key words. Both good; singleness, in the present distress, is better for undivided devotion. Better here is not morally better, but more advantageous in that situation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is morally inferior. Paul says marrying does well.

In a sentence. If anyone is worried that he might not be acting honourably toward the virgin he is engaged to, and if his passions are too strong and he feels he ought to marry, he should do as he wants. He is not sinning. They should get married. But the man who has settled the matter in his own mind, who is under no compulsion but has control over his own will, and who has made up his mind not to marry the virgin, this man also does the right thing. So then, he who marries the virgin does right, but he who does not marry her does better.

On a Tuesday. If you are engaged and unsure, pray, seek counsel, and know that both marrying and waiting can honour God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin,” and that the passage can also be read of a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.

A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. Key words. Marriage is lifelong (Romans 7:2).

But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes. Key words. Death ends the marriage bond. A widow may remarry freely. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is honourable (1 Timothy 5:14).

Only in the Lord. Key words. “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer. A Christian may not marry an unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6:14). This applies to all believers, not only widows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a widow must remarry. Paul’s next verse suggests she may be happier single.

In a sentence. A woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, but he must belong to the Lord.

For worship. If you are single and hoping to marry, commit to marrying only in the Lord, and pray for a godly spouse.
verseByVerse.note: “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. Key words. “Happier” (makarios, blessed). In the present distress, Paul thinks a widow is better off single, free for the Lord.

And I think that I too have the Spirit of God. Key words. A touch of irony. Some in Corinth claimed to be especially spiritual. Paul says: I have the Spirit too. His judgement is Spirit-guided. Here, in what he calls his opinion, he is still writing inspired Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unsure whether he had the Spirit. “I think” is a modest way of making a firm point.

In a sentence. In Paul’s judgement, she is happier if she stays as she is, and he thinks that he too has the Spirit of God.

On a Tuesday. If you have lost a spouse, know that God cares for widows and widowers (Psalm 68:5). Your single life can be blessed and fruitful.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.”<sup>2</sup>But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.<sup>3</sup>The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.<sup>4</sup>For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.<sup>5</sup>Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.<sup>6</sup>Now as a concession, not a command, I say this.<sup>7</sup>I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.<sup>8</sup>To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am.<sup>9</sup>But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.<sup>10</sup>To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband<sup>11</sup>(but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.<sup>12</sup>To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her.<sup>13</sup>If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.<sup>14</sup>For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. God has called you to peace.<sup>16</sup>For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?<sup>17</sup>Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.<sup>18</sup>Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision.<sup>19</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.<sup>20</sup>Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.<sup>21</sup>Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)<sup>22</sup>For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ.<sup>23</sup>You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men.<sup>24</sup>So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.<sup>25</sup>Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.<sup>26</sup>I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.<sup>27</sup>Are you bound to a wife?
