8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
The next question from the Corinthians’ letter is about food offered to idols. Some background makes it vivid. In a Greek or Roman city, most meat came from animals sacrificed at temples: part was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and much of the rest was eaten at banquets in the temple dining rooms or sold in the meat market (the macellum, whose inscription has been found in Corinth). Temples were also the restaurants and party venues of the city; papyrus invitations survive asking guests to dine “at the table of the lord Sarapis”. Excavations at Corinth’s temple of Asclepius found dining rooms with couches. For a Christian, refusing every such meal could mean cutting yourself off from trade guilds, family celebrations and civic life.

Some Corinthian believers, proud of their knowledge, argued that idols are nothing and there is only one God, so they could eat anywhere. Paul agrees with their theology, and gives one of the most important statements of Christian belief: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But knowledge without love puffs people up. Not every believer has that confidence; some, long used to idols, still feel that eating such food is worship, and if they follow the example of the “strong” against their conscience, they are damaged. A believer for whom Christ died must not be ruined by another’s freedom. So Paul would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to fall. (Chapter 10 will add that actually taking part in idol feasts is forbidden.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On food sacrificed to idols, Paul quotes the Corinthians’ claim that “we all have knowledge”, and warns that knowledge inflates people, while love builds them up. Anyone who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he should; but whoever loves God is known by him. So, about eating such food: they say an idol is nothing in the world and there is no God but one. Paul agrees. Though there are many so-called gods and lords in heaven and on earth, for believers there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we live.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is a watershed in NT christology. Paul takes the foundational monotheistic confession of Israel — “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deut 6:4) — and distributes it between the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father receives the title “one God” with the phrase “from whom are all things and for whom we exist”; Jesus Christ receives the title “one Lord” with the phrase “through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” Both titles draw on the divine prerogative of creation. This is not bitheism or subordinationism; it is the Shema expanded to include the Son within the identity of the one God of Israel — which is exactly what Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically sophisticated — probably a mix of those with a Jewish background (who knew the idol was nothing) and educated Gentiles who had absorbed the Stoic critique of popular religion. Their knowledge was real. Their pride was realer. Now: The Reformed tradition is not immune to the Corinthian disease of knowledge-pride. The person who has worked through the doctrines of grace and arrived at the Reformation’s conclusions is in real danger of making theological correctness a platform for contempt of those still confused. Paul’s question applies: have you been known by God? (v. 3). That is the only knowledge that ultimately matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 8–10 answers another question from the Corinthians’ letter: may Christians eat food that has been offered to idols? Chapter 8 lays the foundation. Some Corinthians had knowledge: there is only one God, idols are nothing, so food offered to them is harmless. Paul agrees with their theology (vv. 4–6). But knowledge on its own puffs up; love builds up (vv. 1–3). Not every believer has this knowledge; some, with a past in idol worship, still feel that eating such food is taking part in idolatry, and their weak consciences are defiled if they eat (v. 7). So the strong must not use their freedom in a way that leads a weak brother to act against his conscience, and so to ruin. To sin against a brother like that is to sin against Christ, who died for him (vv. 9–12). Paul’s own resolve: if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat (v. 13). Chapter 9 then gives Paul’s example of giving up rights, and chapter 10 adds a warning about real idolatry.

Setting and background. Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple. Animals were sacrificed; part was burned, part went to the priests, and the rest was eaten at a temple feast or sold at the market. Social life in Corinth revolved around such meals: trade guild dinners, birthday parties and civic festivals were often held in temple dining rooms. To refuse them could cost a Christian business, friends and social standing.

Now concerning food offered to idols. Key words. Eidōlothyta, idol-sacrifices: a Jewish and Christian word. Pagans called it simply sacred offering.

We know that “all of us possess knowledge.” Key words. Probably another Corinthian slogan. They were proud of their theological knowledge (gnōsis).

This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. Key words. The key principle of chapters 8–10. Knowledge alone inflates (physioō, like a balloon). Love (agapē) builds up (oikodomeō, like a house). Knowledge used without love becomes pride.

If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. Key words. Those who are proud of their knowledge show that they do not really understand. True knowledge of God humbles and produces love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge is bad, or that Christians should not study theology. It means knowledge must serve love.

In a sentence. On the question of meat sacrificed to idols: the Corinthians claim that they all have knowledge, but knowledge on its own makes people proud, while love builds others up. Anyone who thinks he has mastered something has not yet understood it as he should.

On a Tuesday. When you know you are right about something, ask: am I using this knowledge to build others up, or to puff myself up?
verseByVerse.note: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple; temples also had dining rooms used for banquets and celebrations. The quoted phrases are probably Corinthian slogans.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.

But if anyone loves God. Key words. The contrast to verse 2. What matters is not how much you know but whether you love God.

He is known by God. Key words. Paul turns it around. We might expect: he truly knows God. Instead: he is known by God. The deepest reality is not our knowledge of God but God’s knowledge of us: his loving, choosing, personal knowledge (Galatians 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:19; Romans 8:29). Our love for God is the evidence that he first knew and loved us (1 John 4:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God only learns about us when we love him. He knew his people before the foundation of the world. It means that love for God is the sign that we are known by him.

In a sentence. But whoever loves God is the one God knows as his own.

For worship. You are known by God. Not just known about, but known and loved. Let that be your joy today.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—

Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols. Key words. Paul returns to the topic.

We know that “an idol has no real existence.” Key words. Probably another slogan: an idol is nothing in the world. There is no real god behind the statue (Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8). Paul agrees, though in 10:20 he adds that demons are behind idol worship.

And that “there is no God but one.” Key words. The confession of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4). Monotheism is foundational.

For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth. Key words. Gods in heaven: sun, moon, Zeus, Apollo. On earth: deified emperors, local gods, heroes.

As indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords.” Key words. In one sense they exist: people worship them, and they hold real power over people’s lives. Lords (kyrioi) was a title for mystery-religion deities like Serapis, and for the emperor.

What it does not mean. It does not mean idolatry is harmless because idols are nothing. Paul will warn that behind idols are demons (10:19–21).

In a sentence. So, about eating food sacrificed to idols: we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is only one God. There may be many so-called gods and lords in heaven or on earth, and people do treat many as gods and lords,

On a Tuesday. Our culture has its own gods and lords: money, pleasure, success, image. Name one in your life and dethrone it today.

parallels.desc: the LORD our God, the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

Yet for us there is one God, the Father. Key words. For Christians, against all the so-called gods, there is one God.

From whom are all things and for whom we exist. Key words. The Father is the source of all creation, and its goal. We exist for him.

And one Lord, Jesus Christ. Key words. Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus. In Deuteronomy 6:4 (the Shema), the two key words are God and Lord: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Paul takes them and applies God to the Father and Lord to Jesus. Jesus is included within the one God of Israel’s confession.

Through whom are all things and through whom we exist. Key words. Jesus is the agent of creation: all things were made through him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). And through him we exist as new creatures, redeemed. Only God creates. So Jesus is God.

Where Christians differ: the deity of Christ. Groups such as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue that this verse distinguishes Jesus from the one God, making him a lesser being. Verdict: Paul is not separating Jesus from the one God of Israel but including him within it. He divides the words of the Shema between the Father and the Son, and gives the Son the divine work of creation. This is the earliest Christian confession of the Trinity in seed form. The Father and the Son are distinct persons, but one God, with the Holy Spirit (Nicene Creed; Westminster 2.3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father is not Lord, or the Son not God. Both titles belong to both. Paul uses them to distinguish the persons while affirming one God.

In a sentence. but for us there is only one God, the Father, the source of everything and the goal of our life, and only one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom everything was made and through whom we have our life.

For worship. Confess it today: one God, the Father; one Lord, Jesus Christ. Worship the Father through the Son.
verseByVerse.note: Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus Christ as the one Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But not everyone has this knowledge. Some, used to idols until recently, still think of the food as offered to an idol when they eat it, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not bring us closer to God; we are no worse off if we do not eat and no better off if we do. But they must be careful that their freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. If someone with a weak conscience sees a knowledgeable believer eating in an idol’s temple, he may be encouraged to eat idol food himself, and so the weak believer, a brother for whom Christ died, is destroyed by the other’s knowledge. Sinning against fellow believers in this way, wounding their weak consciences, is sinning against Christ. So if food makes a brother fall, Paul will never eat meat again, so as not to make him fall.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The category of “weak brother” in Paul is not a permanent spiritual classification but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience is not yet formed to the level of theological maturity the gospel makes possible. The strong are not forbidden to exercise their freedom; they are required to consider the effect of their freedom on those still developing. This is not a silencing of the theologically mature but a school in cruciform love: the pattern of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Cor 8:9), is the paradigm for the voluntary limitation of legitimate freedom in love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific situation — food offered to idols in a pagan temple context — is culturally remote for most Western Christians. But the principle is not: the more mature members of any community regularly face the question of how to use their freedom in ways that do not damage those who are less free. Now: The contemporary applications range from alcohol (where an alcoholic is in the room) to entertainment choices (where a recovering addict might be triggered) to musical styles in worship (where real spiritual associations exist for some). The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.

However, not all possess this knowledge. Key words. In theory, all believers know there is one God. But not all have absorbed it deeply enough to feel free.

But some, through former association with idols. Key words. “Former association” (synētheia, habit, being used to). Gentile believers who had worshipped idols all their lives could not shake the feeling that eating such food meant joining in worship.

Eat food as really offered to an idol. Key words. When they eat, they feel it is an act of idolatry.

And their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Key words. “Weak” (asthenēs): not strong enough to be free. “Defiled” (molynō, stained). If they eat against their conscience, they feel guilty, and in fact they sin, because they act against what they believe is God’s will (Romans 14:23).

Food will not commend us to God. Key words. Probably another slogan of the strong, which Paul accepts. Food does not bring us closer to God.

We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do. Key words. Eating is spiritually neutral. So the strong lose nothing by giving it up.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a weak conscience is good. It is weak. But it must be respected and gently instructed, not overridden.

In a sentence. Yet not everyone grasps this. Some, still used to idols, eat such food as though it were truly offered to an idol, and because their conscience is weak, it is stained. Food will not bring us nearer to God: we lose nothing by not eating, and gain nothing by eating.

On a Tuesday. Be patient with Christians whose past makes them sensitive about things you are free in. Their scruples may come from a painful history.

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?

But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. Key words. “Right” (exousia, authority, freedom). The strong have a right, but it can become a stumbling block (proskomma, something to trip over).

For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple. Key words. The strong were not only eating idol meat at home but attending meals in temple dining rooms. Archaeologists have found such dining rooms at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth.

Will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols? Key words. “Encouraged” is literally built up (oikodomeō), the same word as love builds up (v. 1). Ironic: the strong think they are building up the weak by showing freedom, but they are building them up to sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eating in a temple is fine as long as no weak brother sees. In chapter 10 Paul will say that eating at temple feasts is in fact participating with demons (10:20–21).

In a sentence. But be careful that your freedom does not trip up those whose faith is weaker. If someone with a weak conscience sees you, who know better, eating in an idol’s temple, won’t he be emboldened to eat what has been sacrificed to idols?

For worship. Ask God to make you aware of how your choices affect others watching you.

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.

And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed. Key words. “Destroyed” (apollymi, ruined, perishing). The weak believer, acting against conscience, falls into sin and is spiritually wrecked, perhaps drawn back into idolatry. The very knowledge the strong were proud of becomes the weapon that ruins him.

The brother for whom Christ died. Key words. The supreme reason. He is your brother, and Christ loved him enough to die for him. Will you not give up a meal for him?

Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak. Key words. “Wounding” (typtō, striking, beating). To push a weak conscience is to beat it.

You sin against Christ. Key words. Christ is so united to his people that sin against them is sin against him (Matthew 25:40, 45; Acts 9:4).

Where Christians differ: can a brother for whom Christ died perish? Some take this verse as proof that Christ died for some who will finally be lost. Verdict: Paul describes the real tendency of the strong person’s action: it would lead the brother to ruin. The warning is real. But Scripture also teaches that Christ’s death infallibly saves those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; John 10:15, 28), and God uses warnings like this one as means to keep his people. The point is that the strong should treat every brother as someone precious enough for Christ to die for. This is consistent with definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak have no responsibility. They too should grow in knowledge. But the strong must not take advantage of their weakness.

In a sentence. So this weak believer, the brother Christ died for, is ruined by your knowledge. When you sin against your brothers like this and bruise their fragile consciences, you are sinning against Christ himself.

On a Tuesday. Before you exercise a freedom, look at the person beside you and remember: Christ died for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble. Key words. “Stumble” (skandalizō, cause to fall into sin). Paul turns from argument to personal example.

I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble. Key words. “Never” is emphatic: never, to eternity. Not just idol meat, but any meat, if it would cause a brother to fall. Paul is willing to give up a right entirely for love’s sake. This leads into chapter 9, where he shows how he has given up other rights for the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul became a vegetarian on principle, or that anyone can forbid others anything by claiming offence. The point is the real danger of leading a brother into sin.

In a sentence. So if what Paul eats would cause his brother to fall, he will give up meat for good, rather than make his brother fall.

For worship. Ask God for a heart like Paul’s: one that gladly gives up rights for the sake of others.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 can look like a digression from idol food, but it is Paul’s example. He has just said he would give up meat rather than harm a brother. Now he shows that he lives that way. As an apostle he has every right to financial support: to food and drink, to bring a wife on his travels like Peter and the Lord’s brothers, and to be paid like a soldier, a farmer or a shepherd. The law of Moses says the same, the temple priests lived from the offerings, and Jesus himself commanded that preachers of the gospel should live by it. Yet Paul has used none of these rights in Corinth, because he would rather die than give anyone a reason to say he preached for money.

His freedom is spent in serving others. He has made himself everyone’s slave to win as many as possible: to Jews he lived as a Jew, to Gentiles as one outside the Mosaic law (though never outside God’s law, since he is under Christ’s law), to the weak as weak. He does it all for the gospel. Then Paul turns to the Isthmian Games, held every two years just outside Corinth. Athletes train with fierce self-control for a wreath that withers. Christians run for a crown that lasts, so Paul disciplines his body, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks whether he is not free, whether he is not an apostle who has seen Jesus the Lord, and whether the Corinthians themselves are not the result of his work in the Lord. Even if others doubt his apostleship, the Corinthian church is the seal that proves it. To his critics he offers this defence. He and Barnabas have the right to be fed, the right to take a believing wife with them like the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Peter, and the right not to work for a living. No soldier pays his own wages, no one plants a vineyard without eating its grapes, no shepherd goes without milk. The law of Moses says not to muzzle an ox while it threshes, and that was written for our sake, so that workers can expect a share of the harvest. If Paul has sown spiritual seed among them, it is not too much to reap material support. Others enjoy this right; Paul more so. Yet he has not used it, but puts up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. Those who serve in the temple eat from its offerings, and in the same way the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should get their living from it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Right of Ministers to Financial Support

Paul’s argument from Deuteronomy 25:4 (“You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain”) follows a characteristic pattern in his hermeneutics: the OT command for the benefit of animals carries an “how much more” application to human ministers of the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7, quoted by Paul in 1 Tim 5:18) is embedded in the creation order and confirmed by the Lord’s own command. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on adequate financial support for ordained ministry as a matter of justice, not charity — grounded precisely in passages like this.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The travelling sophist in Corinth charged fees for his teaching; the apostle who did not was, paradoxically, suspected of being less legitimate — not worth paying. Paul’s refusal to accept payment actually undermined his status in the eyes of some Corinthians, which is why he defends the right even while refusing to exercise it. Now: The principle cuts in two directions: congregations should support their ministers generously; ministers should never let financial considerations drive their preaching agenda. The apostle who can preach without anxiety about whether his congregation will like what they hear is the freest preacher in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 9 can look like a change of subject, but it is Paul’s personal illustration of the principle of chapter 8: give up your rights for the sake of others. The strong in Corinth insisted on their right to eat. Paul shows that he, an apostle, has far greater rights: to be supported financially, to bring a wife on his travels, to stop working with his hands. He proves these rights from common sense, the law of Moses, temple practice and the command of the Lord himself (vv. 1–14). Yet he has given them all up, so as not to hinder the gospel. His reward is to preach free of charge (vv. 15–18). More than that, he has made himself a slave to all, becoming like a Jew to Jews, like a Gentile to Gentiles, weak to the weak, all things to all people, to win some (vv. 19–23). Finally, he uses the picture of athletes in training: the Christian life demands self-discipline, so that we win the imperishable prize and are not disqualified (vv. 24–27).

Am I not free? Key words. Free as the strong claimed to be (8:9). Paul has the same freedom, and more.

Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Key words. Some in Corinth questioned Paul’s apostleship. An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord (Acts 1:21–22). Paul saw him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 15:8).

Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? Key words. The Corinthian church itself is proof of his apostleship. It exists because of his ministry.

If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. Key words. A seal (sphragis) authenticated a document, like a signature or a wax stamp. Their conversion is God’s seal confirming Paul’s apostleship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who plants a church is an apostle in Paul’s sense. Paul’s apostleship rested on seeing the risen Lord and being commissioned by him directly. That office ended with the apostolic generation.

In a sentence. Is Paul not free? Is he not an apostle? Has he not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not the result of his work in the Lord? Others may doubt him, but you cannot; your very existence as a church in the Lord is the stamp that proves him an apostle.

On a Tuesday. The best evidence of anyone’s ministry is changed lives. Thank God for those who brought the gospel to you.
verseByVerse.note: An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord. A seal authenticated a document.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?

This is my defense to those who would examine me. Key words. “Defense” (apologia): a legal reply. “Examine” (anakrinō, cross-examine, as in 4:3). Some critics were questioning Paul, perhaps because he refused payment, which they took as a sign he was not a real apostle.

Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Key words. The first right: to receive food and drink at the church’s expense. “We” includes Barnabas and others. “Right” (exousia), the key word of chapters 8–9.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was defending himself out of pride. He was defending the gospel’s integrity and showing the strong how to give up rights.

In a sentence. This is Paul’s answer to those who put him on trial: Do we not have the right to be given food and drink?

For worship. Thank God for those who serve you in the word, and ask how you can support them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?

Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife. Key words. Literally, a sister, a wife: a Christian wife. The right to marry, and to have her travel with him at the churches’ expense.

As do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Key words. Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him (Mark 1:30). The brothers of the Lord were Jesus’ half-brothers, James, Joses, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3), who came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).

Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? Key words. Paul and Barnabas both worked with their hands (Acts 13:2; 18:3). Are they the only ones without the right to be supported?

Where Christians differ: married ministers and the brothers of the Lord. The Roman Catholic Church requires celibacy of most of its priests, and teaches that Mary remained a virgin for life, so that the brothers of the Lord were cousins or children of Joseph by a previous marriage. Verdict: This verse shows that the apostles, including Peter, whom Rome regards as the first pope, had wives. Church leaders may marry (1 Timothy 3:2). Requiring celibacy of ministers has no basis in Scripture. As for the brothers of the Lord, the natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus (Matthew 1:25; 13:55–56). Mary is to be honoured as blessed among women, but nothing in Scripture requires her perpetual virginity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single ministers are less qualified. Paul himself was single. It means marriage is no barrier to ministry.

In a sentence. Don’t we have the right to bring a believing wife with us, as the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Peter all do? Or are Barnabas and Paul the only ones who must earn their own keep?

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor’s marriage and family. Ministry places heavy strains on them.
verseByVerse.note: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him. The Lord’s brothers included James and Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?

Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Key words. Soldiers were paid and supplied by the state. Three examples from everyday life prove the right to support.

Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Key words. The farmer eats from his crop.

Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk? Key words. The shepherd drinks from his flock. All three pictures are used elsewhere of ministry: soldier (2 Timothy 2:3–4), farmer (3:6–9; 2 Timothy 2:6), shepherd (1 Peter 5:2). Workers are supported by their work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should be in it for the money (1 Peter 5:2). It means support is a fair right.

In a sentence. No soldier pays his own wages; no one plants a vineyard and goes without its grapes; no shepherd keeps a flock and never drinks its milk.

For worship. Thank God that he provides for his workers. If you serve him, trust him to supply your needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.

Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? Key words. Not just common sense: Scripture says it too.

For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 25:4. Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor, or pulled a sledge over it, to separate grain from husk. A muzzle would stop them eating as they worked. God’s law forbade it: let the ox eat.

Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Key words. Paul does not mean God does not care about animals (Psalm 145:9; Jonah 4:11). He means that the law’s deeper purpose is not merely about oxen.

Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake. Key words. The principle behind the law: workers should share in the fruit of their labour. If that applies to oxen, how much more to people. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater. Paul uses the same verse for elders’ pay in 1 Timothy 5:18.

Because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop. Key words. Every worker works in hope of a share.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is allegorising the law and ignoring its plain meaning. He draws out the principle behind it, which the law intended (Romans 15:4).

In a sentence. Is this only human reasoning? Doesn’t the law teach it too? Moses wrote, “Do not muzzle the ox while it threshes the grain.” Is God’s real concern here the oxen? Surely he is speaking for our benefit: whoever ploughs or threshes should be able to do it expecting a share of the harvest.

For worship. Thank God that his law is full of kindness, even to animals. And thank him that it was written for your sake.
verseByVerse.note: Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor; the law let them eat as they worked.

parallels.desc: you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.

If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? Key words. Spiritual seed (the gospel) yields material harvest (financial support). A small return for a great gift (Romans 15:27; Galatians 6:6).

If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Key words. Other teachers in Corinth were receiving support. Paul, their founder, has a stronger claim.

Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right. Key words. The surprise. Paul has the right, but refuses to use it. This is the point for the strong.

But we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ. Key words. “Endure” (stegō, bear, put up with, the same word as love bears all things, 13:7). “Obstacle” (enkopē, a cutting in, a roadblock). In Corinth, travelling teachers often charged fees and were seen as greedy. Paul did not want anyone to think he preached for money.

What it does not mean. It does not mean it is wrong for ministers to be paid. Paul defends the right and accepted gifts from other churches (2 Corinthians 11:8–9; Philippians 4:15–16). He refused it in Corinth for the gospel’s sake.

In a sentence. We sowed spiritual seed among you; is it too much to expect a material harvest? If others have that right, we have it more. Yet we never used it; we put up with anything rather than block the way of Christ’s gospel.

On a Tuesday. What right could you give up this week so that the gospel is not hindered?

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.

Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple. Key words. In Israel, the priests and Levites lived from the offerings and tithes (Numbers 18:8–32; Deuteronomy 18:1–5). Pagan priests did the same.

And those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? Key words. Priests ate portions of the sacrifices (Leviticus 7:6–10).

In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel. Key words. The final and highest argument: the Lord Jesus himself commanded it, when he said that the worker deserves his wages (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). Churches have a duty to support those who preach the gospel to them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gospel ministers are priests offering sacrifices. Paul uses the temple only as an analogy for support.

In a sentence. You know that those who work in the temple are fed from the temple, and those who serve at the altar receive part of what is offered there. In the same way the Lord himself directed that those who preach the gospel should be supported by it.

For worship. Give generously to support gospel ministry. It is the Lord’s command.

parallels.desc: the priests’ portion

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has not used any of these rights, and he is not writing to get them now; he would rather die than let anyone empty his boast. Preaching itself gives him no ground for boasting, because he is under compulsion; woe to him if he does not preach. If he did it willingly he would have a reward; but since he is entrusted with it as a duty, his reward is this: to offer the gospel free of charge and not use his rights. Though free from everyone, he has made himself everyone’s slave to win more people. To Jews he became like a Jew, to those under the law like one under it (though not under it himself), to those without the law like one without it (though not free from God’s law, being bound by Christ’s law), to the weak he became weak. He has become all things to all people so that by every possible means he might save some, and he does it all for the gospel, so as to share in its blessings.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missional Identification and the Integrity of the Gospel

Paul’s “all things to all people” has been both one of the most misused and most important principles in Christian mission. Misused, it becomes a pretext for theological drift — adjusting the content of the gospel to make it more acceptable. Properly understood, it describes the willingness to adjust the container — cultural form, communicative register, social entry point — while keeping the content constant. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was an extended application of this principle: enter the cultural world of the highly educated secular professional, learn to speak their language, earn the right to challenge their assumptions — and preach the same crucified Christ that Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s concrete examples — becoming as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak — map onto the social divisions within his own missionary world. He was not fixed in one cultural mode but radically adaptable in form while immovable in content. The Damascus road encounter made him a prisoner of the message; everything else was negotiable. Now: Contextualisation is the ongoing challenge of every missionary enterprise. The line between appropriate adaptation and compromising capitulation is real and requires constant discernment; but the failure to contextualise — treating one’s own cultural form of Christianity as the gospel itself — is at least as dangerous as over-adaptation.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!

But I have made no use of any of these rights. Key words. Paul is not hinting for money. He has deliberately refused.

Nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. Key words. He is not asking them to start paying him now.

For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. Key words. Paul breaks off mid-sentence in Greek, so strongly does he feel. His boast (kauchēma) is not in himself, but in being able to preach without charge.

For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. Key words. Preaching itself is no basis for pride, because he has no choice about it.

For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! Key words. “Necessity” (anankē, compulsion). Christ commissioned Paul (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). Like Jeremiah, he cannot hold it in (Jeremiah 20:9). Woe: he would be under God’s judgement if he refused.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached grudgingly. He preached with joy. But he knew he was under orders.

In a sentence. Paul has used none of these rights, and he is not writing in the hope of being paid now; he would rather die than lose this one thing he can take pride in. Preaching itself gives him nothing to boast about, because he is under orders: woe to him if he does not preach the gospel.

On a Tuesday. You too have been entrusted with the gospel. Share it, not for reward, but because you have been told to and because you love Christ.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.

For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. Key words. If preaching were his own free choice, like a volunteer, he could expect a reward (pay).

But if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. Key words. A steward (oikonomos) was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s affairs; often a slave, not paid but obliged (4:1). Paul is a steward of the gospel. He preaches under compulsion, not for wages.

What then is my reward? Key words. So where is his reward?

That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge. Key words. His reward is the joy of giving the gospel away, as it was given to him. A free gospel offered freely.

So as not to make full use of my right in the gospel. Key words. Paul’s reward is precisely in not using his rights.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers who are paid have no reward. It means Paul found a special joy in giving up what he could rightly have claimed.

In a sentence. If he preached by his own choice, he could expect payment; but since he preaches under orders, he is simply a steward doing what he was given to do. So what is his reward? The joy of offering the gospel without charge, not using the rights it would give him.

For worship. The gospel was given to you free. Give it away freely.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.

For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all. Key words. Free (eleutheros): no one owns him. Yet he made himself a slave (douloō) to everyone. Like Christ, who took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7; Mark 10:45).

That I might win more of them. Key words. “Win” (kerdainō, gain, a business word): win for Christ. Five times in verses 19–22.

To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. Key words. Paul was a Jew, but in Christ he no longer depended on Jewish identity. Yet with Jews he kept Jewish customs: he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), took a vow (Acts 18:18), joined in temple purification (Acts 21:23–26).

To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law). Key words. With people living by the law of Moses, he lived by it too, not as a way of salvation but out of love. But he was not under the law as a covenant or a means of righteousness (Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:19).

That I might win those under the law. Key words. The purpose was always to remove unnecessary barriers to the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul changed the gospel for different audiences. When the gospel itself was at stake, he refused to compromise (Galatians 2:3–5, 11–14). He adapted in matters indifferent, not in truth.

In a sentence. Paul is no one’s slave, yet he has made himself everyone’s slave so as to win as many as possible. With Jews he lived as a Jew to win Jews; with those who keep the law he kept it too, though he himself is not under the law, so that he might win them.

On a Tuesday. What customs or preferences could you lay aside to help someone hear the gospel without unnecessary obstacles?

verseByVerse.quote: To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.

To those outside the law I became as one outside the law. Key words. Those outside the law (anomoi, without law): Gentiles. With them, Paul did not keep Jewish food laws or customs; he ate with them (Galatians 2:12–14).

(Not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ). Key words. A vital qualification. Paul was not lawless. He was under the law of Christ (ennomos Christou, in-lawed to Christ): the moral will of God as taught and fulfilled by Christ, summed up in love (Galatians 6:2; John 13:34). Freedom from Moses’ ceremonies is not freedom from God’s moral law.

To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. Key words. The weak of chapter 8. Paul limited his freedom to serve them.

I have become all things to all people. Key words. In every culture and with every kind of person, Paul adapted himself.

That by all means I might save some. Key words. “Save”: be God’s instrument in their salvation. “Some”: realistic. Not all will believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul became a sinner to reach sinners, or adopted every cultural practice. He never joined in idolatry or immorality. It means he adapted in matters of liberty, never compromising the gospel or holiness.

In a sentence. With Gentiles who do not have the law, Paul lived like them, though he is not free of God’s law but bound to Christ’s, so that he might win them. With the weak he became weak, to win the weak. He has become whatever each person needs him to be, so that by every possible means he might save some.

For worship. Thank God for missionaries who learn new languages and cultures to bring the gospel. Pray for one today.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.

I do it all for the sake of the gospel. Key words. Everything Paul does, every right he gives up, every adaptation he makes, serves the gospel’s advance.

That I may share with them in its blessings. Key words. “Share” (synkoinōnos, a fellow partaker). Paul wants to share in the blessings of the gospel together with those he wins. He is not above them, but a fellow sinner saved by grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul earned his salvation by his ministry. He wants to be a partaker of the gospel’s blessings, which come by grace.

In a sentence. He does all this for the gospel’s sake, so that he may share its blessings along with them.

On a Tuesday. Let the gospel shape your choices today: your words, your spending, your time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the athletic games. In a race all the runners run, but only one wins the prize, so they should run to win. Every competitor trains with strict self-discipline, and they do it for a wreath that will wither; believers do it for a crown that will last for ever. So Paul does not run aimlessly or box like someone throwing punches at the air. He disciplines his body and makes it his servant, so that after preaching to others he himself will not be disqualified.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and Effort: The Perseverance of the Saints

The warning of v. 27 — “lest I myself should be disqualified” — has been debated in relation to the doctrine of perseverance. Reformed theology does not take this as a threat to genuine believers’ final security but as the description of the means by which that security is maintained: the God who sovereignly keeps his people does so through their own disciplined effort, not instead of it. The warning is the mechanism of perseverance: those who are genuinely elect will take the warning seriously, run hard, and thereby demonstrate and maintain their calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the Isthmian Games and would have immediately understood the competitive imagery. Paul makes the comparison in order to shame them slightly: the athletes prepare with greater earnestness for a temporary prize than the Corinthians apply to an eternal one. Now: The contemporary church has, in many quarters, lost the language of spiritual discipline entirely — afraid that any emphasis on effort sounds like works-righteousness. Paul’s athletic imagery corrects this: grace produces effort; the free gift of the gospel generates the runner’s willingness to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.

Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? Key words. The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. The Corinthians knew athletics well. In a race, only one wins.

So run that you may obtain it. Key words. Run the Christian race with the same intensity as a runner aiming to win. The point is not that only one Christian is saved, but that we should run wholeheartedly.

Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. Key words. Athletes trained for ten months, with strict diet and discipline. “Self-control” (enkrateuomai): they say no to many good things for the sake of the prize.

They do it to receive a perishable wreath. Key words. At the Isthmian Games, the winner’s crown was made of withered celery or pine. It soon decayed.

But we an imperishable. Key words. Our crown is eternal life and glory (2 Timothy 4:8; James 1:12; 1 Peter 5:4). If athletes sacrifice so much for a wilting wreath, how much more should we?

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by effort. The prize is given by grace. But the Christian life is not passive; grace trains us to strive (Philippians 2:12–13; Titus 2:11–12).

In a sentence. You know that in a race many run, but only one takes the prize. Run like that, to win. Athletes in training deny themselves in everything, all for a crown that wilts; we do it for one that will never fade.

On a Tuesday. What would spiritual training look like for you this week: early prayer, Scripture memory, fasting from your phone? Train for the imperishable crown.
verseByVerse.note: The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. Winners received a wreath of pine or dried celery.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.

So I do not run aimlessly. Key words. “Aimlessly” (adēlōs, uncertainly): Paul runs toward a clear finish line.

I do not box as one beating the air. Key words. A shadow-boxer swings at nothing. Paul lands real blows against real enemies.

But I discipline my body and keep it under control. Key words. “Discipline” (hypōpiazō, literally to give a black eye, to strike under the eye). Strong language: Paul treats his own body’s sinful desires as an opponent in the ring. “Keep under control” (doulagōgeō, lead as a slave). His body serves him, not the other way round.

Lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified. Key words. “Preaching” (kēryssō): the herald announced the rules and called the contestants at the Games. “Disqualified” (adokimos, failing the test, rejected). Paul fears the herald might himself be disqualified from the race.

Where Christians differ: could Paul lose his salvation? Some take this as proof that even an apostle could fall away and be lost. Others say disqualified means only losing a reward. Verdict: Paul knows that a person can preach to others and yet prove not to be genuine (Matthew 7:22–23). So he takes his own holiness seriously. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. True believers will not finally be lost (Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6), but they persevere by heeding such warnings, not by ignoring them. Assurance and diligence go together (2 Peter 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil. It means sinful bodily desires must be ruled, not obeyed.

In a sentence. So Paul does not run without a goal, and he does not throw punches at the air. He trains his body hard and makes it serve him, so that after calling others to the race he himself will not be found unfit for the prize.

For worship. Ask God to help you take your own holiness seriously, especially if you teach or lead others.
