10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Paul completes his answer about idol food. The strong in Corinth felt secure: they were baptised, they shared the Lord’s Supper, they knew idols were nothing. Paul warns them with Israel’s story. The whole generation that left Egypt enjoyed God’s privileges: led by the cloud, brought through the sea, fed with manna, given water from the rock, which Paul says was Christ himself. Yet most of them died in the wilderness, because they fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling. Their story was written as a warning for us. Whoever thinks he stands should watch out, though God is faithful and will always provide a way through temptation.

So: flee idolatry. At the Lord’s Supper believers share in Christ’s blood and body and are made one body. Israel’s sacrifices likewise bound worshippers to the altar. Idols are nothing, but behind pagan sacrifice stand demons, and believers cannot share both the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Then Paul gives practical rules. Food bought in the market may be eaten without asking questions, for the earth belongs to the Lord. At an unbeliever’s dinner, eat what is served, unless someone points out that it was sacrificed, and then abstain for the sake of that person’s conscience. In everything, eating or drinking, do all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them of Israel in the exodus. All the people were under the cloud and all passed through the sea; all were, as it were, baptised into Moses in the cloud and the sea; all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. Yet God was displeased with most of them, and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness. These things are examples to warn us not to crave evil as they did: not to be idolaters, as when the people sat down to feast and rose up to revel; not to commit sexual immorality, as when twenty-three thousand died in one day; not to put Christ to the test, as some did and were killed by snakes; and not to grumble, as some did and were destroyed by the destroying angel. These events happened to them as examples and were written down to warn us, on whom the climax of the ages has come. So anyone who thinks he is standing firm should take care not to fall. Every temptation they face is the common lot of humanity, and God is faithful: he will not let them be tested beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that they can endure it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Existent Christ and the Typology of the Wilderness

Paul’s identification of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (v. 4) is a claim that the Son of God was the agent of God’s sustaining grace before the incarnation — the “Angel of the LORD” tradition of the OT now understood christologically. This is christological pre-existence applied to redemptive history: the same Christ who died on the cross was present and active in the wilderness, providing the spiritual sustenance that Israel squandered. Reformed typology has always read the OT this way: Christ is not absent from the old covenant; he is present as promise, type, and mediator.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were attending temple meals — eating idol food in an actual pagan temple — needed to hear that spiritual confidence is not the same as spiritual safety. Israel had more obvious privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: The sacramental Christian who trusts in regular communion and baptism as automatic guarantees of spiritual health — without the disciplined effort, the watchful sobriety, the dependency on God that Paul describes — is making exactly the Israelite mistake. The sacraments are genuine means of grace, not magic shields.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 10 completes Paul’s answer about food offered to idols, and adds a sharp warning. The strong Corinthians felt safe: they had knowledge, baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Paul reminds them of Israel in the wilderness. All Israel had their own baptism and their own spiritual food and drink, with Christ himself present; yet most of them fell in the desert through idolatry, immorality, testing God and grumbling. Their story was written as a warning: let anyone who thinks he stands take care not to fall. Yet God is faithful and always provides a way of escape from temptation (vv. 1–13). So flee idolatry. The Lord’s Supper is a real participation in Christ’s body and blood, and pagan sacrifices are offered to demons; you cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons (vv. 14–22). Then Paul gives practical rules: eat whatever is sold in the market, and what an unbeliever serves you at home, without asking questions; but if someone points out that it was sacrificed, do not eat, for his conscience’s sake. Whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved (vv. 23–33).

For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. Key words. A formula for something important (12:1; Romans 11:25).

That our fathers. Key words. Paul calls Israel our fathers, even when writing to mostly Gentile believers. The church is the continuation of Israel; Israel’s history is the church’s family history (Galatians 3:29).

Were all under the cloud. Key words. The pillar of cloud that guided and protected Israel (Exodus 13:21; 14:19–20). Notice “all” five times in verses 1–4. Every Israelite had these privileges.

And all passed through the sea. Key words. The Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14:21–22), the great act of deliverance.

And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Key words. A picture of baptism. As Christians are baptised into Christ, uniting them to him (Romans 6:3), Israel was joined to Moses as their leader and mediator by passing under the cloud and through the sea. They did not get wet, as the Egyptians did; they went through on dry ground. It was a baptism by union, not by immersion in water.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism automatically saves. That is the very point Paul is about to make: they were all baptised, yet most were destroyed.

In a sentence. Paul wants you to remember, brothers and sisters, that our forefathers were all under the cloud and all went through the sea; all of them were baptised into Moses in the cloud and the sea.

On a Tuesday. Israel’s history is your family history. Read the Old Testament as the story of your own spiritual ancestors.

parallels.desc: the pillar of cloud
through the sea on dry ground

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.

And all ate the same spiritual food. Key words. The manna from heaven (Exodus 16). It was real food, but spiritual because it came from God supernaturally and pointed to Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35).

And all drank the same spiritual drink. Key words. The water from the rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Paul sees manna and water as Israel’s equivalent of the Lord’s Supper.

For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them. Key words. Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness, providing water. Paul does not endorse the legend. He means that the source of their water throughout the journey was the spiritual rock who accompanied them: God himself, often called the Rock (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18; Psalm 78:35).

And the Rock was Christ. Key words. A stunning claim. The pre-incarnate Christ was with Israel in the wilderness, providing for them. Christ is the Rock, the God of Israel (Exodus 17:6 says the LORD stood on the rock). This affirms both Christ’s deity and his eternal pre-existence. Verse 9 confirms it: Israel put Christ to the test.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the physical rock was literally Christ. It means the one who gave them water was Christ, and the rock was a sign of him.

In a sentence. All of them ate the same food from heaven and drank the same God-given drink, for they drank from the spiritual Rock that went with them on their journey, and that Rock was Christ.

For worship. The Christ who gave Israel water in the wilderness gives you living water today. Come and drink (John 7:37).
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul says the true source of their water was Christ.

parallels.desc: bread from heaven
water from the rock

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.

Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased. Key words. The shocking turn. All had the privileges; most perished. Of the adults who left Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb entered the promised land (Numbers 14:29–30). “Not pleased” is an understatement.

For they were overthrown in the wilderness. Key words. “Overthrown” (katastrōnnymi, laid low, strewn about): their bodies were scattered across the desert. From Numbers 14:16.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that all who died in the wilderness went to hell. Moses and Aaron died there too, because of their sin, yet were God’s faithful servants. The point is that privileges without faith and obedience do not protect from God’s judgement.

In a sentence. Yet God was displeased with most of them, and their bodies were left scattered in the desert.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised, taking communion and attending church are great privileges, but they do not save by themselves. Make sure you truly trust Christ.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.

Now these things took place as examples for us. Key words. “Examples” (typoi, types, patterns). These events really happened, and God shaped them to serve as warnings for us.

That we might not desire evil as they did. Key words. “Desire” (epithymētas, cravers). The root of Israel’s sins was craving. In Numbers 11:4–34, they craved meat, despised the manna, and God sent quail and a plague at the place called Graves of Craving. The Corinthians’ craving for temple meals is similar. Sin begins with desire (James 1:14–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament stories are merely moral fables. They are history that teaches.

In a sentence. These things happened as warning pictures for us, so that we would not crave evil the way they did.

For worship. Ask God to help you see your cravings clearly, and to make you content with what he gives.

parallels.desc: the graves of craving

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”

Do not be idolaters as some of them were. Key words. The first of four sins. The golden calf (Exodus 32), at the very foot of Sinai, just after receiving the law.

As it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.” Key words. From Exodus 32:6. They ate a sacrificial feast before the calf and then played, a word that includes dancing and sexual revelry. This is exactly what happened at Corinthian temple feasts: eating, drinking and immorality. Paul chooses a verse that connects idolatry with eating.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feasting or playing is wrong in itself. It means feasting in idol worship is.

In a sentence. Do not worship idols as some of them did; Scripture says, “The people sat down to a feast and then got up to revel.”

On a Tuesday. Watch where your celebrations take you. Do they honour God or something else?

parallels.desc: they sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.

We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did. Key words. The second sin. At Baal-peor, Israelite men had sex with Moabite women, who invited them to the sacrifices of their gods (Numbers 25:1–9). Again idolatry and immorality together.

And twenty-three thousand fell in a single day. Key words. Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul says 23,000 fell in a single day. Both may be true: 23,000 died on one day, and the total including others (such as the leaders executed in Numbers 25:4–5) reached 24,000. Or both are round numbers. This is not a contradiction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the precise number is the point. The point is the scale of God’s judgement on immorality joined to idolatry.

In a sentence. Nor should we commit sexual sin as some of them did, and in a single day twenty-three thousand of them died.

For worship. Thank God that Christ took the judgement our sins deserve. And ask him for strength to flee immorality.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul speaks of those who fell in a single day.

parallels.desc: Israel and the Moabite women

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,

We must not put Christ to the test. Key words. The third sin. “Put to the test” (ekpeirazō, try to the limit): to push God, to see how far you can go before he acts. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.” The better reading is “Christ,” which fits verse 4: Christ was with Israel in the wilderness.

As some of them did and were destroyed by serpents. Key words. In Numbers 21:4–9, the people spoke against God and Moses, complaining about the food. God sent fiery serpents. Those who looked at the bronze serpent lived, a picture of Christ on the cross (John 3:14–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean honest questions to God are wrong. Testing God is defiant presumption: daring him to do something about your sin.

In a sentence. We must not push Christ to see how far we can go, as some of them did and were killed by snakes.

On a Tuesday. Are you testing God, telling yourself that he will not mind just this once? Stop, and turn back.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.”

parallels.desc: fiery serpents among the people

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.

Nor grumble. Key words. The fourth sin. “Grumble” (gongyzō, mutter, complain under the breath). Israel grumbled constantly in the wilderness, against God, Moses and Aaron. Perhaps the Corinthians were grumbling against Paul.

As some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer. Key words. After Korah’s rebellion, the people grumbled, and a plague killed 14,700 (Numbers 16:41–49). The Destroyer (olothreutēs) is the angel of destruction, as at the Passover (Exodus 12:23; Hebrews 11:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cannot express sorrow or lament to God. The psalms are full of honest complaint brought to God. Grumbling is complaining against God, not to him.

In a sentence. And do not complain against God, as some of them did and were wiped out by the destroying angel.

For worship. Turn a complaint into a prayer today. Bring it to God honestly, with trust instead of grumbling.

parallels.desc: the destroyer

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.

Now these things happened to them as an example. Key words. “As an example” (typikōs, typically, as warning patterns).

But they were written down for our instruction. Key words. “Instruction” (nouthesia, warning, admonition). God had them written for us (Romans 15:4).

On whom the end of the ages has come. Key words. Literally, the ends of the ages have arrived. Christians live at the climax of history, where all the previous ages meet their fulfilment in Christ (Hebrews 9:26). We are in the last days.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament has no meaning for its first readers. It means its full purpose is seen in Christ and his church.

In a sentence. These things happened to them as warning pictures, and they were written down to warn us, who live when all the ages have reached their goal.

On a Tuesday. You live in the last days. Read the warnings of Scripture as written to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.

Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. Key words. The great warning. The strong in Corinth thought they stood firm. Self-confidence is the danger. Israel thought their privileges guaranteed safety. “Take heed” (blepō, watch out). Peter is the classic example (Mark 14:29–31).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in fear of losing salvation. It means overconfidence is dangerous, and humble watchfulness is the mark of the true believer.

In a sentence. So if you think you are standing firm, watch out that you do not fall.

For worship. Pray: Lord, keep me from overconfidence. Hold me up, for I cannot stand without you.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. Key words. “Temptation” (peirasmos, testing, trial, temptation). “Common to man” (anthrōpinos, human, ordinary). Your temptations are not unique. Others have faced the same and overcome.

God is faithful. Key words. The foundation of hope (1:9). Not our strength, but God’s faithfulness.

And he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability. Key words. God sets the limits of every temptation (Job 1:12; 2:6). He knows our strength and will not allow more than his grace can enable us to bear.

But with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape. Key words. “Way of escape” (ekbasis, way out, exit, like a pass through mountains). With every temptation, God makes an exit. For the Corinthians, the way out of idolatry was to flee (v. 14).

That you may be able to endure it. Key words. The goal is not always removal of the trial but endurance through it.

Where Christians differ: can believers be overcome? Some take this verse to mean believers never actually fall into sin, or that if they do, they were never really tempted beyond ability. Verdict: God always provides a way to resist, so no believer can say, I had no choice. When believers sin, it is because they did not take the way out, not because God failed. This verse does not promise that believers never fall, but that they never have to. And it promises that God’s faithfulness will see them through (Westminster 17.3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never gives us more than we can handle in suffering. Paul himself was burdened beyond his strength (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). The promise is about temptation to sin: God will always enable us to resist, by his grace.

In a sentence. Every temptation you face is the kind others have faced. And God keeps his word: he will not let you be tempted past what you can bear, but when the temptation comes he will also make a way out, so that you can stand up under it.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes today, look for the way out God has provided. Then take it, quickly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So, dear friends, they must run from idolatry. Paul appeals to their good sense to judge what he says. The cup of blessing believers bless is a sharing in Christ’s blood, and the bread they break is a sharing in Christ’s body; because there is one loaf, they who are many are one body, for they all share the one loaf. Look at Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar. Paul does not mean that idol food or idols are anything in themselves. He means that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons, not to God, and he does not want them to be partners with demons. They cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons, or share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Are they trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Do they think they are stronger than he is?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Participation

Paul’s use of koinōnia in vv. 16–17 — the cup of blessing is a koinōnia in the blood of Christ; the bread is a koinōnia in the body of Christ — is the most precise language of eucharistic participation in the NT. It does not specify the mode of Christ’s presence, but it insists on its reality: something genuinely happens in the Supper that is a real sharing in what Christ accomplished. Reformed eucharistic theology (following Calvin rather than Zwingli) has insisted on this real spiritual presence: Christ is truly present in the Supper, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Attending a civic dinner at a Corinthian temple was not optional for many members of the social elite; it was part of the patronage network on which their livelihood depended. Paul’s “flee idolatry” would have carried genuine social cost. Now: The situations where Christian participation in cultural or civic life involves implicit participation in what is spiritually incompatible are multiple and not always obvious. Paul’s principle — you cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — is the test: what are you actually participating in when you participate in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.

Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. Key words. The way of escape (v. 13). Not negotiate with idolatry, or test how close you can get, but flee (pheugō, as with sexual immorality, 6:18). For the Corinthians, this meant: stop attending temple feasts.

I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. Key words. “Sensible” (phronimoi, wise, thoughtful). The Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom. Paul appeals to it: think it through, and you will see I am right.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only ancient-style idol worship is in view. Anything that takes God’s place is an idol (Colossians 3:5; 1 John 5:21).

In a sentence. So, dear friends, run from idolatry. You are thoughtful people; weigh what Paul says for yourselves.

For worship. Name one idol in your heart. Ask God to help you run from it today.

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.

The cup of blessing that we bless. Key words. “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk at the end of a meal with a prayer of thanksgiving, especially at Passover. At the Last Supper, Jesus took this cup and made it the cup of the new covenant (11:25). “That we bless”: over which we give thanks to God.

Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Key words. “Participation” (koinōnia, sharing, fellowship, communion). To drink the cup is to share in the benefits of Christ’s shed blood: forgiveness and the new covenant.

The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Key words. To eat the bread is to share in Christ himself, crucified for us.

Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. Key words. One loaf, shared by all. The Supper expresses and strengthens the unity of the church. The body of Christ here shifts meaning: from Christ’s crucified body to the church, his body.

For we all partake of the one bread. Key words. All believers share in one Christ, and so are one people.

Where Christians differ: what happens in the Lord’s Supper? Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ’s body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many evangelicals hold a memorial view: the Supper is only a reminder. Verdict: The bread and wine remain bread and wine (11:26–28 still calls it bread). But the Supper is more than a memorial: Paul calls it a real participation in Christ. The Reformed view, taught by Calvin, is that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers, by faith, really feed on Christ spiritually, receiving him and all the benefits of his death. Christ’s body is in heaven, but the Spirit lifts us up to commune with him (Westminster 29.7). Christ is truly present, not physically but spiritually, and truly given to faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a sacrifice repeated. Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14).

In a sentence. When we give thanks over the cup, are we not sharing in Christ’s blood? When we break the bread, are we not sharing in Christ’s body? Since there is one loaf, we, though many, are one body, because we all share that one loaf.

For worship. At the next Lord’s Supper, come expecting to meet Christ. Feed on him by faith, and look around at the one body you belong to.
verseByVerse.note: “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk with thanksgiving at a meal, including the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?

Consider the people of Israel. Key words. Literally, Israel according to the flesh: the nation of Israel in its worship.

Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? Key words. Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God at his altar (Leviticus 7:15; Deuteronomy 12:17–18). Eating meant sharing in the worship, being in fellowship with the God to whom it was offered.

What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? Key words. Paul anticipates an objection: are you saying idols are real after all? No; he still holds what he said in 8:4.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the meat itself is changed or defiled. The issue is the act of worship.

In a sentence. Think of Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in what happens at the altar. So is Paul saying that idol offerings are anything, or that an idol is real?

On a Tuesday. What we take part in shapes our loyalty. Think about which tables you sit at, and what they mean.
verseByVerse.note: Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:17. The idol is nothing, but behind idol worship stand real spiritual forces: demons (daimonia). Pagans think they worship gods; in reality they serve demons.

I do not want you to be participants with demons. Key words. “Participants” (koinōnoi, partners). Eating at a temple feast is fellowship with demons.

You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. Key words. Temple feasts included drinking cups of wine offered to the god. You cannot share Christ’s cup and theirs.

You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Key words. Invitations to dinner at the table of the lord Serapis have been found from this period. The Lord’s Supper is the table of the Lord (Malachi 1:7, 12). Divided loyalty is impossible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be afraid of demons, or think demons lurk in every object. It means deliberate participation in false worship is spiritual adultery.

In a sentence. No, what Paul is saying is that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, not to God, and he does not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the demons’ cup too; you cannot eat at the Lord’s table and at the demons’ table.

For worship. Give your whole loyalty to the Lord’s table. Refuse every other altar.

parallels.desc: they sacrificed to demons that were not God

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:21. God is jealous for his people, as a husband for his wife (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). His jealousy is not petty, but holy love that will not share his bride with rivals. Israel provoked him with idols, and was judged.

Are we stronger than he? Key words. A sharp question for the strong in Corinth. You think you are strong. Are you stronger than God?

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s jealousy is like human jealousy, insecure and envious. It is the right zeal of the only true God for the love of those he redeemed.

In a sentence. Do we really want to stir up the Lord’s jealousy? Do we imagine we are stronger than he is?

On a Tuesday. God loves you too much to share you with rivals. Let that move you to loyalty, not fear.

parallels.desc: they have made me jealous with what is no god

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul quotes the slogan “everything is permitted” and answers that not everything is beneficial or builds others up. No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. They may eat anything sold in the meat market without asking questions for conscience’ sake, because, as the psalm says, the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord. If an unbeliever invites them to dinner and they want to go, they may eat whatever is served without asking. But if someone tells them it was offered in sacrifice, they should not eat it, for the sake of the person who told them and for conscience, his conscience, not theirs. Why should Paul’s freedom be judged by someone else’s conscience, and why be blamed for food he thanks God for? Whether they eat or drink or do anything else, they should do it all for God’s glory. They should give no cause for stumbling to Jews, Greeks or the church of God, just as Paul tries to please everyone in everything, seeking not his own benefit but that of many, so that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
Soli Deo Gloria Applied to Ordinary Life

The Reformation’s fifth great watchword — soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory — finds its Pauline root in v. 31. Every meal, every conversation, every commercial transaction, every athletic effort is capable of being an act of worship when performed in the right spirit and with the right orientation. The Reformed conviction that all of life is worship is the systematic development of this verse. The “sacred/secular divide” is not merely unhelpful; by Paul’s logic it is theologically incoherent: all of life, including the most mundane, is lived before the face of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The practical guidelines of vv. 25–28 gave the Corinthians actionable wisdom for the specific daily situations they faced. The principle of “ask no questions” at the market protected them from unnecessary scrupulosity; the principle of sensitivity at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both together are shaped by the glory of God, not by personal preference. Now: “Do all to the glory of God” is not a cliché but a practice — a habit of asking, in any situation: how can this moment, this act, this conversation, be a participation in the glorification of God?

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.

“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. Key words. The Corinthian slogan again (6:12). Paul now turns to the question of meat at home and in the market, outside the temple.

“All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Key words. “Build up” (oikodomeō): the test of love (8:1). The question is not only, may I? but, will this help others grow?

Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor. Key words. The governing principle. Love looks to others’ interests (Philippians 2:4; Romans 15:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should never care for our own needs. It means our own good must not override our neighbour’s.

In a sentence. “Everything is permitted,” you say, but not everything helps; not everything builds others up. No one should look out only for himself, but for the good of others.

For worship. Ask God: whose good can I seek today?

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”

Eat whatever is sold in the meat market. Key words. The meat market (makellon): Corinth’s central meat and fish market, whose remains have been found. Much of the meat had come from temple sacrifices.

Without raising any question on the ground of conscience. Key words. Do not ask where it came from. It is just food. Once it has left the temple, it carries no religious meaning.

For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.” Key words. From Psalm 24:1, which Jews used as a prayer of thanks before meals. All food belongs to God, not to idols. It can be received with thanks (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean contradicting verses 14–22. There, the issue was taking part in temple worship; here, it is buying ordinary meat.

In a sentence. Eat anything sold in the market without asking questions for conscience’s sake, because the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Thank God before you eat. Every meal is a gift from the Lord who owns the earth.

parallels.desc: the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—

If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go. Key words. In a private home, not a temple. Paul assumes Christians will have unbelieving friends and accept their hospitality. “Disposed to go” (thelō, want to): it is your choice.

Eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. Key words. Do not interrogate your host. Enjoy the meal (Luke 10:8).

But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice.” Key words. The pagan word for sacred offering (hierothyton). Perhaps another guest, or the host, points it out, maybe testing the Christian.

Then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you. Key words. Now eating would send a message: that the Christian approves of idol worship, or does not take his faith seriously. The informer, believer or unbeliever, might be confused or led astray.

And for the sake of conscience. Key words. The other person’s conscience (v. 29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid unbelievers’ homes. Paul encourages friendship. It means once the food is publicly identified as an offering, eating it becomes a statement.

In a sentence. If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat what is served without asking questions of conscience. But if someone tells you, “This was offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the person who told you and for conscience’s sake,

For worship. Thank God for unbelieving friends who invite you in. Pray that your presence at their table will point them to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?

I do not mean your conscience, but his. Key words. Your own conscience is clear; you abstain for the other person’s sake.

For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? Key words. The strong person’s objection, or Paul’s own reasoning: in principle, my freedom is not ruled by others’ scruples. I am still free before God.

If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks? Key words. If I thank God for food, how can anyone condemn me? “Denounced” (blasphēmeō, spoken against, slandered). Paul’s point: I give up my freedom voluntarily, not because the other person’s conscience binds mine, but to avoid having my good thing spoken of as evil (Romans 14:16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean others can control what Christians do. Liberty remains; love chooses how to use it.

In a sentence. Paul means the other person’s conscience, not your own. Why should my freedom be put on trial by someone else’s conscience? If I eat with thanks to God, why should I be condemned for something I thank him for?

On a Tuesday. Your freedom in Christ is real. Use it gladly, and lay it down gladly when love calls for it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

So, whether you eat or drink. Key words. The most ordinary actions of life.

Or whatever you do. Key words. Everything: work, rest, play, speech, spending.

Do all to the glory of God. Key words. The governing purpose of the Christian life. To glorify God (doxa) is to show his worth, to honour him, to make him look as great as he is. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: man’s chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever (Q. 1). No part of life is outside this. The Reformers stressed that ordinary work and meals are as sacred as prayer when done for God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must be constantly thinking about God in every second. It means our whole life is offered to him, done in a way that honours him.

In a sentence. So whatever you do, even eating and drinking, do everything for God’s glory.

For worship. At your next meal, pause and give thanks. Then eat to the glory of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.

Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God. Key words. “Give no offence” (aproskopoi, not causing stumbling). Three groups covering all people: Jews, Gentiles and Christians. Do not put an unnecessary obstacle in anyone’s way.

Just as I try to please everyone in everything I do. Key words. Not people-pleasing for approval (Galatians 1:10), but accommodating for their good (9:19–22).

Not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved. Key words. The goal is the salvation of others. Paul’s whole life is shaped by it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding the offence of the cross (1:23). The gospel itself offends; we must not add needless offence of our own.

In a sentence. Do not trip up Jews, Greeks or God’s church, just as Paul tries to accommodate everyone in all he does, looking not to his own benefit but to the benefit of many, so that they may be saved.

For worship. Pray for someone you want to see saved. Ask God to show you how to remove obstacles between them and Christ.

For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.<sup>5</sup>Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.<sup>6</sup>Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.<sup>7</sup>Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”<sup>8</sup>We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.<sup>9</sup>We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,<sup>10</sup>nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.<sup>11</sup>Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.<sup>12</sup>Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.<sup>13</sup>No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. I do not want you to be participants with demons.<sup>21</sup>You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.<sup>22</sup>Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?<sup>23</sup>“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up.<sup>24</sup>Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.<sup>25</sup>Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>26</sup>For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”<sup>27</sup>If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience.<sup>28</sup>But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—<sup>29</sup>I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience?<sup>30</sup>If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?<sup>31</sup>So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.<sup>32</sup>Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God,<sup>33</sup>just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.

11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapters 11–14 deal with problems in the church’s gatherings. The first concerns how men and women appear when they pray or prophesy. In the Roman world clothing and hair sent strong signals. A respectable married woman covered her head in public with a veil or the fold of her mantle; going uncovered could suggest immodesty or rebellion, and shaving a woman’s head was a mark of disgrace. Men, by contrast, did not cover their heads, except in some pagan rituals where Roman priests sacrificed with the toga drawn over the head. Some Corinthian women, perhaps reasoning that in Christ distinctions no longer mattered, were praying and prophesying uncovered. Paul grounds his answer in creation and in the order of headship, God, Christ, man, woman, while insisting that in the Lord men and women depend on each other.

The second problem was worse. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared evening meal in a wealthy member’s house. The host’s friends reclined in the small dining room and ate the best food early; latecomers, often slaves who had worked all day, crowded into the courtyard with little or nothing. Some went hungry while others got drunk. Paul says this is not the Lord’s Supper at all. He repeats the account of the Last Supper that he received from the Lord, reminds them that the meal proclaims Christ’s death until he returns, and warns that eating in an unworthy way, despising Christ’s body, brings judgement. They must examine themselves and wait for one another.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to follow his example as he follows Christ’s, and praises them for holding to the traditions he passed on. But he wants them to understand that Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. A man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head, and a woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours hers; it is as shameful as having her head shaved, so if she will not cover it she might as well cut off her hair. A man should not cover his head, since he is God’s image and glory, while the woman is the glory of man, for woman came from man and was created for him. So a woman should have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels. Yet in the Lord neither is independent of the other: woman came from man, but every man is born of woman, and everything comes from God. Paul asks them to judge for themselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray uncovered, and points to nature: long hair is a disgrace to a man but a glory to a woman, given her as a covering. If anyone wants to argue, the churches of God have no other practice.
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, Order, and the Trinity

Paul’s grounding of the male-female relationship in the Father-Son relationship (v. 3) is one of the most important and most debated texts in trinitarian theology. If “the head of Christ is God” describes an eternal subordination within the Godhead, it supports a permanent hierarchical ordering of human relationships. Most Reformed theologians have understood this as describing the economic Trinity (the Son’s voluntary submission in the incarnation and redemption) rather than ontological subordination within the immanent Trinity. Either way, Paul is using the divine relational order as the theological model for the ordering of human relationships in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific head covering practice was an expression of propriety and social order in a particular cultural context. A woman praying with her head uncovered may have signalled sexual availability or a rejection of the social ordering that the community needed to maintain for the sake of its witness. Now: The head covering practice is not directly applicable in most modern Western contexts. The underlying principle — that worship should reflect an ordered dignity appropriate to the God being worshipped, and that the differentiation of male and female is a gift to be honoured rather than erased — continues to speak into contemporary debates about gender in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 11 begins Paul’s teaching on public worship, which runs through chapter 14. Verse 1 closes chapter 10: imitate Paul as he imitates Christ. Then Paul addresses two problems in their gatherings. First, men and women praying and prophesying (vv. 2–16). Some Corinthian wives were throwing off the head covering, the visible sign in that culture of a married woman’s honour and her relation to her husband. Paul grounds his answer in an order God established: Christ is the head of every man, the husband is the head of his wife, God is the head of Christ. That order comes from creation, and is not cancelled by the gospel, though in the Lord men and women depend on each other completely. Second, the Lord’s Supper (vv. 17–34). The rich were eating and drinking their fill while the poor went hungry, turning the Supper into a display of social division. Paul reminds them of what the Lord himself handed down: the bread and cup proclaim his death until he comes. To eat in a way that despises his body is to eat judgement on oneself. So examine yourselves, and wait for one another.

Be imitators of me. Key words. “Imitators” (mimētai). The conclusion of chapters 8–10: follow Paul’s pattern of giving up rights for the good of others (9:19–23; 10:33).

As I am of Christ. Key words. The qualification and the source. Paul imitates Christ, who did not please himself (Romans 15:3), who gave up everything for others (Philippians 2:5–8). Imitate Paul only so far as he imitates Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any leader can demand blind following. All human examples are measured by Christ.

In a sentence. Follow Paul’s example, as he follows the example of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Find a mature Christian whose life follows Christ, and learn from them. And live so that someone younger can learn from you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.

Now I commend you because you remember me in everything. Key words. Paul begins with praise. Perhaps the Corinthians’ letter claimed they remembered his teaching, and Paul accepts it generously, before correcting where they had gone wrong.

And maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you. Key words. “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them. The word (paradosis) means what is handed over. “Delivered” (paradidōmi) is the technical term for passing on authoritative teaching (as in 11:23; 15:3). These traditions came from the Lord through the apostles, and are now preserved in the New Testament.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church traditions not found in Scripture have equal authority with Scripture. Paul’s traditions are apostolic teaching, which we now have in written form (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Later church traditions must be tested by Scripture.

In a sentence. Paul praises you for remembering him in everything and for holding to the teachings just as he passed them on to you.

For worship. Thank God for the apostolic teaching handed down to you in Scripture. Hold it fast.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.

But I want you to understand. Key words. A new teaching they had not grasped.

That the head of every man is Christ. Key words. “Head” (kephalē). In this context, head means one with authority and responsibility, as in Ephesians 1:22 and 5:23. Some argue it means source, as the source of a river. Both ideas may be present, since verses 8–9 speak of origin. But in Paul’s usage, headship includes leadership.

The head of a wife is her husband. Key words. The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean woman and wife, man and husband. The context, with its focus on the married woman’s head covering, suggests husband and wife. The husband has a God-given responsibility to lead his wife in love (Ephesians 5:23–25).

And the head of Christ is God. Key words. The Son, as incarnate Mediator, submits to the Father (15:28; John 5:19, 30; 14:28). Yet the Son is fully equal with the Father (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). This is the key to the whole passage: headship and submission do not imply inferiority. Christ is not less than God because he submits to the Father; a wife is not less than her husband because she submits to him.

Where Christians differ: headship. Egalitarians argue that head means only source, and that Christ’s coming abolished all role distinctions between men and women. Verdict: Paul grounds this order in creation (vv. 8–9), not in culture or the fall, and compares it with the relation of the Father and the Son. Men and women are equal in worth, dignity and salvation (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7). But God has given husbands the responsibility to lead their families, and qualified men the responsibility to lead and teach in the church (1 Timothy 2:12–13). This is the complementarian view: equal in being, distinct in role. Husbands must lead as Christ leads: by sacrificial love, not domination.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every woman must submit to every man. The headship here is in marriage (and, by extension, the church). It never justifies harshness or abuse.

In a sentence. But Paul wants you to understand that Christ is the head of every man, the husband is the head of his wife, and God is the head of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, lead your wives as Christ leads you: with love that serves. Wives, respect your husbands as the church honours Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife.”

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.

Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. Key words. In public worship, a man covering his head would dishonour his physical head and his spiritual head, Christ. Roman men sometimes pulled their togas over their heads during pagan sacrifices; Paul may have that in mind.

But every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head. Key words. In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and her honour as a wife; to remove it in public could suggest she was unattached or immoral. Her physical head and her husband were both shamed. Notice: Paul assumes women do pray and prophesy in some setting of worship.

Since it is the same as if her head were shaven. Key words. A shaved head was a sign of disgrace for a woman, perhaps associated with punishment for adultery or with certain pagan practices.

Where Christians differ: women praying and prophesying. How does this fit with 14:34 (women should keep silent in the churches) and 1 Timothy 2:12? Verdict: Women may pray and contribute in the church’s life, and in New Testament times some prophesied (Acts 21:9). What is reserved for qualified men is the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church (14:29, 34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12). Since prophecy as new revelation has ceased with the closing of the canon, the question today concerns praying, sharing and teaching; women serve in many ways, but the office of elder and the authoritative preaching of the church belong to qualified men.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are spiritually inferior or have nothing to contribute. Paul expects them to pray and prophesy.

In a sentence. A man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head; and a wife who prays or prophesies with her head bare shames her head, as much as if her head were shaved.

For worship. Men and women both pray to God in his church. Thank God for the prayers of the women in your congregation.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and married status. Christians differ on how the principle applies today.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.

For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. Key words. Paul argues: if you want to go uncovered, go all the way and cut your hair.

But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. Key words. Since that would be shameful, keep the covering.

For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. Key words. From Genesis 1:26–27. Man was made in God’s image and reflects God’s glory.

But woman is the glory of man. Key words. Paul does not say woman is not God’s image; Genesis 1:27 says both male and female are. He says woman is the glory of man: she was made from man and for him (vv. 8–9), and she brings him honour as the crown of creation (Proverbs 12:4; Genesis 2:23). Glory here means that which honours and displays another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women do not bear God’s image or that their glory is only derived. Both sexes bear God’s image equally. Paul is speaking of their relation within creation’s order.

In a sentence. If a wife will not cover her head, she might as well cut off her hair; but if it is shameful for her to have her hair cut or shaved, she should cover her head. A man should not cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.

On a Tuesday. Whether man or woman, you were made to display God’s glory. Live today in a way that honours him and those he has joined you to.

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.

For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Key words. From Genesis 2:21–23. Eve was formed from Adam’s side.

Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. Key words. From Genesis 2:18. God made Eve as a helper fit for Adam. Helper (Hebrew ʿezer) is not a lesser word; it is often used of God himself as Israel’s help (Psalm 33:20). It describes a role, not inferiority.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women exist only to serve men, or that men owe women nothing. Verses 11–12 balance this immediately. Paul is grounding headship in creation, which means it is not merely cultural but reflects God’s design.

In a sentence. Man did not come from woman; woman came from man. And man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man.

For worship. Thank God for his wise design in creating man and woman, different and fitted for each other.

parallels.desc: a helper fit for him; she shall be called Woman

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.

That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head. Key words. Literally, authority on her head. The covering is a sign of her husband’s authority, and perhaps also a sign of her own authority to pray and prophesy in worship, under that order.

Because of the angels. Key words. The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present in worship (Psalm 138:1, in the Greek: before the angels I will sing your praise). They observe God’s order in the church (4:9; Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12), and perhaps are offended when it is disregarded. Some think it refers to the angels who rebelled against their proper place (Jude 6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean angels lust after women, as some ancient interpreters suggested from Genesis 6. The more likely meaning is that angels watch over worship.

In a sentence. For this reason, and because the angels are watching, a wife should wear on her head a sign of authority.

On a Tuesday. When you worship, the angels are present. Worship with reverence and order.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present at worship and to guard God’s order.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.

Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman. Key words. A vital balance. In the Lord, in Christ’s new community, men and women need each other completely. Neither can exist or serve without the other.

For as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. Key words. Eve came from Adam, but every man since has come from a woman, his mother. Mutual dependence.

And all things are from God. Key words. Ultimately both come from God, who designed them and gave them to each other. No room for pride on either side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean headship is cancelled in the Lord. Paul holds both: an order of headship and a deep mutual interdependence.

In a sentence. Yet in the Lord woman is not independent of man, nor man of woman. Just as woman came from man, so every man is born of a woman, and everything comes from God.

For worship. Thank God for the men and women in your life, and in your church, on whom you depend.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.

Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Key words. Paul appeals to their sense of what is fitting (prepō).

Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him. Key words. “Nature” (physis): the natural order of things as people generally sense it, perhaps the instinctive sense of what is masculine and feminine. In Greek and Roman culture, long hair on men was associated with effeminacy.

But if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? Key words. Long hair was considered a woman’s beauty and dignity.

For her hair is given to her for a covering. Key words. Nature itself gives women a covering. The head covering in worship follows that natural pattern.

Where Christians differ: must women wear head coverings today? Some churches require head coverings in worship today; most do not. Verdict: The principle is permanent: the distinction between men and women, and the husband’s headship, rooted in creation, should be honoured in worship. The specific form, a head covering, was the cultural expression of that principle in first-century Corinth, where an uncovered married woman sent a message of shame or rebellion. Where coverings carry no such meaning, the principle should be expressed in other ways: modest dress, and clear distinctions between men and women. Christians who wear coverings out of conviction should be respected.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is a precise rule on hair length. It means men and women should not try to erase the God-given distinction between them.

In a sentence. Decide for yourselves: is it fitting for a wife to pray to God bareheaded? Doesn’t the very nature of things teach you that long hair is a shame for a man but a glory for a woman? For long hair has been given to her as a covering.

For worship. Thank God for making you a man or a woman. Honour that distinction with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.

If anyone is inclined to be contentious. Key words. “Contentious” (philoneikos, fond of quarrelling, loving to win arguments). Paul expects some to argue.

We have no such practice, nor do the churches of God. Key words. No such practice: no practice of women praying with uncovered heads, or of contentiousness. The churches everywhere follow this pattern. Corinth must not go its own way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every church practice must be identical everywhere. It means churches should not break from apostolic patterns in order to be different.

In a sentence. If anyone wants to argue about this, we have no other custom, and neither do the churches of God.

On a Tuesday. Avoid being the person who loves to argue. Seek the peace and unity of the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Paul has no praise for them, because their meetings do more harm than good. He hears that when they gather there are divisions, and he partly believes it; there have to be differences, so that those who are genuine stand out. When they meet, it is not really the Lord’s Supper they eat, because each person goes ahead with his own meal, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk. Do they not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do they despise God’s church and humiliate those who have nothing? Paul will certainly not praise them for this.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Enacted Gospel Equality

Paul’s critique of the Corinthian Supper is grounded in his theology of the cross. The Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26) — the death in which the rich Son of God became poor for the sake of the poor, in which the Lord washed his disciples’ feet, in which social distinctions were overcome in the one body given for all. A Supper that reinforces social stratification is not merely socially unkind; it is a contradiction of what is being enacted. The body and blood of Christ at the table cannot be participated in rightly by those who simultaneously despise the members of his body gathered around the table.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The patronage culture of Roman Corinth structured even the shared meal around social hierarchy: the wealthy ate better food in the inner room; clients and dependents got lesser portions in the outer rooms. The Corinthians had imported this structure wholesale into the church’s gathering. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the place where the social equalisations of the gospel are most visibly enacted — or most visibly denied. The church where wealth, race, or education creates a gradient of welcome and participation has committed the Corinthian error at its most fundamental level.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.

But in the following instructions I do not commend you. Key words. A contrast with verse 2. Here Paul has no praise.

Because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. Key words. Their gatherings were doing more harm than good. A shocking verdict on a church’s worship.

For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. Key words. “Divisions” (schismata, as in 1:10). Here the divisions are social: rich and poor.

And I believe it in part. Key words. Paul is cautious about reports.

For there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized. Key words. “Factions” (haireseis, from which heresies, parties). “Genuine” (dokimoi, tested and approved). Paul speaks with irony and realism: in God’s providence, divisions expose who is truly faithful.

What it does not mean. It does not mean factions are good. Paul condemns them. It means God can use even divisions to show who is true.

In a sentence. In the following instructions Paul has no praise for you, for your meetings do more harm than good. First, he hears that when you gather as a church there are divisions among you, and to some extent he believes it. No doubt there have to be differences among you to show which of you have God’s approval.

On a Tuesday. Ask: does my church’s gathering leave people better or worse? What can I do to make it better?

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.

Setting and background. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal, sometimes called the love feast (Jude 12). The wealthy hosted the church in their homes. In Roman dining custom, the host’s high-status friends reclined in the dining room with the best food, while lower-status guests ate in the courtyard with lesser food. The wealthy, who could arrive early, were starting without the slaves and labourers, who came after work and found little left.

When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. Key words. They called it the Lord’s Supper, but in reality it was their own supper. The Lord’s meal had become a private party.

For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. Key words. “Goes ahead” (prolambanō, takes beforehand, devours). Each ate his own food without sharing.

One goes hungry, another gets drunk. Key words. The poor went hungry; the rich drank too much.

What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Key words. If you want a private feast, have it at home.

Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? Key words. Their behaviour despised the church, God’s people, and shamed the poor. Social snobbery at the Lord’s table is contempt for God’s church.

What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not. Key words. No praise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never share meals in church. It means the Lord’s Supper must not be turned into a display of social division.

In a sentence. When you meet, it is not really the Lord’s Supper you are eating, because each of you rushes ahead with his own food, so one goes hungry while another gets drunk. Don’t you have homes for eating and drinking? Or do you look down on God’s church and shame those who have nothing? What can Paul say? Should he praise you? Certainly not for this.

For worship. At the Lord’s table, rich and poor stand equal before Christ. Come with humility, and look out for others.
verseByVerse.note: The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal. The wealthy, free to arrive early, ate and drank before poorer members — often slaves — could come after work.

parallels.desc: your love feasts

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul passes on what he received from the Lord. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me.” After supper he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; whenever you drink it, do this in remembrance of me.” Every time they eat this bread and drink this cup, they proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. So anyone who eats or drinks in an unworthy way will be guilty of sinning against the Lord’s body and blood. Each person should examine himself before eating and drinking, because whoever eats and drinks without recognising the body eats and drinks judgement on himself. That is why many of them are weak and sick, and some have died. If they judged themselves properly, they would not come under judgement. When the Lord judges, he disciplines them so that they will not be condemned with the world. So when they gather to eat, they must wait for one another. Anyone who is hungry should eat at home, so that their meetings do not lead to judgement. Paul will give further instructions when he comes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Real Presence and the Reformed Understanding of the Supper

Calvin’s eucharistic theology, developed precisely in dialogue with this passage, insisted on a genuine but spiritual presence of Christ in the Supper — against both the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (physical transformation of the elements) and Zwingli’s pure memorialism (the Supper as merely symbolic). Paul’s language of “participation” (10:16) and “proclaiming the Lord’s death” (11:26) supports a real, active, communicative presence of Christ at the table — where Christ genuinely gives himself to be received by faith, and where genuine nourishment of the soul takes place through the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian abuse of the Supper — reducing it to a social meal stratified by class — was the practical outworking of their failure to grasp the gospel. When you understand that Christ died equally for the rich and the poor in your community, you cannot eat well while they starve at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the church’s most powerful enacted proclamation of the gospel — which is why its abuse is so serious, and why its right practice (the community gathered equally around the cross) is so significant as a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. Key words. This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, written about AD 54, before the Gospels. “Received” and “delivered” are technical terms for handing on tradition (15:3). From the Lord: the teaching originates with Jesus himself, passed on through the apostles.
