That the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed. Key words. “Betrayed” (paradidōmi, handed over: the same word as “delivered”). On the night he was handed over to death, he handed this meal to his church. The Supper is rooted in history.

Took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it. Key words. “Given thanks” (eucharisteō, from which the word Eucharist). Jesus followed the Passover pattern of giving thanks over bread.

And said, “This is my body, which is for you.” Key words. “For you” (hyper hymōn, on your behalf): his body given in death for us, in our place. This is substitution.

“Do this in remembrance of me.” Key words. “Remembrance” (anamnēsis): not just recalling, but calling to mind in a way that makes the past event present in its power, as Israel remembered the Exodus at Passover (Exodus 12:14; Deuteronomy 16:3).

Where Christians differ: “This is my body.” Roman Catholics take “is” literally: the bread becomes Christ’s body (transubstantiation). Lutherans say Christ’s body is present in and with the bread. Zwinglians say it is purely a symbol. Verdict: Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said it; the disciples could not have understood him to mean the bread had become his body. Jesus often spoke in metaphors: I am the door, I am the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). The bread signifies his body. But it is not an empty sign: through it, by the Spirit and through faith, believers truly receive and feed on Christ (10:16; Westminster 29.7). Christ is spiritually and really present to faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a re-sacrifice of Christ. He was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28).

In a sentence. What Paul handed on to you came from the Lord himself: on the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, given for you. Do this to remember me.”

For worship. At the table, remember: his body was given for you. Receive him with thanks.
verseByVerse.note: This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

In the same way also he took the cup, after supper. Key words. The third cup of the Passover meal, the cup of blessing (10:16), drunk after the main meal.

Saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood.” Key words. The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31–34: God’s law written on hearts, everyone knowing the Lord, sins forgiven and remembered no more. Covenants were sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8). Christ’s blood ratifies the new covenant (Hebrews 9:15–22).

“Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.” Key words. The Supper is to be repeated regularly. As often: Paul does not say how often. Some churches celebrate it weekly, others monthly or quarterly.

Where Christians differ: how often? Some churches hold the Supper weekly, believing that was the apostolic practice (Acts 20:7). Others hold it less often, to preserve its solemnity. Verdict: Scripture does not command a frequency. The early church seems to have celebrated it each Lord’s Day, and Calvin wished for weekly communion. Frequent celebration is a great blessing, as long as it is done with understanding and self-examination, not mechanically.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cup contains Christ’s literal blood. It signifies and seals the new covenant in his blood.

In a sentence. In the same way, after supper he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant sealed with my blood. Whenever you drink it, do it to remember me.”

On a Tuesday. You belong to the new covenant: your sins are forgiven and remembered no more. Live in that freedom today.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup. Key words. Paul’s comment on the words of Jesus. Notice it is still called bread after the blessing.

You proclaim the Lord’s death. Key words. “Proclaim” (katangellō, announce, preach). The Supper is a visible sermon. Without words, it declares: Christ died for sinners. The Reformers called the sacraments visible words.

Until he comes. Key words. The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the return. It is a meal for the time between, until we eat with him in his kingdom (Matthew 26:29; Revelation 19:9). Every celebration is a prayer: Come, Lord Jesus (16:22).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper replaces preaching. Word and sacrament go together; the Supper confirms the word.

In a sentence. Every time you eat this bread and drink this cup, you are announcing the Lord’s death until he comes back.

For worship. At the table, look back to the cross and forward to his coming. Proclaim his death, and long for his return.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner. Key words. “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating, despising the poor and treating the meal carelessly, not to whether the person is worthy. No one is worthy of the Supper by merit. It is for sinners who trust Christ. “In an unworthy manner” is an adverb: it describes the manner, not the person.

Will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord. Key words. “Guilty” (enochos, liable, answerable). To treat the Supper with contempt is to sin against the one it represents, as if siding with those who crucified him (Hebrews 6:6; 10:29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sinless people may come, or that struggling believers should stay away. The table is for repentant sinners. The danger is coming carelessly or in unrepentant sin.

In a sentence. So anyone who eats the bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way that dishonours him will be answerable for sinning against the Lord’s body and blood.

On a Tuesday. Do not stay away from the table because you feel unworthy. Come as a sinner trusting Christ. Stay away only if you refuse to repent.
verseByVerse.note: “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating — despising the poor — not to whether the individual was worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.

Let a person examine himself. Key words. “Examine” (dokimazō, test, prove). Before coming, look honestly at your heart: Do I trust Christ? Am I repenting of known sin? Am I at peace with my brothers and sisters (Matthew 5:23–24)? Am I coming to honour Christ and his body?

Then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. Key words. The point of self-examination is not to keep away, but to come rightly. Examine, then eat.

Where Christians differ: who may come to the table? Some churches practise open communion, inviting anyone; others closed communion, inviting only members of that church or denomination. Verdict: The table is for baptised believers who trust Christ, are not under church discipline, and examine themselves. Churches should explain this clearly and invite all such believers, whatever their congregation. Unbelievers and those living in unrepentant sin should be lovingly warned not to partake (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 173). This is called fencing the table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you must achieve perfect assurance before coming. Weak faith is still faith. The Supper is given to strengthen it.

In a sentence. Each person should test himself before he eats the bread and drinks the cup.

For worship. Before the next Supper, take time to examine yourself in prayer. Confess, forgive, and then come gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.

For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body. Key words. “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, understanding what it means, or recognising the church as Christ’s body, which the Corinthians were despising by humiliating the poor (v. 22; 10:17). Both fit the context; perhaps Paul means both. To eat without recognising that the meal is about Christ’s body given for us, and that it makes us one body, is to eat wrongly.

Eats and drinks judgment on himself. Key words. “Judgement” (krima): not necessarily eternal condemnation, but God’s judgement in the form of discipline, as the next verse shows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the bread and wine are magically dangerous. It means God takes seriously how his people treat his table and his church.

In a sentence. For anyone who eats and drinks without recognising the Lord’s body brings judgement on himself by doing so.

On a Tuesday. When you take the Supper, remember the body of Christ given for you, and the body of Christ around you: your brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as his body.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. Key words. A startling statement. God’s discipline had come on the Corinthians in the form of illness and even death. “Died” is literally fallen asleep, the Christian word for believers’ death (15:18, 20).

But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. Key words. “Judged ourselves” (diakrinō, discerned, assessed). If we examined ourselves honestly and repented, God would not need to discipline us.

But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined. Key words. “Disciplined” (paideuō, trained, as a father trains a child, Hebrews 12:5–11). God’s judgement on his people is fatherly correction, not final condemnation.

So that we may not be condemned along with the world. Key words. The purpose of discipline is to keep believers from final condemnation. Even the death of some Corinthian believers was discipline, taking them home rather than letting them go on dishonouring Christ; they were not condemned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every illness is a punishment for sin. Scripture warns against that assumption (John 9:2–3; Job). But it does mean that God sometimes disciplines his people through physical affliction.

In a sentence. That is why many of you are weak and sick, and a number of you have died. If we were honest in judging ourselves, we would not come under judgement. But when the Lord judges us, he is disciplining us, so that we will not be condemned with the world.

For worship. Thank God that his discipline is a Father’s love, keeping you from final condemnation. Respond to it with repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. Key words. The practical solution. “Wait for” (ekdechomai, receive, welcome, wait for). Do not start until all have arrived, and share with one another. The poor and slaves who came late must be welcomed.

If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home. Key words. If you cannot wait, eat beforehand. The church meal is not for satisfying appetite at others’ expense.

So that when you come together it will not be for judgment. Key words. Gathering should bring blessing, not discipline.

About the other things I will give directions when I come. Key words. There were other issues about the Supper that Paul would deal with in person. Not everything was written down, but everything necessary was (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean churches must separate the Lord’s Supper from fellowship meals. But many churches did so later, partly to avoid such abuses.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, when you gather to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that your meetings do not lead to judgement. Paul will sort out the other matters when he comes.

On a Tuesday. Wait for one another: notice who arrives late or sits alone at church. Make room for them.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.<sup>2</sup>Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.<sup>3</sup>But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.<sup>4</sup>Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,<sup>5</sup>but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.<sup>6</sup>For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head.<sup>7</sup>For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.<sup>8</sup>For man was not made from woman, but woman from man.<sup>9</sup>Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.<sup>10</sup>That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.<sup>11</sup>Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman;<sup>12</sup>for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.<sup>13</sup>Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered?<sup>14</sup>Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him,<sup>15</sup>but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.<sup>16</sup>If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.<sup>17</sup>But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.<sup>18</sup>For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part,<sup>19</sup>for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.<sup>20</sup>When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.<sup>21</sup>For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.<sup>22</sup>What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.<sup>23</sup>For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread,<sup>24</sup>and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”<sup>25</sup>In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”<sup>26</sup>For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.<sup>27</sup>Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.<sup>28</sup>Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.<sup>29</sup>For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.<sup>30</sup>That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.<sup>31</sup>But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged.<sup>32</sup>But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.<sup>33</sup>So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—<sup>34</sup>if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. The Corinthians were especially impressed by dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, and treated them as marks of superior spirituality. Their pagan background explains some of this. Greek religion prized ecstatic experience: the prophetess at Delphi spoke in a trance, and the worship of Dionysus involved frenzy. Being carried away was taken as a sign of the divine. Paul begins with a test that has nothing to do with excitement: the Spirit always leads people to confess that Jesus is Lord.

Then he insists that the gifts are many but the giver is one, the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God, and that every gift is given for the good of the whole church, not for individual display. He uses the familiar picture of the body, a common image in ancient politics for a community whose members must cooperate. In Corinth the picture had a local twist: at the temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, worshippers left clay models of the body parts they wanted healed, hands, feet, eyes, ears, and many have been dug up. Paul says the church is one body with many parts, all baptised by one Spirit. No member can say it does not belong, and none can say it does not need the others; the weaker parts are indispensable, and all share suffering and honour. God has placed gifts in the church as he chose, and not everyone has the same gift. They should seek the greater gifts, and Paul is about to show them a better way still, the way of love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not want them to be ignorant about spiritual gifts. They remember that as pagans they were swept along and led off to speechless idols. So he gives a test: no one speaking by God’s Spirit says “Jesus is cursed”, and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit. There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit; different kinds of service, but the same Lord; different kinds of working, but the same God works all of them in everyone. To each person the Spirit is shown in some way for the common good. To one the Spirit gives a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another faith, to another gifts of healing, to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish spirits, to another different kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes them to each person as he decides.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

The explicit trinitarianism of vv. 4–6 is remarkable as a casual structural feature of Paul’s argument: he assumes the Trinity without arguing for it. Reformed pneumatology has always grounded the discussion of spiritual gifts in this trinitarian framework: the gifts are not the Spirit’s autonomous productions but the common work of Father, Son, and Spirit. This prevents both the elevation of the Spirit over Christ (a common charismatic error) and the neglect of the Spirit’s ongoing work (a temptation in cessationist circles): all genuine gifts are simultaneously the work of the triune God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian believers were apparently competing for the most impressive gifts, using spiritual gifts as social capital. Paul’s trinitarian grounding removes the competition from its foundation: you cannot boast in a gift that was sovereignly given to you by the Spirit who gives as he wills. Now: The same gift-competitive dynamic operates in charismatic and Reformed communities alike, in different directions: charismatics sometimes elevate dramatic gifts (tongues, healing) over quiet ones; cessationists sometimes elevate intellectual gifts (teaching, wisdom) over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both hierarchies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 12–14 answers the Corinthians’ question about spiritual gifts. They prized the spectacular gifts, especially speaking in tongues, as signs of spiritual superiority, and this was dividing and disordering the church. Chapter 12 lays the foundation. The test of the Spirit’s work is not ecstasy but the confession that Jesus is Lord (vv. 1–3). The gifts are many but come from one Spirit, one Lord, one God; each is given for the common good, and the Spirit distributes them as he wills (vv. 4–11). The church is one body with many members, all baptised by one Spirit into it. Every part is needed, the weaker and less honoured most of all, so that there is no division but mutual care (vv. 12–26). God has appointed different gifts and roles; not all are apostles, not all speak in tongues. Desire the greater gifts, those that most build up, and Paul will show the way that surpasses them all: love (vv. 27–31).

Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers. Key words. “Spiritual gifts” is literally spiritual things or spiritual people (pneumatika). The Corinthians’ word, perhaps, for the gifts they valued. Paul will use charismata, grace-gifts (v. 4), shifting the focus from spirituality to grace.

I do not want you to be uninformed. Key words. They thought they knew about spiritual things. Paul says they need teaching.

You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols. Key words. “Mute” (aphōna, voiceless): idols cannot speak (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18). Yet pagan worship was full of ecstatic speech and frenzy, especially in the cults of Dionysus. Being carried away by powerful spiritual experiences is not proof of the Holy Spirit.

However you were led. Key words. “Led” (agō, carried off, driven). They had been swept along by forces beyond their control. The Holy Spirit does not work by mindless compulsion (14:32).

What it does not mean. It does not mean all strong experiences are demonic. It means experience alone is not the test. The test is what it says about Jesus.

In a sentence. Now about the gifts of the Spirit, brothers and sisters, Paul does not want you to be ignorant. You remember that when you were pagans you were swept off, in one way or another, to idols that cannot speak.

On a Tuesday. Do not judge spirituality by how intense it feels. Judge it by whether it honours Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore I want you to understand. Key words. The first test of genuine spiritual activity.

That no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” Key words. “Accursed” (anathema). Perhaps some in ecstatic speech, or some unbelievers in synagogues, cursed Jesus (Acts 26:11). Whatever the source, the Holy Spirit never speaks against Christ.

And no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions (Romans 10:9; Philippians 2:11). To say it sincerely, submitting to Jesus as God and master, requires the Spirit’s work. Every believer who confesses Jesus as Lord has the Spirit. There are no second-class Christians without the Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who mouths the words has the Spirit (Matthew 7:21–23). It means sincere confession is the Spirit’s work. The mark of the Spirit is a Christ-centred life, not spectacular gifts.

In a sentence. So Paul wants you to know that no one speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can truly say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.

For worship. If you can say “Jesus is Lord” from your heart, thank the Holy Spirit. He is at work in you.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.

Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. Key words. “Varieties” (diaireseis, distributions, different allotments). “Gifts” (charismata, grace-gifts). The Spirit gives them.

And there are varieties of service, but the same Lord. Key words. “Service” (diakoniai, ministries). The gifts are for serving, under one Lord, Jesus.

And there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone. Key words. “Activities” (energēmata, workings, effects). God the Father works through all.

The Trinity. Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God. Each person of the Trinity is involved in every gift. Unity in diversity in the church reflects unity in diversity in God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts, services and activities are three separate categories. They are three ways of describing the same thing: gifts of grace, used in service, by God’s power.

In a sentence. There are different kinds of gifts, but one Spirit gives them; different kinds of service, but one Lord is served; different kinds of working, but one God is at work in all of them in everyone.

For worship. Thank the Father, the Son and the Spirit for every gift in your church, including those very different from yours.
verseByVerse.note: Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

To each is given. Key words. Every believer has received at least one gift. No one is left out. “Is given”: received, not earned.

The manifestation of the Spirit. Key words. “Manifestation” (phanerōsis, display, showing). Each gift is a way the Spirit shows himself at work.

For the common good. Key words. “Common good” (sympherō, for benefit, what helps). Gifts are not for personal display, status or private enjoyment. They are given to serve others. This is the key to chapters 12–14.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer has a spectacular gift. Many gifts are quiet: helping, giving, showing mercy (Romans 12:6–8).

In a sentence. To every believer the Spirit shows himself through some gift, given for the good of all.

On a Tuesday. Your gift is not for you. Ask: who in my church needs what God has given me?

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,

For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom. Key words. A word of wisdom (logos sophias): the ability to speak God’s wisdom, applying the gospel to life (2:6–7).

And to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit. Key words. A word of knowledge (logos gnōseōs): the ability to explain the truths of the faith. Probably close to teaching. The Corinthians loved knowledge (8:1).

To another faith by the same Spirit. Key words. Not saving faith, which all believers have, but a special gift of faith: confidence in God for great things, wonder-working faith (13:2; Matthew 17:20).

To another gifts of healing by the one Spirit. Key words. Plural: gifts of healings. The ability to bring God’s healing in specific cases, as the apostles did (Acts 3:6–8; 5:15–16; 28:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts, or that each person has only one. Paul gives several lists, all different (Romans 12; Ephesians 4; 1 Peter 4).

In a sentence. To one person the Spirit gives a message of wisdom, to another, by the same Spirit, a message of knowledge, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit,

For worship. Thank God for those in your church who speak wisely and explain the faith clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.

To another the working of miracles. Key words. Literally, workings of powers (energēmata dynameōn): acts of power beyond healing, such as Paul blinding Elymas (Acts 13:11) or raising Eutychus (Acts 20:9–12).

To another prophecy. Key words. Speaking a message revealed by God for the church’s strengthening, encouragement and comfort (14:3).

To another the ability to distinguish between spirits. Key words. Discerning which messages and powers are from God and which from false spirits (1 John 4:1). Prophecies needed testing (14:29).

To another various kinds of tongues. Key words. Speaking in languages one has not learned (Acts 2:4–11), by the Spirit. Listed last here, perhaps deliberately, since the Corinthians ranked it first.

To another the interpretation of tongues. Key words. The ability to explain what was spoken in a tongue, so the church could understand (14:13, 27–28).

All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills. Key words. The Spirit decides. “As he wills” (bouletai): the Spirit is a person with a will, not a force. No one can demand a particular gift or boast in having one.

Where Christians differ: do the miraculous gifts continue? Continuationists hold that all these gifts are available today. Verdict: The gifts of miracles, healings, prophecy and tongues served as signs confirming the apostolic message while Scripture was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation of apostles and prophets laid and the canon closed, these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased as ordinary gifts in the church. God still heals in answer to prayer and does wonders as he pleases, and the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, faith, discernment, teaching, serving and mercy continue. This cessationist view is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters, with whom we share the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God no longer works powerfully. It means his normal way now is through the word, prayer and the ordinary gifts.

In a sentence. to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All of these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who gives them to each person as he chooses.

On a Tuesday. Accept the gifts the Spirit has given you, without envy of others’ gifts. He chose wisely.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The body is one, though it has many parts, and so it is with Christ. All believers, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, were baptised by one Spirit into one body and were all given the one Spirit to drink. The body is not one part but many. If the foot said it does not belong because it is not a hand, it would still belong; if the ear said it does not belong because it is not an eye, it would still belong. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell? God has placed each part in the body just as he wanted. If all were one part, there would be no body. As it is, there are many parts but one body. The eye cannot tell the hand it does not need it, nor the head the feet. In fact the parts that seem weaker are essential, the parts we think less honourable we treat with more honour, and our less presentable parts are treated with more modesty, while the presentable ones need no special care. God has put the body together, giving greater honour to the parts that lacked it, so that there should be no division in the body, but its parts should care equally for each other. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part shares its joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Ecclesiology and Soteriology United

Paul’s body metaphor is not merely sociological (a useful way to describe community life) but soteriological: the church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised all believers into the one body of the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real — not metaphorical — which is why the suffering of one member is genuinely felt by the whole (v. 26). The theology of the body of Christ is the foundation of Paul’s entire ethic of community: you cannot be indifferent to the suffering of a fellow member of Christ’s body any more than your left hand can be indifferent to the pain in your right foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had produced both contempt (the tongues-speakers dismissing those with lesser gifts) and despair (those with lesser gifts feeling excluded). Paul’s body metaphor addresses both directly: the despairers are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church community has its impressive and its unimpressive members by the world’s standards. Paul’s insight is that the one who seems indispensable and the one who seems marginal are both placed by the same God — and the functioning of the body requires both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.

For just as the body is one and has many members. Key words. The analogy that fills the rest of the chapter. One body, many parts.

So it is with Christ. Key words. Paul does not say so it is with the church, but with Christ. The church is so united to Christ that it is his body (v. 27; Ephesians 1:22–23).

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. Key words. “In one Spirit” (or by one Spirit). All believers were baptised by the Spirit into the body of Christ at conversion. “All”: even the immature, quarrelsome Corinthians. This is the Spirit’s work of uniting us to Christ, of which water baptism is the sign.

Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. Key words. The deepest divisions of the ancient world, ethnic and social, are overcome in the one body (Galatians 3:28).

And all were made to drink of one Spirit. Key words. The Spirit is like water poured out and drunk (John 7:37–39; Isaiah 44:3). All believers have drunk deeply of him.

Where Christians differ: baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals often teach that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues. Verdict: Paul says all believers, including the immature Corinthians, were baptised in the one Spirit into the one body. Spirit baptism happens at conversion; it is the Spirit’s work of joining us to Christ and his body. It is not a second blessing for some. Believers may and should seek to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), which is different from the once-for-all baptism in the Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean water baptism unites us to Christ by itself. The Spirit does; water baptism signifies and seals it.

In a sentence. A body is one unit made of many parts, and though its parts are many they form one body; so it is with Christ. For we were all baptised by one Spirit into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given the one Spirit to drink.

For worship. Thank God that you were baptised by the Spirit into Christ’s body, together with believers of every race and class.

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.

For the body does not consist of one member but of many. Key words. Diversity is essential to a body.

If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body.” Key words. The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united society; the Roman Menenius Agrippa told a famous fable of the body’s parts rebelling. Paul uses it first to address those who feel inferior: the foot envying the hand, the ear envying the eye.

That would not make it any less a part of the body. Key words. Your feelings of inferiority do not change the fact that you belong. Those without spectacular gifts are no less part of Christ’s body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feelings of inadequacy are sinful. It means they are untrue. Every believer belongs.

In a sentence. The body is made of many parts, not one. If the foot says, “I am not a hand, so I don’t belong to the body,” it does not stop being part of the body. And if the ear says, “I am not an eye, so I don’t belong to the body,” it does not stop being part of the body.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you have nothing to offer your church, you are wrong. You belong, and you are needed.
verseByVerse.note: The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united community.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?

If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? Key words. A comic picture: a giant eyeball. A church where everyone had the same gift would be a monster.

If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell? Key words. Diversity is not a problem to be fixed; it is necessary. A church full of tongue-speakers, or preachers, or anyone else, would not function.

What it does not mean. It does not mean some gifts are unimportant. It means all are necessary.

In a sentence. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell?

For worship. Thank God that your church is not made of people just like you.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.

But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. Key words. “Arranged” (tithēmi, placed, set). God designed the body and put each member where he wanted it. Your place in the church is God’s decision, not an accident (v. 11).

If all were a single member, where would the body be? Key words. A single member is not a body.

As it is, there are many parts, yet one body. Key words. Unity and diversity together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you cannot grow in your gifts or seek new ways to serve. It means you should accept your place with contentment.

In a sentence. But in fact God has placed every part in the body just as he wanted. If all were one part, there would be no body. As it is, there are many parts and one body.

On a Tuesday. God has put you exactly where he wants you in his church. Serve there gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”

The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you.” Key words. Now Paul addresses the opposite problem: those who feel superior. The gifted eye looking down on the hand.

Nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.” Key words. The head, the most honoured part, cannot dismiss the feet. The spectacularly gifted cannot do without the ordinary members.

What it does not mean. It does not mean head here refers to Christ, the head of the church. Paul is using the physical body as an analogy.

In a sentence. The eye cannot tell the hand, “I don’t need you,” and the head cannot tell the feet, “I don’t need you.”

For worship. Confess any pride that looks down on others in your church. Thank God for those you have overlooked.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,

On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable. Key words. The weakest-seeming parts, internal organs perhaps, are the ones you cannot live without. In the church, those who seem weakest may be the most vital: the prayer warriors, the faithful elderly, the quietly serving.

And on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor. Key words. We clothe some parts more carefully. “Honour” here may mean clothing.

And our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty. Key words. The private parts are covered with special care.

Which our more presentable parts do not require. Key words. The face needs no covering.

But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it. Key words. “Composed” (synkerannymi, blended, mixed together). God deliberately designed the body so that the less honoured get more honour. So in the church, God honours the lowly (1:27–28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should despise the gifted. It means we should give special honour to those the world overlooks.

In a sentence. On the contrary, the parts that seem weaker are the ones we cannot do without, and the parts we regard as less honourable we treat with special honour; the parts we keep private we treat with special modesty, while the presentable parts need no such care. God has put the body together so as to give greater honour to the parts that lacked it,

On a Tuesday. Find the overlooked person in your church this Sunday and honour them.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.

That there may be no division in the body. Key words. “Division” (schisma, as in 1:10; 11:18). God’s design of the body aims at unity.

But that the members may have the same care for one another. Key words. “Care” (merimnaō, be concerned for). Each member cares for the others equally.

If one member suffers, all suffer together. Key words. When you stub a toe, the whole body hurts. When one believer suffers, the whole church should feel it (Romans 12:15; Hebrews 13:3).

If one member is honored, all rejoice together. Key words. When one is honoured, the whole body shares the joy, without envy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we feel every pain automatically. It means love makes us feel with others, and acts on it.

In a sentence. so that there should be no split in the body, but each part should have equal concern for the others. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part shares in its joy.

For worship. Pray today for a suffering member of your church. And rejoice with one who has been blessed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them plainly that they are Christ’s body, and each one of them is a part of it. God has placed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and different kinds of tongues. Are all apostles, prophets or teachers? Do all work miracles, have gifts of healing, speak in tongues or interpret? Obviously not. So they should eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now Paul will show them the most excellent way of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The list of gifts in vv. 28–30, with its implied ordering (first, second, third), suggests that Paul does see a hierarchy of value in gifts — not because some are intrinsically superior but because some are more directly edifying for the whole community. Apostles and prophets lay the doctrinal foundation; teachers expound it; the other gifts serve the body in various ways. But the “still more excellent way” of chapter 13 is not a further gift above tongues and prophecy; it is the character quality that makes the exercise of any gift genuinely excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had inverted the hierarchy: tongues (the most self-focused gift in Paul’s analysis) was being treated as the most prestigious. Paul’s list puts tongues last. The correction is not to dismiss tongues but to reorder values: gifts that build the community outrank gifts that edify only the speaker. Now: The principle applies in every community: the gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up the body has missed what gifts are for. The “excellent way” is available to every gift-user who submits his gift to love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.

Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. Key words. The application. You, the Corinthian church, are Christ’s body. Each of you is a part.

And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. Key words. “Appointed” (tithēmi, the same word as v. 18). A ranked list. Apostles: the foundational witnesses of Christ (Ephesians 2:20). Prophets: those who spoke revelation in the early church. Teachers: those who explained the faith. These three word ministries come first because they build the church most.

Then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues. Key words. Helping (antilēmpseis, acts of assistance): care for the needy. Administrating (kybernēseis, steering, like a ship’s pilot): leadership and guidance. Tongues come last. The Corinthians had the order upside down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that those with lower-ranked gifts are less valuable as persons. The ranking concerns how much each gift builds up the church (14:5).

In a sentence. You are Christ’s body, and each of you is one of its parts. In the church God has placed first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and of different kinds of tongues.

On a Tuesday. Value the ministry of the word in your church. Pray for your teachers. And honour those who help and administer behind the scenes.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Key words. Each question in Greek expects the answer no. Not everyone has the same gift.

Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Key words. No.

Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Key words. No. Not every Christian speaks in tongues.

Where Christians differ: tongues as the evidence of the Spirit. Some Pentecostal groups teach that speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of being baptised in the Spirit. Verdict: Paul’s question expects the answer: no, not all speak in tongues. Yet all were baptised in the Spirit (v. 13). So tongues cannot be the required evidence of Spirit baptism. The evidence of the Spirit is confessing Jesus as Lord (v. 3) and the fruit of the Spirit, above all love (Galatians 5:22–23; 1 Corinthians 13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts are unimportant. It means no single gift is for everyone, or proves spiritual status.

In a sentence. Is everyone an apostle? Is everyone a prophet or a teacher? Does everyone work miracles or heal? Does everyone speak in tongues or interpret? Of course not.

For worship. Thank God for the gift he gave you, and stop comparing it with others’.

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

But earnestly desire the higher gifts. Key words. “Earnestly desire” (zēloō, be zealous for). The higher gifts are those that build up the church most, such as prophecy and teaching (14:1–5). The church as a whole should seek them. Some read it as a statement: you are eagerly desiring the supposedly greater gifts; but Paul will show a better way.

And I will show you a still more excellent way. Key words. “More excellent” (kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond comparison, surpassing). Not another gift, but the way in which all gifts must be used: love. This introduces chapter 13.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is a gift for some. It is the way for all.

In a sentence. Be eager for the gifts that do the most good. And now Paul will show you a way that is better than all of them.

On a Tuesday. Seek gifts that build others up. But above all, seek love.

If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?<sup>18</sup>But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.<sup>19</sup>If all were a single member, where would the body be?<sup>20</sup>As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.<sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”<sup>22</sup>On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,<sup>23</sup>and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,<sup>24</sup>which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,<sup>25</sup>that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another.<sup>26</sup>If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.<sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.<sup>28</sup>And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.<sup>29</sup>Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?<sup>30</sup>Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?<sup>31</sup>But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
This famous chapter is often read at weddings, but it was written to rebuke a quarrelsome, proud church that valued spectacular gifts above everything. Paul sets it between his teaching on gifts in chapters 12 and 14, as the “more excellent way” in which every gift must be used. The Greek word for love here, agapē, was rare in ordinary Greek; the Christians filled it with new meaning from the love God showed in Christ. Read the chapter with Jesus’ name in place of “love” and it describes him; read it with your own name and it shows how far you fall short.

First Paul shows that love is essential. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, even giving away everything or sacrificing one’s body, are worth nothing without love. Then he describes love in action, mostly by what it does not do, and almost every phrase corrects something in Corinth: envy, boasting, arrogance, rudeness, self-seeking. Finally he shows that love lasts. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge are partial and temporary, suited to the present age, like a child’s speech or a dim reflection in a bronze mirror. When the complete arrives, at Christ’s return, they will give way to seeing God face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Paul could speak every human language and even the language of angels, but had no love, he would be no more than a noisy gong or a clashing cymbal. If he had the gift of prophecy and understood every mystery and all knowledge, and had faith enough to move mountains, but had no love, he would be nothing. If he gave away everything he owned and handed over his body to hardship, but had no love, he would gain nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Aquinas, following Augustine, called love (caritas) the form of all virtues — the quality without which no virtue is genuinely virtuous. Paul’s three strophes make the same point: spiritual gifts without love are not merely incomplete but negated. Reformed theology has grounded this in the law of love (Matt 22:37–40): the whole law is fulfilled in love, and therefore the whole Christian life, including the exercise of spiritual gifts, finds its telos and criterion in love. The gift that is not exercised in love has been severed from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-speaker who exercised his gift in a public meeting, leaving the congregation uninstructed and himself privately edified, was exhibiting Paul’s noisy gong in practice. The spiritual trophy was real; the love was absent; the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than the people he is preaching to, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he is arguing with, the worship leader who loves the experience he generates more than the congregation he is leading — all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 13 is the most famous chapter on love ever written, but it is not a wedding poem; it is a rebuke to a gifted, proud, divided church, set in the middle of Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts. It has three movements. First, without love, even the greatest gifts and sacrifices are worthless: tongues become noise, prophecy and knowledge and faith amount to nothing, and giving everything away gains nothing (vv. 1–3). Second, love is described in action, fifteen verbs that read like a portrait of Christ and a mirror held up to the Corinthians: patient, kind, not envious, boastful, arrogant, rude, selfish, irritable or resentful; rejoicing in truth, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring all things (vv. 4–7). Third, love lasts forever. The gifts are for this age and will pass away when the perfect comes; now we see dimly, then face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love (vv. 8–13). The word throughout is agapē: self-giving love that seeks the good of others, the love God showed in Christ.

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels. Key words. Paul starts with the gift the Corinthians prized most. The tongues of angels: perhaps what some Corinthians believed they spoke in ecstatic speech. Even if Paul could speak every human and heavenly language,

But have not love. Key words. Love (agapē): not mainly a feeling, but a self-giving commitment to another’s good, defined by God’s love in Christ (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9–10).

I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. Key words. Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship, especially in the cults of Cybele and Dionysus. Corinth was famous for its bronze. Tongues without love are just noise, no better than pagan racket.

And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge. Key words. Prophecy, the gift Paul ranks highest (14:1), and complete understanding of God’s truth.

And if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains. Key words. Wonder-working faith (12:9; Matthew 17:20).

But have not love, I am nothing. Key words. Not just the gift is nothing, but I am nothing. A gifted person without love is spiritually zero.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts do not matter. Paul has just urged them to desire the higher gifts (12:31). It means gifts without love have no value before God.

In a sentence. If Paul could speak every human language and even the speech of angels, but had no love, he would be only a booming gong or a crashing cymbal. If he could prophesy, understand every mystery and know everything, and had faith enough to move mountains, but had no love, he would be nothing.

On a Tuesday. You may be gifted, knowledgeable and busy for God. Ask honestly: is it all done in love?
verseByVerse.note: Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.

If I give away all I have. Key words. “Give away” (psōmizō, dole out in morsels, feed). Giving all one’s possessions, piece by piece, to feed the poor.

And if I deliver up my body to be burned. Key words. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body that I may boast.” The manuscript evidence is close. Burned fits the idea of martyrdom; boast fits the Corinthian pride. Either way, the ultimate sacrifice of self.

But have not love, I gain nothing. Key words. Even generosity and martyrdom can be done for pride, reputation or self-justification. Without love, they profit nothing before God (Matthew 6:1–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving and sacrifice are bad. It means motive matters. God looks at the heart.

In a sentence. If Paul gave everything he had to the poor and even handed over his body to the flames, but did it without love, he would gain nothing.

For worship. Ask God to purify your motives. Give and serve out of love for him and others, not for recognition.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body [to death] that I may boast.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love is patient and kind. It is not envious, boastful or proud. It does not behave disgracefully, does not seek its own advantage, is not easily provoked, and keeps no record of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing but is glad when truth wins. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes and always perseveres.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Christological Description

The point deserves full weight: replace “love” in vv. 4–7 with “Jesus Christ” and the sentences remain true. Christ is patient — he waited thirty years before beginning his public ministry; he bore with his disciples for three years; he endured the cross. Christ is kind — he touched lepers, welcomed children, ate with sinners. Christ does not insist on his own way — “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Christ does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth. Christ bears all things, believes all things (his faith was perfect toward the Father), hopes all things (the joy set before him, Heb 12:2), endures all things (the cross). Love is not primarily a commandment to be obeyed but a Person to be united with — and as Christ is formed in us (Gal 4:19), his character becomes our character.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth. Every community that reads 1 Corinthians 13 should see itself in it — not as an aspiration but as a diagnostic. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? The catalogue of love’s character is simultaneously a catalogue of the community’s failures. Now: The most powerful apologetic for Christianity in the twenty-first century is not a philosophical argument but a community that actually loves this way — that bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The watching world knows what love looks like; it is waiting to see if the church produces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant

Love is patient. Key words. “Patient” (makrothymeō, long-tempered): slow to anger, putting up with people who wrong you. God is patient with sinners (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9). Notice Paul describes love with verbs, not adjectives: love acts.

And kind. Key words. “Kind” (chrēsteuomai, be useful, gracious): actively doing good to others. Patience endures injury; kindness repays it with good.

Love does not envy. Key words. “Envy” (zēloō, be jealous). The Corinthians envied each other’s gifts (3:3). Love rejoices in others’ blessings.

Or boast. Key words. “Boast” (perpereuomai, brag, show off): parading oneself. The Corinthians boasted in their gifts and leaders.

It is not arrogant. Key words. “Arrogant” (physioō, puffed up), the Corinthians’ besetting sin (4:6, 18–19; 5:2; 8:1). Love is humble.

A portrait of Christ. Every quality here was perfectly shown by Jesus. You can put his name in place of love and the sentences remain true: Jesus is patient and kind. Put your own name in, and you see how far you fall short, and how much you need him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love tolerates everything. It means love responds to others with patience, kindness and humility.

In a sentence. Love is patient and kind. Love does not envy and does not show off; it is not proud,

On a Tuesday. Who tests your patience? Be patient and kind to them today, deliberately.

parallels.desc: love covers all offences

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;

Or rude. Key words. “Rude” (aschēmoneō, behave disgracefully, improperly). The Corinthians were behaving shamefully at the Lord’s Supper (11:21–22) and in worship.

It does not insist on its own way. Key words. Literally, it does not seek its own things. The heart of love: not self-seeking (10:24, 33; Philippians 2:4). The strong were insisting on their rights.

It is not irritable. Key words. “Irritable” (paroxynomai, provoked, easily angered, touchy).

Or resentful. Key words. Literally, it does not count up the wrong. “Resentful” (logizetai to kakon, keep a record of wrongs). Logizomai is the accounting word used for righteousness being credited (Romans 4). Love does not keep a ledger of offences. God does not count our sins against us (2 Corinthians 5:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean love ignores serious sin or abuse. Love confronts sin for the person’s good (Galatians 6:1). But it does not nurse grudges.

In a sentence. and does not behave badly. It is not selfish, not quick to take offence, and keeps no list of wrongs.

For worship. Is there a record of wrongs you are keeping against someone? Tear it up before God, as he has torn up yours.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.

It does not rejoice at wrongdoing. Key words. “Wrongdoing” (adikia, unrighteousness). Love takes no pleasure in sin, whether its own or others’. It does not enjoy gossip about others’ failures. The Corinthians were proud even of the man living with his stepmother (5:2).

But rejoices with the truth. Key words. Love is glad when truth prevails: the truth of the gospel and truthful living. Love and truth go together (Ephesians 4:15; 2 John 1–3). Love is not opposed to truth; it delights in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is soft on doctrine. Love rejoices in truth, and so it cares that people believe and live the truth.

In a sentence. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but is glad whenever the truth wins.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s sin, refuse to enjoy it. When you hear of someone’s faithfulness, rejoice.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

Love bears all things. Key words. “Bears” (stegō, covers, protects, like a roof; or puts up with). Love covers others’ faults rather than exposing them (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12), and carries burdens. Paul used the same word of himself in 9:12.

Believes all things. Key words. Not gullibility, but a readiness to think the best, to give the benefit of the doubt. Love does not assume the worst motives.

Hopes all things. Key words. Love does not give up on people. It keeps hoping for their good, because it trusts God’s power to change them.

Endures all things. Key words. “Endures” (hypomenō, stands firm under pressure). Love keeps going when it is hard, persecuted or rejected. Christ endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is naive, or must stay in danger, or must believe lies. All things means in every situation, love keeps bearing, trusting, hoping and enduring, within the bounds of truth and wisdom.

In a sentence. Love always shelters, always trusts, always hopes, and always keeps going.

For worship. Thank Christ that he bore all things, believed, hoped and endured, for you. Ask for that love in your heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love never fails. Prophecies will come to an end, tongues will stop, and knowledge will pass away, because our knowledge and our prophecy are only partial, and when completeness comes, the partial will be done away with. When Paul was a child he talked, thought and reasoned like a child, but when he became a man he put childish ways behind him. At present we see only a blurred reflection in a mirror, but then we shall see face to face. Now Paul knows in part; then he will know fully, just as he is fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of them is love.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatology of the Gifts and the Permanence of Love

Paul’s teaching that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away is often taken as the foundation of the cessationist argument — the gifts being provisional for an age of incomplete revelation and superseded when the perfect comes. Whether the perfect means the completion of the New Testament canon, the maturity of the church, or the return of Christ has been debated for centuries; but Paul defines his own terms in verse 12, where then is when we see face to face and know fully even as I have been fully known. Since no one began to see God face to face when the canon closed, this passage by itself does not settle the question, and the stronger arguments for cessation are made from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4 rather than from here. Those arguments are the stronger.

What the passage does settle is the structure: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever. A church that pours its energy into the spectacular while neglecting love has it exactly backwards, clinging to the provisional and letting go of the permanent — and that is true of every party to the argument, whichever side it takes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian community that prized tongues above all else was, on Paul’s analysis, investing heavily in something that would not survive the transition to the coming age, while neglecting the one quality that would. Now: The church that is rich in programmes, gifts, and spiritual activity but thin in genuine love has the Corinthian problem in contemporary dress. Every spiritual tradition — charismatic, Reformed, liturgical — can produce communities that are impressively gifted and loveless. Paul’s word is the same to all of them: love never ends; everything else is provisional.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.

Love never ends. Key words. “Ends” (piptō, falls, fails). Love never collapses or becomes obsolete. It will continue into eternity, because God is love (1 John 4:8).

As for prophecies, they will pass away. Key words. “Pass away” (katargeō, be done away with, rendered inoperative).

As for tongues, they will cease. Key words. “Cease” (pauō, stop).

As for knowledge, it will pass away. Key words. The same word as prophecy. Our present partial knowledge will be replaced by full knowledge.

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge itself ends in heaven. We will know more, not less (v. 12). It means the present gift of partial knowledge will give way to something far greater.

In a sentence. Love will never fail. But prophecies will come to an end, tongues will stop, and knowledge will be set aside.

On a Tuesday. Invest in what lasts. Gifts will end; love never will.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.

For we know in part and we prophesy in part. Key words. Even the best present gifts give only partial understanding.

But when the perfect comes. Key words. “The perfect” (to teleion, the complete, the goal reached). “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things at Christ’s return, when we see him face to face (v. 12).

The partial will pass away. Key words. When the complete arrives, the incomplete is no longer needed.

Where Christians differ: what is “the perfect”? Some cessationists argue that the perfect is the completed New Testament canon, so that tongues and prophecy ceased when Scripture was finished. Continuationists argue that since the perfect is Christ’s return, the gifts must continue until then. Verdict: The perfect is best understood as the return of Christ and the age to come, when we will see face to face and know fully. This verse says that these gifts will certainly end by then; it does not say whether some of them might end sooner. The case for the cessation of the revelatory and sign gifts rests on other texts: the foundational and unrepeatable role of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), the confirmation of the apostolic message by signs (Hebrews 2:3–4), and the closing of the canon (Jude 3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Scripture is partial or imperfect. Scripture is complete and sufficient for this age (2 Timothy 3:16–17). But our knowledge, even with Scripture, is partial compared to seeing Christ.

In a sentence. Our knowledge is incomplete and our prophesying is incomplete; but when completeness comes, what is incomplete will be done away with.

For worship. Long for the day when the perfect comes and you see Christ. Pray, Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things when Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.

When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. Key words. An illustration. A child speaks, thinks and reasons in limited, immature ways. That is right for a child.

When I became a man, I gave up childish ways. Key words. “Gave up” (katargeō, the same word as pass away in vv. 8, 10). The present gifts are like childhood speech compared with the maturity of the age to come. There may also be a gentle rebuke: the Corinthians, proud of tongues, were acting like children (3:1; 14:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gifts are childish or bad. They are right for this stage, as childhood speech is right for a child.

In a sentence. As a child Paul talked, thought and reasoned like a child. When he grew up, he left childish ways behind.

On a Tuesday. Grow up in love. Leave behind childish attitudes: sulking, competing, showing off.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.

For now we see in a mirror dimly. Key words. Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect image. Corinth was known for its bronze mirrors. “Dimly” (en ainigmati, in a riddle, an enigma). Now we see God truly but indirectly, through his word and works, like a reflection.

But then face to face. Key words. As God spoke to Moses face to face, not in riddles (Numbers 12:8). At Christ’s return we will see him as he is (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). This is the beatific vision, the great hope of the Christian.

Now I know in part; then I shall know fully. Key words. “Know fully” (epiginōskō, know thoroughly). Our knowledge will be complete, not infinite as God’s is, but without the distortions and gaps of the present.

Even as I have been fully known. Key words. God already knows us completely (8:3; Galatians 4:9). One day we will know him as truly as he now knows us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become God or know everything. We will always be creatures. But we will know God directly and truly.

In a sentence. For now we see only a dim reflection, as in a metal mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now Paul knows in part; then he will know fully, just as he is already fully known.
