What it does not mean. It does not mean the cross alone has no significance. It means the cross and resurrection belong together; the resurrection shows the cross worked.

In a sentence. More than that, we would be shown to be false witnesses about God, for we have testified that God raised Christ, which he did not do if the dead are not raised. If the dead are not raised, Christ was not raised either; and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is worthless and you are still guilty of your sins.

For worship. Because Christ is raised, you are not in your sins. Rejoice in your forgiveness today.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.

Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. Key words. If there is no resurrection, believers who have died are simply gone. No reunion, no future. Every Christian funeral would be a lie.

If in Christ we have hope in this life only. Key words. If Christianity offers only benefits for this life: meaning, morals, community.

We are of all people most to be pitied. Key words. Christians give up pleasures, face persecution, and stake everything on a future life. If there is no resurrection, they have been fooled and have wasted their lives. Paul does not accept that Christianity is worth it merely as a helpful way of life. It is true, or it is pitiable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christianity has no benefits in this life. It does. But they are not the main point.

In a sentence. Then those who have died believing in Christ are lost. If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we deserve more pity than anyone in the world.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one whose hope reaches beyond this life. What would you do differently if you truly believed in the resurrection?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first portion of the harvest of those who have died. Since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in turn: Christ first, then, at his coming, those who belong to him. Then the end will come, when he hands the kingdom over to God the Father after destroying every rule, authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Scripture says God has put everything under his feet; this plainly does not include God himself, who put everything under Christ. When all things have been subjected to him, the Son himself will also be subject to the one who put everything under him, so that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Adam/Christ Typology and the Scope of Redemption

The Adam/Christ typology here (cf. Rom 5:12–21) is the cornerstone of Paul’s understanding of both sin and salvation. Adam’s representative headship means that his sin brought death to all who are “in Adam” — which is every human being by natural birth. Christ’s representative headship means that his obedience, death, and resurrection bring life to all who are “in Christ” — which is every believer by the new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: “in Christ shall all be made alive” refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being universally. The typology demands that the domain of redemption be at least as real and significant as the domain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had lost members to death needed to know that those deaths were not permanent losses but sleeps awaiting a harvest. The firstfruits language gave them a specific, liturgically resonant image: the resurrection of Christ is God’s pledge that the full harvest of resurrection is coming. Now: The Christian stands at the graveside of a believer with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared; the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who made the pledge. The resurrection is not a hope against hope but a certainty grounded in a historical event.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead. Key words. The great turning point. Not if, but in fact (nyni de, but now). Christ is risen.

The firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. Key words. The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–14). The feast of firstfruits fell on the day after the Sabbath following Passover, the very day Christ rose. His resurrection is the first part of the great harvest; ours will follow.

For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. Key words. Death came through Adam’s sin (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12). Resurrection comes through Christ, a man. Christ had to be truly human to undo what a human did.

For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. Key words. Two heads of humanity. All who are in Adam, every natural human, die. All who are in Christ, united to him by faith, will be made alive in resurrection glory.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Universalists read “all” in both halves the same way: as all die in Adam, all humans will be saved in Christ. Verdict: The two “alls” are defined by in Adam and in Christ. All who are in Adam die; all who are in Christ, those who belong to him (v. 23), will be made alive to glory. Paul is not saying every human will be in Christ. Scripture is clear that some will rise to judgement and eternal punishment (John 5:28–29; Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Paul here speaks only of the resurrection to life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers will not be raised at all. All will rise, some to life, some to judgement (Acts 24:15). This chapter focuses on believers.

In a sentence. But Christ really has been raised from the dead, the first part of the harvest of those who have died. Since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes through a man too. As everyone joined to Adam dies, so everyone joined to Christ will be made alive.

For worship. Christ is the firstfruits. Your resurrection is as certain as his. Praise him.
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come — at the time of the Passover festival.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.

But each in his own order. Key words. “Order” (tagma, rank, a military term for a company of soldiers). There is a sequence.

Christ the firstfruits. Key words. First, Christ’s resurrection, already accomplished.

Then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Key words. Second, at his coming (parousia, arrival, the word for a king’s visit), all believers will be raised. Those who belong to Christ: believers only. This happens at one event, his return.

Then comes the end. Key words. “The end” (to telos): the goal, the consummation of history.

When he delivers the kingdom to God the Father. Key words. Christ, having completed his work as Mediator, hands the kingdom to the Father.

After destroying every rule and every authority and power. Key words. Every power opposed to God: spiritual forces of evil, human rebellion, and death itself.

Where Christians differ: the millennium. Premillennialists see a gap between his coming (v. 23) and the end (v. 24), filled by a thousand-year earthly reign of Christ. Verdict: The most natural reading is that the end follows Christ’s coming directly. Christ is reigning now (v. 25), from heaven, and will reign until his return, when the dead are raised and death is destroyed. This is the amillennial view: the millennium of Revelation 20 describes Christ’s present reign during the church age. There is one return of Christ, visible and public, not a secret rapture followed by a later coming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule ends. He hands the kingdom over in the sense that his mediatorial work is complete, but he reigns forever with the Father (Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15).

In a sentence. But each in proper order: Christ, the firstfruits; then, when he comes, those who belong to him. Then the end will come, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, having destroyed every ruler, authority and power.

On a Tuesday. Every evil power you see is on borrowed time. Christ will destroy them all. Take courage.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. Key words. From Psalm 110:1, the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament: the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool. Christ is reigning now, at the Father’s right hand (Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 10:12–13). “Must” (dei): it is God’s plan. His reign is now, not only in the future.

The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Key words. “Destroyed” (katargeitai, abolished, rendered powerless). Death is an enemy, not a friend or a natural process to be welcomed. Christ has already defeated it by his resurrection; at his return it will be abolished entirely (Revelation 20:14; 21:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not grieve death. Death is an enemy, and Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb (John 11:35). But we grieve with hope.

In a sentence. For Christ must go on reigning until he has put every enemy under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death.

For worship. Christ is reigning now. And death, your last enemy, will be destroyed. Praise him.

parallels.desc: until I make your enemies your footstool

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.

For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” Key words. From Psalm 8:6, about God giving humanity dominion over creation. Christ, the true man and last Adam, fulfils it (Hebrews 2:6–9).

But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. Key words. All things except God the Father, who did the subjecting.

When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him. Key words. The Son, as Mediator, will hand his completed work to the Father and remain subject to him.

That God may be all in all. Key words. The goal of history: God’s rule complete and unchallenged, filling everything (Ephesians 1:23; Colossians 3:11).

Where Christians differ: is the Son inferior to the Father? Arians, ancient and modern, use this verse to argue that the Son is a lesser being. Verdict: The subjection here is of the Son as incarnate Mediator, in his role of redemption, not of the Son in his divine nature. In his divine nature, the Son is equal with the Father, of the same substance (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). In his role as Mediator, he submits to the Father’s will (John 6:38). This is the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, as summarised in the Nicene Creed and Westminster 2.3 and 8.2.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s kingdom will end, or that he will stop being king.

In a sentence. For Scripture says, “He has put everything under his feet.” When it says everything has been put under him, clearly this does not include God himself, who put everything under Christ. When he has done this, the Son himself will be made subject to the one who put everything under him, so that God may be all in all.

On a Tuesday. History is heading toward one goal: God all in all. Let that goal shape your goals today.

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Otherwise, Paul asks, what are people doing when they are baptised on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why do it? And why do the apostles face danger every hour? Paul faces death every day; he swears it by his pride in them in Christ Jesus. If, humanly speaking, he fought wild beasts at Ephesus, what did he gain, if the dead are not raised? Then, as people say, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. They must not be misled: bad company corrupts good character. They should come back to their senses and stop sinning, because some of them have no knowledge of God; Paul says this to their shame.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Rational Grounds of Christian Ethics

Paul’s argument here anticipates the famous wager logic: if there is no resurrection, Christian ethics (self-denial, risk, suffering for others) is irrational. The person who lives as if the resurrection were true is either right (and has invested wisely) or wrong (and has lived a meaningful but ultimately futile life). The Epicurean is consistent: if there is no resurrection, maximise pleasure now. Paul’s whole life is a living argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes no sense on any other hypothesis.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s reference to “fighting with beasts at Ephesus” may be literal (arena animals) or metaphorical (violent opponents); either way it describes the real mortal danger of apostolic ministry. The question is: for what purpose? If the dead are not raised, the purpose has no transcendent ground. Now: Every Christian who chooses a harder path for the sake of the gospel — the missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who refuses to compromise his convictions, the layperson who sacrifices career advancement for integrity — is making an implicit resurrection bet. Their lives only make sense if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?

Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? Key words. One of the most puzzling verses in the Bible. The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; over forty interpretations have been suggested. Some think certain Corinthians were being baptised in place of believers who had died unbaptised. Others think it means being baptised because of the dead: new converts were baptised in order to be reunited with believing loved ones who had died, or in response to their testimony. Paul does not approve the practice; he simply uses it to show the inconsistency of those who deny the resurrection.

If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Key words. Whatever it was, it only made sense if there was a resurrection.

Why are we in danger every hour? Key words. Paul turns to his own life. Why would the apostles risk death constantly if there were no resurrection?

Where Christians differ: baptism for the dead. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, based on this verse. Verdict: Paul mentions the practice without endorsing it, and notice he says “people,” not “we.” Nowhere else does Scripture teach it. The New Testament is clear that each person must believe for themselves, and that after death comes judgement, with no second chance (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:26). Baptism is for those who personally repent and believe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an uncertain verse should be used to build a doctrine. Clear passages must interpret unclear ones.

In a sentence. Otherwise, what will those who are baptised for the dead do? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptised for them? And why do we put ourselves in danger every hour?

For worship. Thank God that salvation comes through personal faith in Christ, and that your loved ones who died in Christ will rise.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; most likely some Corinthians were being baptized as proxies for the dead. Paul mentions the practice without approving it, only to show that it assumes a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! Key words. A solemn oath. “I die every day”: Paul faced the threat of death daily, and daily gave up his life for Christ (2 Corinthians 4:10–11; 11:23–27).

What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? Key words. Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition, since a Roman citizen was unlikely to be thrown to animals, and Paul does not mention it in his list of sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Perhaps it refers to the riot of Acts 19, or to opponents who acted like wild animals.

If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Key words. From Isaiah 22:13, the words of people in Jerusalem who partied instead of repenting. If there is no resurrection, why not live for pleasure? This was the creed of the Epicureans and of many ordinary people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians live morally only for reward. It means the resurrection changes everything about how we live.

In a sentence. Paul faces death every day, brothers and sisters; he swears it by the pride he takes in you in Christ Jesus our Lord. If he fought wild beasts at Ephesus for merely human reasons, what has he gained? If the dead are not raised, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.

On a Tuesday. Because of the resurrection, you can give your life away. It is not wasted.
verseByVerse.note: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition; a Roman citizen could not normally be sent to the arena.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

Do not be deceived. Key words. Some in Corinth were being misled by those who denied the resurrection.

“Bad company ruins good morals.” Key words. “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander’s comedy Thais, which had become a proverb. Those who deny the resurrection influence others toward sinful living.

Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right. Key words. “Wake up” (eknēphō, sober up). Wrong beliefs about the future had made them spiritually drunk.

And do not go on sinning. Key words. Wrong doctrine leads to wrong living. Doctrine and ethics belong together.

For some have no knowledge of God. Key words. “No knowledge” (agnōsia, ignorance). Ironic for a church that prided itself on knowledge. To deny the resurrection is to be ignorant of God’s power (Matthew 22:29).

I say this to your shame. Key words. They should be ashamed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid all contact with unbelievers. It means they should not be influenced by false teaching and bad examples.

In a sentence. Do not be misled: bad company corrupts good character. Come back to your senses as you should, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God, and Paul says this to shame you.

For worship. Ask God to show you any influences in your life that are pulling you away from him.
verseByVerse.note: “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Someone will ask how the dead are raised and what kind of body they will have. Paul calls that a foolish question: a seed does not come to life unless it dies, and what is sown is not the plant that will grow but a bare grain, of wheat or something else. God gives it the body he has chosen, and each kind of seed its own body. Not all flesh is alike: people, animals, birds and fish differ. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies with different splendour, and even sun, moon and stars differ in glory. So it will be with the resurrection. The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in dishonour and raised in glory, sown in weakness and raised in power, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body. Scripture says the first man, Adam, became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. The natural came first, then the spiritual. The first man was made of earth’s dust; the second man is from heaven. Those of the earth are like the earthly man, and those of heaven are like the heavenly man. Just as believers have borne the image of the earthly man, they will bear the image of the heavenly one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The Reformed tradition has insisted, against all forms of Gnosticism and spiritual idealism, on the bodily nature of the resurrection. The creeds confess “the resurrection of the body” — not the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed analogy establishes both poles: continuity (the seed and the plant are the same organism in different stages) and transformation (the glory of the plant exceeds anything visible in the seed). The specific body that is buried — your body, with its particular history, its particular wounds, its particular scars — is the body that will be raised. This is why the bodily resurrection of Christ is the paradigm: the same body that was crucified was raised — still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), yet transformed into resurrection glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection to bodily resurrection was that the body is the problem, not the solution; the soul’s liberation from the body is the goal, not its resurrection. Paul refuses this framing entirely: the body is God’s creation, declared good, destined for resurrection. The problem is not embodiment but mortality, not physicality but corruption. The resurrection is the redemption of the body, not its abolition. Now: Every theology that treats the goal of salvation as the soul going to heaven (leaving the body behind) has the Corinthian problem. The goal is the new creation, the resurrection body, the renewed earth — the full embodied flourishing of redeemed humanity in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised?” Key words. The objection: resurrection is impossible. Bodies decay, are eaten by worms, scattered, burned. How can they be raised?

“With what kind of body do they come?” Key words. And what would such a body be like? The same decaying body? That sounded absurd to Greeks.

You foolish person! Key words. “Foolish” (aphrōn, without sense). The objection shows a failure to think, and to know God’s power.

What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. Key words. The analogy of a seed. A seed must be buried and decay before the plant grows (John 12:24). Death is not the end; it is the way to new life. Burial is sowing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean resurrection is a natural process. God does it (v. 38). The seed is an illustration.

In a sentence. But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? What sort of body will they have?” How foolish! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

On a Tuesday. When you bury a believer, you are sowing a seed. Grieve, but with hope of the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.

And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. Key words. A seed looks nothing like the plant. A bare kernel becomes a stalk of wheat. Continuity and transformation: the same life, a different form.

But God gives it a body as he has chosen. Key words. God is the one who gives the new body. Resurrection is his power at work.

And to each kind of seed its own body. Key words. Each seed becomes its own kind of plant: wheat becomes wheat. So each person will be raised as themselves, recognisably the same person, but transformed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection body has no connection to the present body. The seed becomes the plant; it is the same life. The body sown is the body raised.

In a sentence. When you sow, you do not plant the body that will grow, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. Then God gives it the body he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.

For worship. God will give you a resurrection body as he chooses. Trust his wisdom and power.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.

For not all flesh is the same. Key words. A second analogy. God has made many kinds of bodies.

But there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. Key words. Echoes Genesis 1. God the Creator is able to make bodies of every kind suited to every sphere.

There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. Key words. Heavenly bodies: sun, moon, stars. Earthly: plants and animals.

But the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. Key words. Each has its own splendour (doxa, glory, brightness).

There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. Key words. Even among the heavenly bodies, there is variety. If God can make all these, he can make a resurrection body with a glory beyond anything we know.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers will become stars, or that there will be ranks of glory among the saved based on merit, though some interpreters have taken it that way. Paul’s point is about God’s creative power.

In a sentence. Not all flesh is alike: people have one kind, animals another, birds another, fish another. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; the splendour of the heavenly is one kind, the splendour of the earthly another. The sun has one splendour, the moon another and the stars another, and star differs from star in splendour.

On a Tuesday. Look at the night sky. The God who made the stars will make your resurrection body.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

So is it with the resurrection of the dead. Key words. The application. Four contrasts (vv. 42–44) between the present body and the resurrection body.

What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. Key words. First: perishable (phthora, decay, corruption) to imperishable (aphtharsia). The present body ages, sickens and decays. The resurrection body will never decay or die.

It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. Key words. Second: dishonour to glory. A corpse is a humiliating thing. The raised body will shine with glory, like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21; Matthew 13:43).

It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. Key words. Third: weakness to power. The present body tires and fails; the dead body is utterly helpless. The resurrection body will be full of strength.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a different person is raised. “It” is sown and “it” is raised: the same body, transformed.

In a sentence. So it will be with the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown in decay and raised never to decay; sown in humiliation and raised in splendour; sown in weakness and raised in power.

For worship. Your weak, aging body will one day be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful. Thank God for that hope.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

It is sown a natural body. Key words. Fourth contrast. “Natural” (psychikos, soulish): a body animated by ordinary human life, suited to this age (2:14).

It is raised a spiritual body. Key words. A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit. “Spiritual” (pneumatikos) describes what governs and empowers it, not what it is made of. Paul uses the same word of spiritual people (2:15), who are not made of spirit.

If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. Key words. Just as there is a body suited to this age, there will be one suited to the age to come.

Where Christians differ: a physical resurrection? Some say the resurrection body is immaterial, a spirit body, and that Jesus’ resurrection was spiritual rather than physical. Verdict: Christ’s resurrection body was physical: he ate, was touched, had flesh and bones and the marks of his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27). The tomb was empty. Ours will be like his (Philippians 3:21). The spiritual body is physical, but transformed and wholly governed by the Holy Spirit (Westminster 32.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will be ghosts or disembodied spirits. That is the opposite of resurrection.

In a sentence. It is sown a body fit for this life; it is raised a body ruled by the Spirit. If there is a body for this life, there is also a body for the Spirit’s life.

For worship. Thank God that he will redeem your body, not discard it. Honour your body now as one God will raise.
verseByVerse.note: A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being.” Key words. From Genesis 2:7. God breathed into Adam, and he became a living soul (psychē zōsa), the word behind natural body.

The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Key words. Christ is the last Adam, the head of the new humanity (Romans 5:12–21). By his resurrection, he became the giver of life through the Spirit. Adam received life; Christ gives it (John 5:21; 6:63). “Spirit” here does not mean Christ is no longer bodily; it means he gives the Spirit’s life to his people.

But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. Key words. The order of history: first the natural (Adam and this age), then the spiritual (Christ and the age to come). Some Corinthians thought they already had the spiritual in full. Paul says it comes later, at the resurrection.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Adam was created evil. He was good, but natural, not yet glorified. Christ brings humanity to its intended goal.

In a sentence. So Scripture says, “The first man Adam became a living person”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. The spiritual did not come first, but the natural, and after that the spiritual.

On a Tuesday. You are now in Adam’s body but united to the last Adam. The best is still to come.

parallels.desc: the man became a living creature

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.

The first man was from the earth, a man of dust. Key words. Adam was made from the ground (Genesis 2:7; 3:19). Dust to dust.

The second man is from heaven. Key words. Christ came from heaven, and his risen body belongs to the heavenly realm.

As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust. Key words. All Adam’s descendants share his earthly, mortal nature.

And as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Key words. All who belong to Christ will share his heavenly, glorious nature.

Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. Key words. “Image” (eikōn). We were born in Adam’s likeness (Genesis 5:3). We will be raised in Christ’s likeness (Romans 8:29; 1 John 3:2). Some manuscripts read “let us bear,” making it an exhortation; the ESV note mentions this. The future “we shall” fits the context of the resurrection better.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become divine. We will be glorified humans, like Christ in his humanity.

In a sentence. The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man is from heaven. Those of the earth are like the earthly man, and those of heaven are like the heavenly man. And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so we will bear the likeness of the heavenly man.

For worship. One day you will look like Jesus. Let that hope purify you now (1 John 3:3).

parallels.desc: you are dust

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul declares that flesh and blood, our present mortal nature, cannot inherit God’s kingdom, nor can the perishable inherit the imperishable. He tells them a mystery: not all believers will die, but all will be changed, in a flash, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. The trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and the living will be changed. The perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. When that happens, the saying of Scripture will come true: death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is death’s victory, where is its sting? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power comes from the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. So, dear brothers and sisters, they must stand firm and immovable, always giving themselves fully to the Lord’s work, because they know their labour in the Lord is not wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The practical conclusion of the resurrection argument — “your labour is not in vain” (v. 58) — is the most comprehensive positive statement about Christian ethics in the letter. The resurrection does not merely give hope for the future; it validates the present. Every act of love, faithfulness, service, and endurance that has been poured out for Christ is stored up in a creation that will be renewed, not discarded. Herman Bavinck’s great theme was that grace restores nature: the resurrection does not annul creation but redeems and glorifies it.

Anthony Hoekema makes the same point in his study of biblical eschatology: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that the deaths of their beloved dead were not permanent losses, that their own present labour was not ultimately futile, and that the God who raised Christ had the power and the intention to complete what he had begun in them. The resurrection doctrine is not abstract comfort; it is the concrete ground of the community’s ability to bear all things, believe all things, hope all things, endure all things (ch. 13). Now: Every generation of the church faces the question that faces every human being: does my life mean anything beyond this brief span? Paul’s answer is the most radical possible: yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who inhabits your story, and he wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,

I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Key words. “Flesh and blood” is a Hebrew phrase for human nature in its present weak, mortal state (Matthew 16:17; Galatians 1:16). It does not mean physical bodies cannot enter the kingdom; it means bodies as they now are, mortal and corruptible, cannot. They must be changed.

Nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Key words. What decays cannot possess what is eternal. Transformation is necessary.

Behold! I tell you a mystery. Key words. A truth previously hidden, now revealed by God.

We shall not all sleep. Key words. Not every believer will die. Those alive at Christ’s return will not experience death. “We” means believers generally; Paul did not know whether he would be alive then.

But we shall all be changed. Key words. All believers, dead and living, will be transformed. “Changed” (allassō, transformed, exchanged).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection body is not flesh. Jesus’ risen body had flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). It means our bodies must be changed from mortality to immortality.

In a sentence. Paul declares to you, brothers and sisters, that flesh and blood as they are now cannot inherit God’s kingdom, nor can what decays inherit what never decays. Listen, he tells you a mystery: we will not all die, but we will all be changed,

On a Tuesday. Whether you die before Christ returns or are alive when he comes, you will be changed. Either way, the future is glory.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.

In a moment. Key words. “Moment” (atomos, from which atom: what cannot be divided). Instantly.

In the twinkling of an eye. Key words. As fast as a blink. The change will not be gradual.

At the last trumpet. Key words. A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people (Exodus 19:16; Joel 2:1; Zechariah 9:14). The last trumpet signals the end of history and the return of Christ (Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. Key words. First the dead are raised, then the living are changed (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). All together meet the Lord.

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists teach a secret rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers away before a seven-year tribulation, and then return again visibly later. Verdict: Paul says this happens at the last trumpet, which suggests the end, not a stage before further events. The New Testament describes one return of Christ, visible, public and glorious (Matthew 24:27, 30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7), at which the dead are raised, the living changed, and all are judged. There is no secret rapture. Believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, to welcome him as he comes, and then be with him forever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know when it will happen. The day is unknown (Matthew 24:36).

In a sentence. in a flash, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised never to decay, and we will be changed.

For worship. Listen for the last trumpet. Pray, Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”

For this perishable body must put on the imperishable. Key words. “This”: the body we have now. The same body will be clothed (endyō, put on, like clothing) with imperishability (2 Corinthians 5:2–4).

And this mortal body must put on immortality. Key words. “Immortality” (athanasia, deathlessness). Only God has immortality in himself (1 Timothy 6:16); he will give it to his people.

When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality. Key words. Paul repeats it for emphasis.

Then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.” Key words. From Isaiah 25:8: the LORD will swallow up death forever, and wipe away tears from all faces. “Swallowed up” (katapinō, gulped down, devoured). Death, which swallowed everyone, will itself be swallowed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean death is defeated by human progress. Only God can swallow it up.

In a sentence. For this body that decays must be clothed with what never decays, and this mortal body with immortality. When that happens, the saying in Scripture will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

On a Tuesday. At the next funeral you attend, remember: death will be swallowed up. It does not have the last word.

parallels.desc: he will swallow up death forever

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” Key words. From Hosea 13:14. A taunt song over defeated death. Death is like a scorpion or bee whose sting has been removed. It may still frighten, but it cannot destroy believers.

The sting of death is sin. Key words. What makes death deadly is sin. Death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). Sin brings death, and with it judgement. Christ removed the sting by bearing our sin.

And the power of sin is the law. Key words. The law gives sin its power, by exposing it, condemning it, and even provoking it (Romans 7:7–13). Without the law, sin is not counted (Romans 5:13). Christ fulfilled the law and bore its curse (Galatians 3:13). So sin has no power to condemn believers, and death has no sting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is sin. The law is holy (Romans 7:12). But it condemns sinners.

In a sentence. “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law.

For worship. Taunt death today with Paul’s words. Its sting has been drawn by Christ.

parallels.desc: O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

But thanks be to God. Key words. The only fitting response: thanksgiving (Romans 7:25).

Who gives us the victory. Key words. Present tense: God is giving us the victory now, over sin, death and the law. The victory is a gift, not an achievement.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Through his death, which removed sin’s sting, and his resurrection, which defeated death. His victory is ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never struggle with sin or face death. It means the outcome is certain.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

For worship. Thank God for the victory he has given you through Christ. Say it out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

Therefore, my beloved brothers. Key words. The practical conclusion of the whole chapter. After rebuking them throughout the letter, Paul calls them beloved.

Be steadfast. Key words. “Steadfast” (hedraios, firmly seated, settled). Do not be shaken in your faith in the resurrection.

Immovable. Key words. “Immovable” (ametakinētos, not to be moved). Not moved by false teaching or hardship.

Always abounding in the work of the Lord. Key words. “Abounding” (perisseuō, overflowing). Give yourself fully to the Lord’s work: serving, witnessing, loving.

Knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain. Key words. “Labour” (kopos, toil to exhaustion). “Not in vain” (ouk kenos, not empty), the same word as v. 14. Because Christ is risen, nothing done for him is wasted. Every act of faithful service will count in eternity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you will always see the results of your labour now. It means God sees and will reward it.

In a sentence. So then, dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing shift you. Always give yourselves fully to the Lord’s work, because you know that what you do for the Lord is never wasted.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection means your ordinary faithfulness today matters forever. Get on with the Lord’s work.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand,<sup>2</sup>and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.<sup>3</sup>For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>4</sup>that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>5</sup>and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.<sup>6</sup>Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep.<sup>7</sup>Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.<sup>8</sup>Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.<sup>9</sup>For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.<sup>10</sup>But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.<sup>11</sup>Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.<sup>12</sup>Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?<sup>13</sup>But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.<sup>14</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.<sup>15</sup>We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.<sup>16</sup>For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised.<sup>17</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.<sup>18</sup>Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.<sup>19</sup>If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.<sup>20</sup>But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.<sup>21</sup>For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead.<sup>22</sup>For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.<sup>23</sup>But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ.<sup>24</sup>Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.<sup>25</sup>For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.<sup>26</sup>The last enemy to be destroyed is death.<sup>27</sup>For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him.<sup>28</sup>When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.<sup>29</sup>Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?<sup>30</sup>Why are we in danger every hour?<sup>31</sup>I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!<sup>32</sup>What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”<sup>33</sup>Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”<sup>34</sup>Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.<sup>35</sup>But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”<sup>36</sup>You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.<sup>37</sup>And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.<sup>38</sup>But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.<sup>39</sup>For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish.<sup>40</sup>There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another.<sup>41</sup>There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.<sup>42</sup>So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable.<sup>43</sup>It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.<sup>44</sup>It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.<sup>45</sup>Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.<sup>46</sup>But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.<sup>47</sup>The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven.<sup>48</sup>As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven.<sup>49</sup>Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.<sup>50</sup>I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.<sup>51</sup>Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,<sup>52</sup>in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.<sup>53</sup>For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality.<sup>54</sup>When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”<sup>55</sup>“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”<sup>56</sup>The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.<sup>57</sup>But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>58</sup>Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
After the soaring end of chapter 15, the letter comes down to practical matters, which is itself a lesson: the hope of the resurrection makes ordinary faithfulness “not in vain”. First the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (described more fully in 2 Corinthians 8–9). Each believer should set aside money regularly on the first day of the week, in proportion to income, so that there is no last-minute scramble when Paul comes; the church will choose its own trusted messengers to carry it.

Then Paul’s travel plans. He is writing from Ephesus, where a great opportunity has opened amid much opposition, and he plans to stay until Pentecost before travelling through Macedonia to Corinth, perhaps for the winter, when sea travel stopped. Timothy may arrive first and must be made welcome, and Apollos will come later. Paul gives five brisk commands, watch, stand firm, be courageous, be strong, do everything in love, and commends the household of Stephanas and the three men who brought the Corinthians’ letter. He sends greetings from the churches of Asia, from Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house, writes the final words in his own hand, pronounces a curse on anyone who does not love the Lord, prays the earliest Christian prayer, “Maranatha”, “Our Lord, come!”, and ends with grace and his own love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About the collection for the Lord’s people, the Corinthians should do what Paul told the churches of Galatia. On the first day of every week each of them should set aside a sum in keeping with their income and save it up, so that no collections need to be made when Paul arrives. When he comes, he will send the people they approve, with letters of introduction, to take their gift to Jerusalem. If it seems right for Paul to go too, they will travel with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s collection theology, most fully developed in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds financial generosity in the grace of Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). The collection is not a tax but a participation in the logic of the cross — the voluntary sharing of material blessing across economic and ethnic lines that enacts the gospel’s claim that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The Gentile churches supporting the Jewish church in Jerusalem is the financial expression of Romans 15:27: “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was impoverished, possibly as a result of the famine of Acts 11:28 or the social cost of Jewish Christians being excluded from economic networks following their conversion. The collection was an act of solidarity across the most significant social divide of the ancient world. Now: The principle of systematic, proportionate, habitual giving as a spiritual discipline remains the most practically effective and most theologically grounded approach to Christian financial stewardship. The “first day of every week” rhythm connects giving to worship — it is part of how the community orients itself toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Giving to the needy should be planned, regular and proportionate, set aside each first day of the week.

The collection. For the poor believers in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–28), a sign of the unity of Jewish and Gentile churches.

The first day of the week. Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection, when the churches met: “On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread” (Acts 20:7). John calls it “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10).

Sabbath or Lord’s Day? Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians should keep Saturday as the Sabbath. Some Reformed Christians (the Westminster tradition) hold that the Sabbath command transfers to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, to be kept with rest and worship. Others say the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, “a shadow of the things to come” (Colossians 2:16–17). Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10); the Lord’s Day, Sunday, is the church’s day of gathering from the apostles’ time. Keeping it for worship and rest is a privilege and wisdom, not a law imposed on conscience.

Each of you. Every believer, rich and poor.

As he may prosper. Proportional giving: according to income. No fixed percentage (see on 2 Corinthians 8).

Regularly. Weekly, planned, not impulsive.

On a Tuesday. Set up a regular plan for giving: weekly or monthly, proportional to your income. Planned giving is usually more generous than impulse giving.
verseByVerse.note: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The first day of the week is Sunday, the day Christians met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The collection will be carried by approved representatives, with accountability.

Accountability. The church chooses its own representatives to carry the money. Paul does not handle it alone (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

Letters. Of recommendation, introducing them to the Jerusalem church.

Grace. The word translated “gift” is charis, grace.

On a Tuesday. Churches and charities: have more than one trusted person handle money, and be transparent about where it goes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul plans to come to them after passing through Macedonia. He may stay with them for a while, perhaps the winter, so that they can help him on his journey wherever he goes next; he does not want just a brief visit in passing, but hopes to spend some time with them, if the Lord permits. But he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a wide door for effective work has opened for him, and there are many opponents. If Timothy comes, they should make sure he has nothing to fear among them, for he is doing the Lord’s work as Paul is. No one should look down on him; they should send him on his way in peace so that he can return to Paul, who is expecting him with the brothers. As for Apollos, Paul strongly urged him to visit them with the brothers, but he was quite unwilling to go now; he will come when he has the opportunity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are not merely logistical; they reflect the theology of the one body of Christ extended across geography. The early church was not a collection of independent local congregations operating in isolation; it was a network of communities bound together by the gospel, by apostolic ministry, by financial sharing, and by personal relationship. Paul’s letters are themselves the literary expression of this network — the apostle’s presence extended across distance through writing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ease with which Paul mentions Timothy and Apollos as co-workers, and the genuine care he shows for Timothy’s reception, models the pastoral culture of the early church: mutual submission, personal warmth, collaborative ministry. Now: The temptation to treat Christian ministry as competitive rather than collaborative is ancient and persistent. Paul’s warmth toward Apollos — the man whose followers had been used as a weapon against him — is a lesson in the largeness of a gospel-formed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul plans to visit after Macedonia, if the Lord permits.

The plan. Overland from Ephesus north to Troas, across to Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica), then south to Corinth. These plans later changed, which caused the accusations of 2 Corinthians 1:15–17.

The winter. Sea travel in the Mediterranean largely stopped from about November to March. Travellers wintered where they were (Acts 27:9–12; 28:11).

If the Lord permits. Paul’s plans are always subject to God’s will (James 4:13–15).

On a Tuesday. Make plans, but hold them loosely. Say, and mean, “if the Lord wills”.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stays in Ephesus, where a great door is open and there are many adversaries.

Ephesus. The great city of the province of Asia, where Paul stayed nearly three years (Acts 19–20), so that “all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord” (Acts 19:10).

Pentecost. The Jewish Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, in early summer. A sign that Paul, though free from the law, still marked time by the Jewish calendar.

Door and adversaries. Opportunity and opposition often come together. The riot of the silversmiths (Acts 19:23–41) shows how much opposition there was.

On a Tuesday. Opposition is not a sign that God has closed a door. Sometimes it shows the door is wide open.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must be welcomed and supported.

Timothy. Young, perhaps timid (1 Timothy 4:12, “Let no one despise you for your youth”; 2 Timothy 1:7). Sent to remind them of Paul’s ways (4:17).

Without fear. A proud church might bully a young man.

As I am. Timothy carries Paul’s authority.

On a Tuesday. Encourage the young or new leaders in your church. Do not despise them for inexperience.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos will come when he can; Paul respects his freedom.

Now concerning. Perhaps the Corinthians had asked for Apollos. Some preferred him (1:12).

Paul urged him. No rivalry between Paul and Apollos. Paul wanted him to go.

Not his will. Perhaps Apollos did not want to feed the faction around him. Paul respected his decision: apostles did not order colleagues around.

On a Tuesday. Christian workers can disagree about plans and still respect each other.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives five short commands: stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong, and do everything in love. He reminds them that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia and have devoted themselves to serving God’s people, and urges them to submit to such people and to everyone who joins in the work and labours at it. He is glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from the Corinthians; they have refreshed his spirit and theirs. Such people deserve recognition.
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love: The Paradox of Gospel Character

The sequence of imperatives in vv. 13–14 — watchful, firm, courageous, strong, then loving — captures the full paradox of the Christian character that Paul has been cultivating throughout the letter. The cross demands both: the courage to stand for truth (as Paul has done in every hard section of this letter) and the love that is patient, kind, and bears all things (as chapter 13 demands). Neither without the other is Christian; together they describe the character of Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept on the way to Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed all five imperatives in exactly the order Paul gave them. They needed watchfulness against the false teachings threatening them; firmness against the cultural pressure to conform; courage to exercise church discipline; strength to endure the costs of faithful community. And they needed all of this wrapped in love, or it would produce the cold and harsh community that pride produces rather than the warm and strong community that grace produces. Now: Every generation of the church needs the same five imperatives in the same order. The church that is watchful and firm but unloving is a fortress, not a family. The church that is loving but not watchful and firm is a sentimentality, not a community.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be watchful, stand firm, be courageous and strong, and do everything in love.

Five commands. Military language, like a commander’s final orders.

Watchful: alert for Christ’s return and against error.

Stand firm: hold your ground in the faith (15:1, 58).

Act like men: andrizesthe, be brave, show courage. Addressed to the whole church, women included. “Be strong and courageous” (Joshua 1:9).

Be strong: in the Lord’s strength (Ephesians 6:10).

In love: the final command, summing up the letter. Courage without love becomes harshness; love without courage becomes weakness.

On a Tuesday. Write these five commands on a card for your desk or fridge this week.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should submit to devoted servants like the household of Stephanas.

Stephanas. His household was among the first converts in the province, baptised by Paul himself (1:16). The “firstfruits” of Achaia.

Devoted themselves. Literally “appointed themselves” to service. They took initiative.

Be subject. Respect and follow those who serve. Leadership in the church is earned by service, not status.

On a Tuesday. Who are the faithful, long-serving people in your church? Thank them and support them.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful visitors refreshed Paul’s spirit, and deserve recognition.

Three men. Probably the delegation that brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul (7:1). Fortunatus (“lucky”) and Achaicus (“the man from Achaia”) were common names for slaves or freedmen. A wealthy householder and two men of humble status travelled together as brothers.

Made up for your absence. They brought the church’s fellowship to Paul in person.

Refreshed. Good company is a gift (Philemon 7).

On a Tuesday. Who refreshes your spirit? Who could you refresh this week with a visit?
verseByVerse.note: These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The churches of the province of Asia send greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church that meets in their house, send warm greetings in the Lord, and so do all the believers there. They should greet one another with a holy kiss. Paul writes this greeting in his own hand. If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under God’s curse. Our Lord, come! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with them, and Paul’s love be with them all in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Eschatological Pulse of the Church

“Maranatha” is either maran atha (“Our Lord has come,” a declaration of the incarnation) or marana tha (“Our Lord, come!” a prayer for the Parousia). The context — following the anathema, preceding the benediction, echoing Revelation 22:20’s “Come, Lord Jesus” — strongly favours the prayer. The church that lives with the cross at its centre (ch. 1–2), that loves without condition (ch. 13), that proclaims the resurrection (ch. 15), lives with this prayer on its lips: come. The present is not all there is; the best is yet to come; the One who died and rose is coming again. Maranatha is the heartbeat of the community that has understood what Paul has been saying all letter long.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church’s Aramaic prayer preserved in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small but moving piece of evidence for the unity of the early church across language and culture. Jewish and Gentile believers shared the same prayer in the same words. Now: The prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” is a prayer Christians in every tradition and century have prayed. It is the prayer that the Revelation ends with; it is the prayer that this letter ends with. To pray it is to join the whole church across time — to live, with Paul, as one on whom the end of the ages has come, watching and waiting for the One whose coming makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches send greetings, and believers should greet one another with a holy kiss.

Asia. The churches around Ephesus: Colossae, Laodicea, Hierapolis and others (Revelation 2–3).

Aquila and Prisca. A Jewish couple, tentmakers like Paul, expelled from Rome under Claudius, who worked with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:1–3) and moved to Ephesus. They taught Apollos: “they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). The Corinthians knew them well.

The church in their house. Churches met in homes for the first three centuries. A husband and wife opened theirs.

A holy kiss. See 2 Corinthians 13:12.

A textual note. Some manuscripts use the fuller form “Priscilla”; the earliest have “Prisca”. They are the same name.

On a Tuesday. Is your home open for Christian fellowship? A meal, a Bible study, a place for new believers.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul signs the letter with his own hand.

His own hand. Paul dictated his letters to a secretary (Romans 16:22) and added the final greeting himself as proof of authenticity (2 Thessalonians 3:17; Galatians 6:11).

On a Tuesday. A handwritten note still means more than a typed one. Write one this week.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who does not love the Lord is under a curse; come, Lord.

Accursed. Anathema: under God’s judgement (Galatians 1:8). A sobering line: loving Christ is not optional.

Love the Lord. The verb is phileō, warm personal affection. Not merely doctrine or behaviour, but love for Jesus.

Maranatha. An Aramaic phrase left untranslated, from the earliest Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem. It can be divided two ways: marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (a prayer), or maran atha, “Our Lord has come” (a confession). Verdict: most likely the prayer, as in Revelation 22:20, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” An early Christian manual, the Didache, uses it in prayers at the Lord’s Supper.

The earliest worship of Jesus. Aramaic-speaking Jewish Christians, strict monotheists, prayed to Jesus as “Lord”. This is evidence that Jesus was worshipped as divine from the very beginning, not as a later Greek development.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “Jesus Christ” after “the Lord”. The earliest have simply “the Lord”.

For worship. Pray “Maranatha” today, the prayer of the first Christians.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Our Lord, come!” translates Maranatha, an Aramaic prayer of the earliest church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul ends with grace and his love for them all in Christ.

Grace. The letter that began with grace (1:3–4) ends with it.

My love. Unique among Paul’s endings. After a letter of rebuke, he sends his love to all of them, the factions, the proud, the confused. Not to some, to all.

A textual note. Some manuscripts omit the final “Amen”; it may have been added from liturgical use.

For worship. Thank God for a church that, for all its faults, is loved by Christ and by his apostle. Then love your own church that way.

I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.<sup>8</sup>But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,<sup>9</sup>for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.<sup>10</sup>When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am.<sup>11</sup>So let no one despise him.
